You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Later Vedic Society – Varnas, Ashramas, Gotra, Status of Women

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Four Varnas and Caste
Varna | Role
Brahmana | Priests, teachers; most powerful
Kshatriya (Rajanya) | Rulers, warriors
Vaishya | Farmers, traders, artisans; tribute-payers
Shudra | Service; no upanayana, no Vedas
First reference to four varnas: Purusha Sukta, Rigveda 10th Mandala.
Dvija (twice-born) = upper three, entitled to upanayana.
Varna became birth-based and rigid in the Later Vedic period; spread of jatis is post-Vedic (Gupta era).
Aitareya Brahmana: Shudra = "servant of another", could be driven out or beaten anytime.
Outside the varna order: Vratyas, Nishadas.
## Untouchability, Guilds, Money-lending
Chandala = despised birth in the Chhandogya Upanishad; formal untouchability = post-Vedic Dharmasutras / Dharmashastra phase (early Christian era).
First reference to money-lending (usurer, kusidin): Shatapatha Brahmana; ⚠ APPSC key (2010) gave Atharvaveda.
Vaishya guilds (gana) headed by a shreshthin; Sarthavaha (Srenipramukh) = head of trade guilds; rules = Samay, Srenidharma.
AP: Gautamiputra Satakarni protected varnashrama dharma; anuloma offspring = Ugra, pratiloma = Chandala.
# Ashramas and Purusharthas
Ashrama | Duty
Brahmacharya | Vedic study
Grihastha | Household; daily Pancha Mahayajnas
Vanaprastha | Gradual withdrawal
Sannyasa | Complete detachment; added last
First three in Chhandogya Upanishad; all four first in Jabala Upanishad. Varna + ashrama = Varnashrama Dharma.
Pancha Mahayajnas: Brahma, Deva, Pitra, Bhuta, Atithi (Nri/Manushya); Bhuta = living beings; Nri = hospitality.
Purusharthas: Dharma (duty), Artha (wealth), Kama (desire) = trivarga (Later Vedic-Sutra phase); Moksha (liberation) added later (Upanishadic).
# Gotra and Kinship
Gotra = literally cow-pen (Rigveda); lineage sense first in Atharvaveda; as descent from one male ancestor, set up in Later Vedic times.
Gotra exogamy: no marriage within the same gotra, with caste endogamy and sapinda rules.
Kula = family; Vamsha = lineage; Kosa = treasury (odd one out).
Irawati Karve: *Kinship Organization in India* (1953); four kinship zones.
# Samskaras and Education
Samskaras: 16 (shodasha). Upanayana = sacred thread, boy's 8th year; full description in Shatapatha Brahmana; Shudras and women excluded.
Varna | Upanayana metre
Brahmana | Gayatri
Kshatriya | Trishtubh
Vaishya | Jagati
Gurukula: pupil lived with the guru; education mostly for Dvija.
Term | Meaning
Acharya | Initiated the pupil; taught whole Veda free
Upadhyaya | Taught Veda/Vedangas for a livelihood
Adhvaryu | Performed sacrificial acts
Hotri / Udgatri | Recited Rigveda / chanted Samaveda
Purohita | Chief priest
# Marriage
Form | Nature
Brahma | Daughter given to a Veda-learned man of good conduct
Daiva | Given to the officiating priest
Arsha | Groom gives a token cow and bull
Prajapatya | No dowry; couple jointly perform dharma
Asura | Purchase of bride
Gandharva | Mutual consent
Rakshasa | Capture
Paishacha | Seducing a sleeping/drunk girl; lowest
First four approved; 8 forms in Manu and Kautilya.
Anuloma = higher-varna man, lower-varna woman; Pratiloma = reverse (disapproved).
# Status of Women
Declined: lost upanayana, limited education, barred from Sabha and public rites; child marriage and sati appear.
Text | Statement
Aitareya Brahmana | Daughter = source of misery; son = protector
Shatapatha Brahmana | Wife is half her husband
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad | Gargi debated Yajnavalkya
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
Samskaras | 16
Marriage forms | 8
Pancha Mahayajnas | 5
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First four varnas: Purusha Sukta; last ashrama added: Sannyasa.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
APPSC Group 1, 2012 | Marriage by bride purchase = Asura
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Asura = purchase; Rakshasa = capture.
2. Kshatriya upanayana = Trishtubh.
3. Pancha Mahayajnas = Grihastha.
4. 3 ashramas Chhandogya, 4 Jabala.
5. Kosa is not a kinship term.
6. Upadhyaya paid; Acharya free.
7. Aitareya = daughter misery; Shatapatha = wife half.
8. Moksha added last to purusharthas.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Varnas → role; groups outside the varna order — The fourfold order
## 1. The fourfold order
Origin: Purusha Sukta (Rigveda, 10th mandala) = first statement of the four-fold order
"varna" and "shudra" words also occur in the Rigveda
Varna | Role in later Vedic texts
Brahmana | Priests and teachers; seeker of livelihood; initially one of 16 classes of priests, became the dominant priestly class; APP notes call them the most powerful class
Kshatriya/Rajanya | Rulers, warriors; political power and protection
Vaishya | Farmers, traders, cattle-rearers, some artisans; the tribute payers (tribute-payers)
Shudra | Service to upper three; no Upanayana, no right to study the Vedas
Dvija: Upper three = dvija / Dvija (twice-born, via upanayana)
Aitareya Brahmana: Shudra = "servant of another", could be expelled and beaten/slain/struck at will; Vaishya = tribute payer
# Varnas → role; groups outside the varna order — Rigidity and emergence of caste
## 1. Rigidity and emergence of caste
Later Vedic shift: Birth-based occupation + rigid hierarchy set in during the later Vedic period; social mobility fell
Jatis: Proliferation (sub-castes, mixed castes) is post-Vedic
Gupta-era diversification; post-Satavahana mixed castes in Andhra
Exam angle: "caste as a new form of social organisation" questions test that varna rigidified after the Rig Vedic phase.
## 2. Occupational groups, guilds and FIRSTs
Specialisation: Iron-age economy → specialised crafts
Money-lending: Satapatha Brahmana = first reference to money-lending
Guilds: Guild-like bodies of Vaishyas (gana, headed by a shreshthin) in later Vedic texts
## 3. Outside the varna order
Outside the varna order: Vratyas, Nishadas / Vratyas and Nishadas
Rathakaras kept sacred-thread privilege
Discrimination: Against Shudras and Chandalas in later Vedic society
Chandala: Named as a despised birth in the Chhandogya Upanishad
Formal rule: Untouchability as a formal rule = post-Vedic Dharmasutras
# Gotra and kinship terms → meaning
## 1. Gotra
Meaning: Literally "cow-pen" → lineage from a common male ancestor
Word:
First occurs in the Rig Veda (UPPSC key)
Atharvaveda / Atharva Veda uses it in the lineage sense
Institution: Established in Later Vedic times
Rule: gotra exogamy = no marriage within the same gotra
+ caste endogamy + sapinda prohibition ("sasan" rule) → North Indian pattern
## 2. Kinship terms
Kula | Family/household
Vamsa / vamsha | Lineage/dynasty
Gotra | Exogamous clan
Kosa | Treasury
⚠ Trap: Kosa (treasury) is the odd one out (UPSC 1996)
## 3. Scholar → work
Scholar | Work
Irawati Karve | Kinship Organization in India (1953); analysed sapinda + gotra rules; divided India into four kinship zones
# Ashramas and purusharthas — stages, duties and goals
## 1. Four ashramas
Ashrama | Stage | Key duty
Brahmacharya | Student | Vedic study under a guru
Grihastha | Householder | Marriage, family, economic duties; performs the Pancha Mahayajnas
Vanaprastha | Forest-dweller | Gradual withdrawal
Sannyasa | Renunciate | Complete detachment; added later (added last)
Prevalence: Only the first three prevalent in Later Vedic times; Sannyasa not well established
Earliest references:
First three = Chhandogya Upanishad
All four = Jabala Upanishad (fully listed in post-Vedic texts)
Varna + ashrama = Varnashrama dharma
Women: Followed the ashrama chosen by their husbands
⚠ 3 – 4 ashramas = Chhandogya – Jabala
## 2. Pancha Mahayajnas (daily duties of the Grihastha)
Yajna | Meaning
Brahma yajna | Vedic study
Deva yajna | Offerings to gods
Pitri yajna | Ancestors
Bhuta yajna | All/living beings
Nri/Manushya yajna | Hospitality to guests
Exam angle: "Pancha Mahayajna performed in which ashrama?" - Grihastha (MPPSC 2025).
## 3. Purusharthas — four goals of life
Goal | Meaning
Dharma | Duty
Artha | Wealth
Kama | Desire
Moksha | Liberation
Trivarga: First three; older, took shape in the later Vedic-Sutra phase
Moksha: Added as the fourth with Upanishadic ideas of karma, samsara and liberation
Core Vedic-Upanishadic concepts (legacy list): dharma, karma, moksha
# Samskaras and upanayana → purpose
## 1. Samskaras
Total: 16 (shodasha samskaras) (MPPSC 2015)
From Garbhadhana (conception) → Antyeshti (funeral)
Key ones: Upanayana + Vivaha
Samskara | Purpose
Garbhadhana | Conception
Pumsavana | To procure a male child
Simantonnayana | Safety of the child in the womb
Jatakarma | At birth, before cutting the cord
Chudakarma | Tonsure, in the 3rd year
Upanayana | Sacred thread - entry (initiation) into Vedic study; makes one dvija; boy's 8th year
Vivaha | Marriage
Antyeshti | Funeral
## 2. Upanayana
Access: Upanayana only for the upper three varnas; Shudras and women excluded
Source: Elaborate description in the Shatapatha Brahmana / Satapatha Brahmana
Varna | Upanayana metre/mantra
Metre-varna pairing: Per the MPPSC 2024 key and standard Grihya texts
⚠ Gayatri – Trishtubh – Jagati = Brahmana – Kshatriya – Vaishya
Exam angle: "mantra in the Kshatriya upanayana" = Trishtubh (MPPSC 2024).
# Marriage — eight forms and types
## 1. Eight forms of marriage (Manu)
Form | Nature | Approved?
Brahma | Father gives daughter, with gifts, to a learned man of good conduct | Approved
Daiva | Daughter given to the officiating priest in lieu of sacrificial fee | Approved
Arsha | Groom gives a token cow and bull to the bride's father | Approved
Prajapatya | Given without dowry or demand, with the blessing; couple told to jointly perform dharma together | Approved
Asura | Purchase of the bride - groom pays a bride price (price paid to her kin) | Disapproved
Gandharva | Love marriage by mutual consent | Disapproved
Rakshasa | Marriage by capture/abduction | Disapproved
Paishacha | Seduction of a sleeping, intoxicated or incapacitated girl; lowest form | Disapproved
Classification: Standard Dharmashastra
Count: 8 forms in both Manu and Kautilya
⚠ Asura = purchase; Rakshasa = capture; Paishacha = lowest; Arsha = cow and bull
Exam angle: "marriage by purchase of bride" = Asura (APPSC-G1 2012); capture = Rakshasa.
## 2. Types of marriage → meaning
Type | Meaning
Anuloma | Higher-varna man + lower-varna woman (tolerated)
Monogamy | Serial or non-serial
Polyandry | Fraternal among the Khas (Uttarakhand), Ladakh and Toda
Polygyny | Sororal or non-sororal; permitted for Muslims
Group marriage | Several men with several women
# Teachers and priests → terms
## 1. Gurukula
Access: Education confined largely to the Dvija
Gurukula: Pupils lived with the guru
## 2. Teachers and priests
Term | Distinction
Acharya | Teacher who initiated the pupil (upanayana) and taught the whole Veda, not for a fee [GK]
Upadhyaya | Taught Veda or Vedangas for a livelihood (paid teacher) (UKPSC 2007 key)
Adhvaryu | Yajurveda priest who performs the sacrificial acts
Hotri / Udgatri | Rigveda reciter / Samaveda chanter [GK]
Purohita | Family/royal priest, adviser of the king (a ratnin)
⚠ Acharya = not for a fee; Upadhyaya = paid
# Women — texts → statements on status
## 1. Decline in status
Status: declined
Lost Upanayana; restricted education
Excluded from religious rites/rituals
Lost attendance at assemblies (Sabha): in Rig Vedic times women attended Sabha; Atharva Veda mentions women in the Samiti
Family: Joint family; rising paternal authority (father could disinherit a son)
Social evils: References to sati and child marriage appear
## 2. Texts → statements
Maitrayani Samhita | Three evils = liquor, dice, women
Satapatha/Shatapatha Brahmana | "wife is half her husband and completes him"
## 3. Exceptions — women philosophers
Women philosophers: Some women received higher learning
Gargi debated Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
Maitreyi (Yajnavalkya's wife)
⚠ Aitareya = daughter a misery; Shatapatha = wife is half her husband
# Universal angles
Significance:
Varna + ashrama = Varna-ashrama-dharma, normative frame of later Hindu society
Later Vedic society fixed varna, gotra, samskaras and ashramas → base of later Dharmashastra society + target of Buddhist/Jain protest
Comparative note:
Rig Vedic = relatively fluid, egalitarian; flexible varna; women in assemblies
Later Vedic = birth-based varna, gotra exogamy, women excluded
Harappan = differentiation but no textual caste
AP angle:
Gautamiputra Satakarni opposed varna-sankara and protected varnashrama dharma
Post-Satavahana (Ikshvaku) society: mixed castes and sub-castes
Satavahana Andhra: anuloma offspring = Ugra; pratiloma offspring = Chandala

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Decline of the Mauryan Empire – Competing Explanations

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Theories of Decline → Historian
Theory | Historian | Core argument
Brahmanical reaction | H.P. Shastri | Pro-Buddhist policy and ban on sacrifices angered Brahmins; Sunga coup = Brahmin revolt
Ashoka's pacifism | H.C. Raychaudhuri | Non-violence after Kalinga dulled the army's spirit
Financial crisis | D.D. Kosambi | Army, bureaucracy and Dhamma spending emptied the treasury
Over-centralisation, no national consciousness | Romila Thapar | Rule depended on the king; weak successors → collapse
Oppressive provincial rule | Divyavadana evidence | Revolts at Taxila against wicked officials (Bindusara's and Ashoka's reigns)
No single theory is accepted; historians stress structural weakness and weak successors over religious reaction.
## Evidence for the Financial Crisis
Heavy spending on Dhamma missions and gifts to the Sangha.
Debasement of later punch-marked silver coins (more alloy).
## Against the Brahmanical-Reaction Theory
Pushyamitra was himself a Mauryan general; Sanchi and Bharhut grew under Sunga rule.
Shastri = Brahmanical; Raychaudhuri = pacifism; Kosambi = finance; Thapar = centralisation.
Heavy taxation: Kosambi also points to very heavy taxes, raised even on actors and prostitutes, as a sign of the money crisis of the later Mauryas.
# Later Mauryas and Division of the Empire
Usual list: Kunala, Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha.
Part | Rulers
Western (north-west) | Kunala, later Samprati; replaced by Indo-Greeks by c. 180 BC
Eastern (Pataliputra) | Dasharatha … Brihadratha (last)
Samprati: Ashoka's grandson, Jain patron, ruled c. 230–215 BCE.
# Foreign Threats and Breakaway Regions
Threat / region | Power
North-west | Bactrian (Indo-Greek) Demetrius, later Menander
Hindu Kush, c. 206 BC | Antiochus III (Seleucid); tribute from Subhagasena
Great Wall of China (c. 220 BC) | Turned Scythian tribes west and south towards India
Andhra / Deccan | Satavahanas, earlier Mauryan feudatories
Vidarbha | Yajnasena (Malavikagnimitram)
Neglect of the north-west frontier; Indo-Greek raids drained resources.
Menander = Milinda; capital Sagala (Sialkot); dialogue with monk Nagasena in the Milindapanha.
Indo-Greek pressure was a cause; a permanent alliance with them was NOT.
# End of the Dynasty and the Sungas
Brihadratha, 7th king after Ashoka, killed by his senani Pushyamitra Sunga at a military review – a military coup (APPSC 2023).
Sunga dynasty founded in Magadha in 187 BC; Sungas = immediate successors of the Mauryas (APPSC G2 2003).
Pushyamitra: Brahmana, Bharadvaja gotra; held the Ganga heartland against Demetrius and Menander.
Rituals: two Ashvamedhas – Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva.
Buddhism debate: Divyavadana calls him a persecutor; yet Sanchi and Bharhut grew.
Core: Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha, Narmada valley.
Malavikagnimitram (Kalidasa): love story of the son of Pushyamitra; grandson Vasumitra defeated a Yavana army on the Sindhu.
# Kanvas
Founder Vasudeva Kanva, Brahmana minister, killed the last Sunga Devabhuti.
Four kings (c. 73–28 BC): Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susharman.
Susharman, last Kanva, overthrown by the Satavahanas (Andhras), not Menander.
Order in Magadha: Mauryas → Sungas → Kanvas → Satavahana conquest.
# Kharavela and the Satavahanas
Hathigumpha inscription (2nd c. BC): year-by-year record of Kharavela; at Udayagiri (not Khandagiri), near Bhubaneswar.
Udayagiri 18 caves, Khandagiri 15; natural and artificial.
Kharavela: Jaina, Chedi (Mahameghavahana) line; raided Magadha and recovered the Jina image taken by the Nandas; sent an army west ignoring Satakarni.
Satavahanas: founder Simuka (Srimukha); Puranas call them Andhra-bhrityas; first to unite the Krishna-Godavari region.
Rudradaman – Nanaghat = wrong pair; Nanaghat = Naganika.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
Brihadratha | 7th king after Ashoka
Sunga founding | 187 BC
Antiochus III | c. 206 BC
Kanva kings | 4 (c. 73–28 BC)
Pushyamitra's Ashvamedhas | 2
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
Last Mauryan: Brihadratha; last Sunga: Devabhuti; last Kanva: Susharman.
End of the first pan-Indian empire → regional kingdoms and Brahmanical revival.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2, 2003 | Immediate successors of the Mauryas – Sungas
APPSC 2023 | Brihadratha killed at army review
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Sungas, not Kanvas, directly followed the Mauryas.
2. Pushyamitra was a senani, not a minister; Vasudeva Kanva was the minister.
3. Kosambi = financial crisis, not Brahmanical reaction.
4. Hathigumpha is at Udayagiri.
5. Nanaghat belongs to Naganika.
6. Susharman fell to the Satavahanas.
7. Antiochus III took tribute from Subhagasena.
8. Vasumitra, grandson of Pushyamitra, beat the Yavanas on the Sindhu.

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Arab Conquest of Sindh; Ghaznavid and Ghurid Invasions; Battles of Tarain

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Invasions in Order
Year | Event
712 CE | Muhammad bin Qasim defeats Raja Dahir; Sindh taken
1000-1027 | Mahmud of Ghazni: 17 raids
1025-26 | Somnath sacked (Solanki Bhima I)
1175 | Ghori's first attack: Multan (Multan and Uch 1175-76)
1178 | Ghori's first defeat: Gujarat, near Mount Abu
1191 | First Tarain: Prithviraj won
1192 | Second Tarain: Ghori won
1194 | Chandawar: Ghori beats Jaichand
1206 | Qutbuddin Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate
Chronology: Mahmud Ghaznavi (1000-1027) → Muhammad Ghori (1175-1205) → Genghis Khan → Taimur.
Mahmud raided for plunder; Ghori conquered and stayed.
# Arab Conquest of Sindh (712 Ce)
## Commander and Ruler Defeated
First Muslim invaders of India: the Arabs, under Muhammad bin Qasim, Sindh, 712.
Qasim: nephew and son-in-law of Al-Hajjaj (Hajjaj bin Yusuf), the Umayyad governor; sent by Caliph al-Walid at the age of 17.
Removed Raja Dahir, capital Alor (Aror/Arod), near modern Karachi.
Places taken: Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad, Multan (not Somnath).
Dahir's capital was Alor (Aror); Brahmanabad was only one of the places taken.
## Chachnama
Arabic chronicle of the conquest of Sindh (680-718); original author unclear.
Persian translation by Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi (BPSC 2024).
## Causes and Effects
Factor | Fact
Causes | Arab maritime interests, expansion, piracy against Arab ships
Religion | No mass Islamisation; Hindus and Buddhists given dhimmi status
Limited reach | Confined to Sindh by the Thar and Aravallis, strong Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Palas, weak resources
Knowledge transfer | Indian decimal and place-value maths, astronomy, medicine → Islamic world → Europe
Nagabhata I (Pratihara) drove back the Arabs, keeping them in Sindh; Arab writers said Pratiharas had the strongest cavalry in India.
# Ghaznavids and Mahmud of Ghazni
## Founders
Person | Role
Alptigin | Founder of the Ghaznavid line; Turkish slave of the Samanid governors
Sabuktigin | Real founder
Mahmud (998-1030) | The raider; 17 raids
Alptigin = founder; Sabuktigin = real founder; Mahmud = the raider.
## Raids → Target
Target | Year | Note
Nagarkot (Kangra) | 1009 | Temple treasure
Thanesar (Chakraswamin temple) | 1014 | 
Mathura | 1018 | 
Kanauj | 1018 | Pratihara king submitted
Somnath (Gujarat) | 1025-26 | Solanki Bhima I; loot said to be 20 million dinars
Raids were repeated, not systematic conquest; he did not aim at a permanent empire.
Issued silver coins with Arabic and Sanskrit legends; built the Ghazni minarets.
After Mahmud, the Ghaznavids weakened under Seljuk pressure.
## Indian Rulers Who Resisted
Jayapala and Anandapala (Hindu Shahis): first to resist Mahmud.
Chandela Vidyadhara: faced and repulsed Mahmud (1019-20), not defeated (MPPSC 2021). Chandelas ruled Central India, 9th-13th c.; first capital Khajuraho.
Bhimadeva I ruled during the Somnath attack and reconstructed the temple.
## Motives and Effects
Motives: more than religion; temple wealth to fund the state, political expansion.
Effect: exposed India's military weakness and opened the north-west frontier.
Somnath Swabhiman Parv (launched January 2026): 1,000 years since Mahmud's attack.
# Scholars in Mahmud's Court
Scholar | Work / Role
Firdausi ("Homer of the East") | Shahnama
Al-Biruni | Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind); Kitab Patanjal
Utbi | Court historian; Kitab-ul-Yamini (Tarikh-i-Yamini)
Baihaqi | Tarikh-i-Subuktigin
Unsuri | Poet laureate (Malik-ush-Shuara)
Uzari | Persian court poet
## Al-Biruni
Born 973 in Khwarizm (Khiva); came with Mahmud; "father of Indian historical writing".
Kitab-ul-Hind: fair account of 11th-century Indian society, religion, science, customs. Translated into English by Edward Sachau, Hindi by Rajnikant Sharma.
Kitab Patanjal: Arabic translation of Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra.
Not a secular author: no kind word about the Somnath raid.
# Muhammad Ghori and the Battles of Tarain
## Route and Conquests
Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori (Ghurid, 1173-1206) entered through the Gomal Pass; aimed at permanent occupation.
Multan (1175) → Peshawar (c. 1179) → Sindh (c. 1182) → Punjab and Lahore (c. 1190).
## Battles → Opponent + Victor
Battle | Year | Opponent | Victor
Gujarat (Kasahrada/Kayadara, near Mount Abu) | 1178 | Mularaja II (Bhimdev II), Chaulukya/Solanki; regent mother Naika Devi | Gujarat; Ghori's first defeat
First Tarain (near Karnal, Haryana) | 1191 | Prithviraj Chauhan (Prithviraja III, Chahamana of Ajmer) | Prithviraj; Ghori barely escaped
Second Tarain | 1192 | Prithviraj Chauhan | Ghori; turning point, opened North India
Chandawar (Firozabad, UP, on the Yamuna near Agra) | 1194 | Jayachandra (Jaichand), Gahadavala of Kannauj | Ghori
Cause of Tarain I: Tabarhinda (Bhatinda); Prithviraj took it but left no strong garrison.
Aibak (Ghori's slave, Master of Stables) got the first Iqta in India (1192); capital Lahore; first Sultan of Delhi on Ghori's death (1206). Delhi Sultanate 1206-1526: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.
Somnath = Bhima I (Mahmud); Ghori beaten by Mularaja II (1178).
# Bakhtiyar Khalji
Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji: Ghori's slave/general; real founder of Turk rule in Bihar (BPSC 2022).
Conquered Bihar and Bengal (1193-1203); sacked Nalanda, Vikramashila, Odantapuri.
Entered Nadiya, drove Lakshmana Sena to East Bengal (1204); ruled from Lakhnauti.
# Causes of Turkish Success
Factor | Point

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Timur's Invasion; Sayyid and Lodi Dynasties; First Battle of Panipat, 1526

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# From Timur to Babur – Timeline
Year | Event
1398 | Timur sacks Delhi (Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq)
1412-13 | Last Tughlaq dies (1412); Daulat Khan Sultan (1413)
1414 | Khizr Khan takes Delhi; Sayyid dynasty
1451 | Alam Shah gives throne to Bahlol Lodi
1498 | Vasco da Gama arrives; Delhi ruler Sikandar Lodi
1504 | Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
1517 | Khatauli: Rana Sanga defeats Ibrahim
21 April 1526 | First Panipat: Babur kills Ibrahim
# Delhi Sultanate Dynasties
Order | Dynasty | Period | Founder | Origin
1 | Mamluk (Slave) | 1206-90 | Qutbuddin Aibak | Turk
2 | Khalji | 1290-1320 | Jalaluddin Khalji | Turk (Khalji)
3 | Tughlaq | 1320-1414 | Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq | Turk
4 | Sayyid | 1414-51 | Khizr Khan | Claimed descent from the Prophet
5 | Lodi | 1451-1526 | Bahlol Lodi | Afghan
Longest dynasty: Tughlaq (94 years); shortest: Sayyid (37 years) after the Khaljis (30 years).
Lodis = first Afghan dynasty and last dynasty of the Sultanate; Ibrahim Lodi = last Delhi Sultan.
Chronology item: Rukn-ud-din (1236) → Mubarak Khan (1316-1320) → Firuz Shah Tughluq (1351-88) → Alam Shah (1445-51).
Rukn-ud-din ruled after Iltutmish's death though Iltutmish had named Raziyya.
# Timur's Invasion, 1398
Route: crossed the Indus → Punjab via Multan and Bhatnair → sacked Delhi (December 1398).
Sultan on the throne: Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq, the last Tughlaq (d. 1412).
Effects: Tughlaq state broke into regional kingdoms (Jaunpur, Malwa, Gujarat); Timur's nominee Khizr Khan later founded the Sayyid dynasty.
The Mughal Empire was not an effect of Timur; it was founded by Babur in 1526.
# Sayyid Dynasty (1414-51)
Khizr Khan (1414-21), Timur's viceroy: arrested/defeated Daulat Khan Lodi, took Delhi in 1414.
Ruled as Timur's deputy, without the title of Sultan.

1 | Khizr Khan | 1414-21
2 | Mubarak Shah | 1421-34
3 | Muhammad Shah | 1434-45
4 | Alauddin Alam Shah | 1445-51

End: Alam Shah voluntarily gave the throne to Bahlol Lodi (1451), without a battle.
Sayyid order: Khizr Khan → Mubarak Shah → Muhammad Shah → Alam Shah.
# Lodi Dynasty (1451-1526)
Ruler | Reign | Key points
Bahlol (Bahlul) Lodi | 1451-89 | Founder; Governor of Punjab; throne from Alam Shah; conquered Jaunpur; ruled longest
Sikandar Lodi | 1489-1517 | Founded Agra; Gaz-i-Sikandari; pen name Gulrukhi
Ibrahim Lodi | 1517-26 | Arrogant to nobles; killed at Panipat
Order: Bahlol → Sikandar → Ibrahim (son follows father each time).
Lodi kingship: Sultan as "first among equals" among Afghan nobles.
## Sikandar Lodi
Nizam Khan, third son of Bahlol; crowned 17 July 1489.
Founded Agra (1504); shifted the capital there from Delhi.
Gaz-i-Sikandari (Gaj-i-Sikandari): yard to measure land.
Tax remissions: abolished the tax on grains, several taxes and trade restrictions; used audits and spies; punished embezzlement by nobles.
Rule from Punjab to Bihar; took Jaunpur; defeated Bengal rulers and Rajput chiefs.
Wrote Persian poetry under the pen name Gulrukhi.
Destroyed Jwalamukhi (Nagarkot) images and Mathura temples, imposed jizya; yet had a Sanskrit medical work translated into Persian.
Built Moth ki Masjid and royal tombs of the Lodi Gardens.
## Ibrahim Lodi
Nobles plotted to enthrone his brother Jalal Khan.
Seized Gwalior (which had sheltered Jalal Khan); Vikramajit of Gwalior made a vassal.
Khatauli (1517): defeated by Rana Sanga of Mewar.
Contemporaries: Krishnadevaraya, Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk (Golconda, independent 1518), Rana Sanga (not Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq).
# Invitation to Babur
Person | Role
Daulat Khan Lodi | Governor of Punjab; invited Babur
Alam Khan | Ibrahim's uncle and pretender to the Delhi throne; invited Babur
Rana Sanga | Offered to join against Ibrahim (as per Babur)
Cause: Ibrahim's arrogance alienated the Afghan nobles.
Babur's descent: Timur (father's side), Chengiz Khan (mother's side).
Krishnadevaraya (1509-29) was a contemporary of Babur.
# First Battle of Panipat, 1526
Date: 21 April 1526; Babur (about 12,000) beat Ibrahim (about 1,00,000) by skilled warfare and skilled commandants despite a smaller army.
## Tactics
Term | Meaning
Tulughma | Flanking (side) attack
Araba | Carts chained together as a defence line ("Rumi"/Ottoman device)
Field artillery and muskets | Decisive factor; gunners Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa
Artillery first used in India at Panipat; Babur first mentions guns at Bajaur (1519).
## Consequences
Ibrahim = only Delhi Sultan to die on the battlefield.
Babur captured Delhi and Agra and the Lodi treasure.
End of the Delhi Sultanate, start of the Mughal Empire (founded by Babur; consolidated by Akbar; Sher Shah = Sur dynasty).
21 April 2026 = 500th anniversary of the battle.
# Babur's Battles
Battle | Year | Defeated
First Panipat | 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi
Khanwa | 1527 | Rana Sanga
Chanderi | 1528 | Medini Rai
Ghaghra | 1529 | The Afghans
Khanwa (16 March 1527): Babur declared Jehad, took the title Ghazi; broke Rajput power.
Khanwa was more decisive than Panipat: Rana Sanga was a stronger enemy; it set up Mughal supremacy in North India.
Mughal-period battle order: Khanwa → Ghaghra → Chausa → Samugarh. Later: Second Panipat 1556; Plassey 1757.

Item | Fact
Timur sacks Delhi | December 1398
Sayyid / Lodi | 1414-51 / 1451-1526
Agra founded | 1504
First Panipat | 21 April 1526
Babur's army / Ibrahim's | 12,000 / 1,00,000
Khanwa | 16 March 1527
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First Afghan dynasty and last Sultanate dynasty: Lodi.
Last Delhi Sultan, only one to die in battle: Ibrahim Lodi.
First use of artillery in an Indian battle: First Panipat.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area

Group 1 Prelims | Delhi Sultanate dynasties: order and founders
Group 1 Prelims 2025 | Lodi rulers: contribution and succession
# High-probability Mcq Traps

2. Khizr Khan ruled without the title Sultan.
3. Alam Shah gave the throne voluntarily, no battle.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Mughal Empire – Babur: Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra; Tuzuk-i-baburi

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Babur – Background and Career
Given name: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad; "Babur" = tiger (a nickname/title).
Born 1483 in Farghana (Central Asia).
Descent: Timur on father's side, Chingiz Khan on mother's side.
Mughals were Chagatai Turks – named after Chagatai, Genghis Khan's second son, ruler of Central Asia and Turkistan.
Babur's arrival set up the Timurid dynasty in India.
## Career Timeline
Year | Event
1483 | Born, Farghana
1501 | Took Samarkand (held only 8 months)
1504 | Took Kabul; dropped "Mirza", took title "Padshah"
1526 | First Battle of Panipat – Lodis displaced
1527 | Khanwa – Rajput power broken
1528 | Chanderi – Medini Rai
1529 | Ghaghra – Afghans of Bihar and Bengal
1530 | Died at Agra; buried at Kabul (Bagh-e-Babur)
## Invited to Invade India
Inviter | Who
Daulat Khan Lodi | Governor of Punjab
Alam Khan | Ibrahim Lodi's uncle
Rana Sanga | Ruler of Mewar
# Mughal Battles – Chronology
Battle | Year | Mughal side | Opponent | Winner
Panipat I | 1526 | Babur | Ibrahim Lodi | Babur
Khanwa | 1527 | Babur | Rana Sanga | Babur
Chanderi | 1528 | Babur | Medini Rai | Babur
Ghaghra | 1529 | Babur | Mahmud Lodi's Afghans + Nusrat Shah of Bengal | Babur
Chausa | 1539 | Humayun | Sher Shah | Sher Shah
Kannauj / Bilgram | 1540 | Humayun | Sher Shah | Sher Shah
Panipat II | 1556 | Akbar (Bairam Khan) | Hemu | Akbar
Haldighati | 1576 | Akbar (Man Singh) | Maharana Pratap | Akbar
Order: Panipat I → Khanwa → Chanderi → Ghaghra → Chausa → Kannauj → Panipat II → Haldighati.
# First Battle of Panipat – 1526
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last Delhi Sultan (Lodis = last Sultanate dynasty).
Ended the Delhi Sultanate; began Mughal rule.
Numbers: Babur's 12,000 vs about 1,00,000 of Ibrahim's troops.
Gains: Delhi and Agra (APPSC 2023) + the Lodi treasure.
He shared the treasure lavishly → nickname "Qalandar"; treasury left depleted for Humayun.

Tactics: trenches and barricades against Sanga's elephants; artillery decisive again.

Extent: Kabul, Badakhshan → Punjab, Delhi, Agra → borders of Bihar (after Ghaghra).

Ruled through jagirs and paraganas; Badakhshan was given to Humayun.

Mughal authority had shallow roots; Bengal unconquered; Afghans still claimed Delhi.

No administrative system was set up; treasury empty.

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Akbar's Institutions – Mansabdari System, Todar Mal's Bandobast, Dahsala, Zabti and Other Revenue Systems

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Road to the Dahsala
Mansabdari + zabti-dahsala = a salaried, transferable nobility + predictable cash revenue.
Sher Shah's survey system → Karori experiment (1574) → karoris collect revenue and cultivation data → Dahsala (1580), Todar Mal.
## Karori Experiment – 1574
Core provinces split into circles, each to yield one crore dams, under officers called karoris.
Karoris collected revenue and reported cultivation data – groundwork for the dahsala.
1574 = Karori experiment; 1580 = Dahsala.
# Raja Todar Mal
Earlier served Sher Shah; built on his survey-based system.
Diwan (finance minister) of the empire; one of the Navratnas.
Muzaffar Khan Turbati was first given the proper status of Diwan by Akbar, with Todar Mal as assistant; Todar Mal and Khwaja Shah Mansur came later.
Unit | Fact
Gaz-i-Ilahi | Unit of length, about 82 cm
Jarib | Bamboo pieces joined with iron rings – replaced hemp rope, which shrank or stretched
State share | One-third of average produce, paid in cash (dam); kind allowed in some areas
# Revenue Systems
System | Meaning | Region / year
Zabti (Bandobast) | Land measured; dasturs with cash rates per crop per bigha | Core North Indian provinces (Lahore to Allahabad, Malwa, Gujarat)
Dahsala (Ain-i-Dahsala) | Average produce and prices of the last ten years (1571-1580), turned into cash | 1580 (APPSC G2 2017)
Batai / Ghalla-bakhshi (Bantai) | Crop-sharing – actual produce divided between state and peasant | Thatta, Kabul, Kashmir
Nasaq | Rough assessment from past revenue records, no fresh measurement | Mainly Bengal
Kankut | Yield estimated on the standing crop | Where measuring was impractical
Plough assessment | By number of ploughs | Parts of the Deccan (J.N. Sarkar, History of Aurangzeb)
"Bandobast system" = Dahsala (JPSC 2013); also called "Zabti or Bandobast".
Zabti was introduced by Akbar.
Sher Shah's three systems: Nasq / Muktai / Kankut, Nakadi or Jabti, Galla Bakshi or Bantai.
Iqta = Sultanate revenue assignment (Iltutmish).
# Land Classification
Class | Status
Polaj | Cultivated every year
Parauti | Fallow 1-2 years
Chachar | Fallow 3-4 years
Banjar | Fallow 5+ years
Parauti (1-2) vs Chachar (3-4) vs Banjar (5+).
# Revenue and Grant Terms
Term | Meaning
Maal (mal) | Land revenue – the principal state income
Khalisa | Crown land; revenue straight to the imperial treasury; reserve for cash (naqd) salaries
Jagir | Right to collect revenue in lieu of salary – not ownership
Madad-i-maash | Revenue-free grant to scholars, holy men, the needy
Suyurghal | Another name for such charitable revenue-free grants
# Mansabdari System
Introduced by Akbar; of Central Asian / Mongol military origin.
Mansabdars held combined civil-military, non-hereditary ranks, paid by jagir (or cash).
Ranks: 10 to 5,000 for nobles (later raised to 7,000); higher ranks only for royal princes.
Zat = personal rank and pay; Sawar = number of horsemen to maintain – dual ranks from 1595-96.
Three classes by the sawar-zat ratio: sawar equal to zat = 1st class.
Dagh (horse branding) – 1573-74.
Du-aspa sih-aspa – troopers with two/three horses without raising zat – introduced by Jahangir.
Mansabdar | civil-military, non-hereditary | paid by jagir
ICS | purely civil | fixed salary
# Jagirdari System
Type | Feature
Tankha | In lieu of salary; transferable every 3-4 years
Watan | Zamindar's homeland; hereditary, not transferable
Mashrut | Conditional, tied to specified duties
In'am | Reward; no service obligation
Frequent transfers prevented local power bases.
# Central Ministers
Office | Function
Wakil | Highest in rank; lost financial powers
Wazir / Diwan-i-kul | Finance – revenue, treasury, accounts
Mir Bakhshi | Military – dagh, chehra, promotions
Sadr-us-sudur | Religious affairs, charitable grants, Shariat
Mir Saman | Royal household and karkhanas
# Provincial and Local Administration
Unit | Officials
Suba (12 in 1580) | Subedar (head), diwan, bakhshi, sadr, qazi
Sarkar | Faujdar (law and order), amalguzar (revenue)
Pargana | Shiqdar, amil, qanungo
Town | Kotwal – law and order in the city
Village | Muqaddam (headman), patwari, chowkidar
## Revenue Officials
Official | Duty
Amalguzar | Sarkar revenue collector; extend cultivation
Bitikchi | Records on land and produce
Qanungo | Pargana land and revenue records
Karori | Circle yielding one crore dams
Potdar | Treasurer
Patwari | Village accountant
AP angle: Qutb Shahi Golconda took one-third (not one-half); lands wet, dry, garden, waste. Deshmukh collected land revenue for the state treasury.

First proper Diwan: Muzaffar Khan Turbati.

Only non-transferable jagir: Watan.

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Trade Centres of Coastal Andhra – Masulipatnam, Nizampatnam, Bheemunipatnam, Yanam

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Exports from Coastal Andhra
## Export → Centre
Export | Centre | Point
Handloom cotton textiles: chintz, palampores, muslins, kalamkari | Machilipatnam | The handloom port of the 16th-17th centuries (APPSC 2019)
Saltpetre / gunpowder | Machilipatnam, Narsapur, Pulicat | Bulk export
Diamonds | Golconda mines; Kollur (Guntur) | Kollur gave the Koh-i-Noor
Indigo | Nagulavancha, Nalgonda | Dye
Salt | Pedaganjam, Chinaganjam | APPSC 2019
Cheap calico | Narasapuram | Coarse cloth
Taanis | Injaram | Cloth variety
Rumaals | Nellore | Kerchiefs
Dominant pre-colonial industry = textiles, second only to diamonds in the Qutb Shahi economy.
Textile ports shipping to England, France and Holland: Kalingapatnam, Srikakulam, Vizag, Bhimunipatnam, Corangi, Kakinada, Narsapur, Machilipatnam.
Salt = Pedaganjam, Chinaganjam; indigo = Nagulavancha; Koh-i-Noor = Kollur, not Golconda town.
## Textile Terms → Meaning
Term | Meaning
Chintz | Glazed textile; became brighter after washing
Pintado | Printed textile
Palampores, kalamkari | Masulipatnam textile names (painted and printed cotton)
Odaberam | Sea-going ships (mentioned in Shuka Saptati)
# Machilipatnam (masulipatnam)
## Ruler and Periods
Period / ruler | Point
Ancient | Ptolemy's Mysolia / Maisolia – "great market"
Qutb Shahis of Golconda | Principal maritime gateway; customs revenue made Golconda one of the richest states
1600s | Famous for textile and diamond trade
Mughals | Aurangzeb took Golconda in 1687; Masulipatnam passed to the Mughals
Present | Lighthouse near Manginapudi, from 1984
Machilipatnam = most famous textile port of the 16th-17th centuries (chintz/kalamkari); linked Andhra weavers to the European companies.
English calico bans (1700, 1721) did not hurt Andhra – other markets stayed open.
## Merchant Communities
Komatis: the key merchant community at Masulipatnam.
Andhra weavers sold to all four European companies.
Machilipatnam was the Qutb Shahi port; Aurangzeb's capture of Golconda (1687) brought it under the Mughals.
# Shipbuilding Centres
Narasapuram / Narsapur (West Godavari, Godavari delta): major shipbuilding centre of the 16th-17th centuries; good timber and a safe river mouth.
Methold saw large, strong ships built there under the Qutb Shahis.
Machilipatnam: ship and boat building with Narasapuram.
Corangi: Company-era shipbuilding site.
The medieval shipbuilding centre on the Godavari = Narasapuram, not Machilipatnam alone.
# European Factories at Trade Centres
## Centre → Power → Year
Centre | Power(s) | Year / note
Masulipatnam | Portuguese first to arrive; Dutch factory 1605; English 1611 | First English factory in South India
Pulicat | Dutch; English | 1610; 1621
Nizampatnam (Petapoli) | Dutch and English | Early 17th century
Bheemunipatnam | Dutch → English | Dutch subordinate factory; English from the late 17th century
Palakollu (Palicol) | Dutch | Godavari delta
Madapollam | English (not French) | In records from 1676
Vizagapatnam | English | 1682
Yanam | French | 1723
First English factory in South India = Masulipatam, 1611.
Madapollam = English; Yanam = French (1723); Vizagapatnam = English (1682).
# Imports Into Andhra Ports
Import | Source / use
Bullion (gold, silver) | From Europe – financed English purchases of chintz, calico, muslin
Horses | Ormuz / Persia
Elephants | Ceylon (Simhala)
Camphor | Punjab
Golden sprouts | Jalanogi
Rice and grains | Brought back by coastal boats from Bengal, Rangoon, Chittagong
Company era: coastal boats carried salt and groceries to Yanam, Bengal, Rangoon and Chittagong and returned with rice and grains.
Reddi-period merchant Tippa (Avachi Tippaya Setti) is credited with importing horses, elephants and camphor.
# Yanam
Particular | Fact
European owner | French
Acquired | 1723 – only French territorial possession in Andhra
Merger with India | Indian Union 1954; de jure (in law) 1962
Present status | Part of the Union Territory of Puducherry; an enclave in AP's Godavari delta
Yanam is not part of Andhra Pradesh; it belongs to Puducherry UT.
# Bheemunipatnam (bhimili)
Dutch subordinate factory → later an English factory.
Dutch cemetery: tombs from 1661, the oldest European tombs in the Northern Circars.
A Dutch fort was allowed after Maratha troops plundered the town in 1754.
St Peter's Church – British-period church.
Bhimili = first municipality in Andhra (1861).
Bhimili: Dutch cemetery (1661) + first Andhra municipality (1861).
# Other Historic Ports and Centres
## Motupalli
Also called Desiyakondapattanam; the most important Kakatiya port (APPSC 2011).
Satavahana east-coast seaport; important Ikshvaku port with Ghantasala.
Marco Polo visited it in 1287, under Rudrama Devi, and described its busy trade.
Ganapatideva's Abhaya inscription (Abhaya Sasanam) protected foreign traders.
Reddy period: held by Mallaya Reddy; minister Somaya issued another Abhaya Sasana for trade. Anavota Reddi lifted customs duties; sea trade ran through Motupalli.
## Ghantasala and Others
Centre | Period | Point
Ghantasala (Kantakasela), Krishna district | Satavahana / Ikshvaku | Ptolemy's Kantakossyla; Roman coins found
Koddura | Satavahana | Ancient east-coast port with Ghantasala
Penugonda | Medieval | Central trade centre of medieval Andhra (APPSC 2012)
Nagapattinam | Dutch | Dutch HQ in India from 1690 (APPSC 2005)
Kondapalli, Golconda, Narsapur, Madras | Post-European | Major trade centres
Visakhapatnam | 19th century | Port for agricultural products
## Ptolemy's Names
Ptolemy's name | Place
Mysolia | Machilipatnam
Kantakossyla | Ghantasala
## Texts on Trade
Srinatha dedicated Haravilasam to overseas trader Avachi Tippaya Setti: the Reddi sea-trade text (APPSC 2019).
Kashikhandam is another Srinatha work, but not the sea-trade text.
Shuka Saptati mentions odaberam ships; Vedanta Rasayanam by Subbarayudu.
Reddi sea trade = Haravilasam, not Kashikhandam (APPSC 2019 key).
# Decline and Present Ports
High Company-era duties ruined Andhra's domestic and foreign trade.
Four new AP ports under construction: Machilipatnam, Mulapeta, Ramayapatnam, Kakinada SEZ.
Proposed Nizampatnam (Guntur) and Vodarevu (Prakasam) ports under PPP-BOOT model – on hold during a CBI investigation (2024-25).

Marco Polo at Motupalli | 1287
Dutch HQ at Nagapattinam | 1690
Machilipatnam Dutch / English | 1605 / 1611
Golconda to Aurangzeb | 1687
English calico bans | 1700, 1721
Yanam French / India / de jure | 1723 / 1954 / 1962
Bhimili municipality | 1861
Manginapudi lighthouse | 1984
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First municipality in Andhra: Bhimili (1861).
Only French territory in Andhra: Yanam. Most important Kakatiya port: Motupalli.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Arya Samaj and Dayananda Saraswati – Satyarth Prakash, Shuddhi, Dayanand Anglo-vedic Schools

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Dayananda Saraswati – Life
Item | Fact
Original name | Mool Shankar (Tiwari)
Born | 1824, Tankara, Morvi (Gujarat)
Guru | Swami Virajananda (Virjanand) of Mathura
Died | 1883, Ajmer
Main work | Satyarth Prakash (1875), in Hindi
Body founded | Arya Samaj, Bombay, 1875
200th birth anniversary of Dayananda and 150 years of the Arya Samaj were marked at the International Arya Mahasammelan 2025 (Jnana Jyoti Festival), New Delhi (Nov 2025).
Guru = Virajananda of Mathura; died at Ajmer, not Lahore (Lahore was later the Arya Samaj HQ).
# Titles, Slogans and Firsts
Title / slogan | Fact
"Martin Luther of India" | Title given by Lala Lajpat Rai
"Grandfather of the Indian Nation" | Dayananda
"India for the Indians" | Dayananda's slogan
Swaraj | Dayananda credited as the first to use the term
"Back to the Vedas" ("Go Back to the Vedas") | His call on the Vedas
Hindi | Wrote his main work in Hindi; promoted Hindi as a link language
## "Back to the Vedas"
The four Vedas infallible = primordial (original) word of God.
Rejected later accretions of the Puranas (myths, rituals, idol worship).
Claimed the Vedas held all true knowledge, including science → countered the colonial idea of Western intellectual superiority.
'Prophet of Indian Nationalism': this title is given to Swami Vivekananda, not to Dayananda Saraswati.
# Satyarth Prakash
Point | Fact
Author | Swami Dayananda Saraswati, 1875 – his greatest work
Language | Hindi
Meaning | "The Light of Truth" (also "The True Exposition")
Themes | His religious and social philosophy; Vedic religion explained; critique of Hindu orthodoxy and of other religions (Islam, Christianity, Jainism, Buddhism)
Attacked | Orthodoxy, idolatry, caste by birth, child marriage
Satyarth Prakash did NOT support orthodoxy – it attacked it. Its language is Hindi, not Sanskrit.
# Arya Samaj, 1875 – Founding and Base
Founder: Swami Dayananda Saraswati.
Founded at Bombay, 10 April 1875 (Girgaon).
Name means "Society of Nobles".
Strongest base: Punjab; HQ later moved to Lahore; also strong in Rajasthan and the United Provinces.
Ten Principles drafted by Dayananda – truth, rational thought, moral action, welfare of all.
The principles stress that God is the source of all true knowledge, that the Vedas are the books of true knowledge, that one must accept truth and give up untruth, and that the aim of the Samaj is to do good to the whole world – physical, spiritual and social.
Caste was to be decided by merit and conduct, not by birth.
Founded in Bombay, NOT Calcutta; it rejects idol worship (never "promotes idol worship").
## Programme
Rejected / opposed | Supported
Idol worship, polytheism, ritualism | Widow remarriage
Caste by birth, untouchability | Inter-caste marriage
Child marriage, purdah | Women's education
Nature: revivalism + reform; revivalist like Deoband, unlike the reformist Brahmo and Prarthana Samajes.
## Arya Samaj vs Other Reform Bodies
Feature | Arya Samaj | Brahmo Samaj | Prarthana Samaj
Founder | Dayananda Saraswati | Rammohan Roy | Atmaram Pandurang
Year, place | 1875, Bombay | 1828, Calcutta | 1867, Bombay
Nature | Revivalist + reform | Reformist (reason) | Reformist, milder
Scripture | Vedas infallible | No scripture final; Vedas not faultless | Reform within Hinduism
Idol worship | Rejected | Rejected | Not forbidden
Main base | Punjab (HQ Lahore) | Bengal | Maharashtra
Conversion work | Shuddhi (reconversion) | None | None
Arya Samaj was an open body, not a secret society (unlike the Paramahansa Mandali).
Like the Deoband movement, it looked back to its own sacred tradition for reform.
"Nursery of militant nationalists": influenced Lala Lajpat Rai, Swami Shraddhanand, Bhagat Singh's family.
# Reform Bodies – Year of Founding
Body | Year | Founder
Brahmo Samaj (Sabha) | 1828 | Rammohan Roy
Prarthana Samaj | 1867 | Atmaram Pandurang
Satyashodhak Samaj | 1873 | Jyotiba Phule
Arya Samaj | 1875 | Dayananda Saraswati
Ramakrishna Mission | 1897 | Vivekananda
Order: Brahmo (1828) → Prarthana (1867) → Satyashodhak (1873) → Arya (1875) → Ramakrishna Mission (1897).
## Related Pairs (asked in the same question)
Al Hilal (Urdu weekly, 1912) – Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
Presidency College (formerly Hindu College), Calcutta – Rammohan Roy.
Lala Lajpat Rai – associated with 'The People'.
# Shuddhi Movement
Started by: Arya Samaj (Dayananda) – NOT Brahmo Samaj, Satyashodhak Samaj or Ramakrishna Mission.
Aim: ritual "purification" to reconvert Hindus who had become Muslims or Christians, and admit outsiders into the Hindu fold.
Later leader: Swami Shraddhanand – 1920s campaign through the Bharatiya Hindu Shuddhi Sabha (1923).
Shraddhanand gave a speech on Hindu-Muslim unity from the pulpit of Jama Masjid, Delhi, on 4 April 1919; assassinated 1926.
Method: a purification ritual after which the person was accepted back into Hindu society; it also opened the fold to outsiders.
Impact: contributed to the communalisation of social life and, later, to communal political consciousness.
"Shuddhi was started by ___" → Arya Samaj.
# Dav and Gurukul – the Split
## Dayanand Anglo-Vedic Schools
DAV school, Lahore, opened 1886 in Dayananda's memory, with Lala Hansraj as headmaster; grew into DAV College, Lahore.
Blended Vedic values with English-medium modern education.
## Split of 1893
Faction | Leaders | Stand
College (DAV) party | Lala Hansraj, Lala Lajpat Rai | Kept control of DAV College; modern English education
Gurukul party | Munshi Ram (later Swami Shraddhanand) | Vedic, Gurukul education; set up Gurukul Kangri (1902) near Haridwar
# Arya Samaj in Hyderabad State
Satyagraha of 1938–39 in Hyderabad State against the Nizam's curbs on religious and civil rights.
Ran alongside the Hyderabad State Congress satyagraha.
Helped build political awakening against Nizam rule in the Telangana region.
Hyderabad satyagraha = 1938–39, against the Nizam's curbs on religious and civil rights – not a Shuddhi campaign.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Correct Fact
Dayananda born | 1824
Arya Samaj founded | 10 April 1875, Bombay
Satyarth Prakash | 1875
Dayananda died | 1883, Ajmer
DAV Lahore | 1886
Split | 1893
Gurukul Kangri | 1902
Shuddhi Sabha | 1923
Hyderabad satyagraha | 1938–39
Principles | 10
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First to use the term Swaraj: Dayananda.
Main work written in Hindi, not Sanskrit.
Arya Samaj HQ shifted from Bombay to Lahore.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2 Screening 2024 | Movement – started by; Samaj (Shuddhi / Arya Samaj)
APPSC Group 1 Prelims | Arya Samaj founder, year and place
APPSC Group 1 Prelims | "India for the Indians" slogan
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Arya Samaj founded in Bombay, not Calcutta or Lahore.
2. Shuddhi = Arya Samaj, not Brahmo or Satyashodhak.
3. Satyarth Prakash = Hindi, "Light of Truth".
4. "Martin Luther of India" title given by Lajpat Rai.
5. Original name Mool Shankar; guru Virajananda.
6. Dayananda died at Ajmer, 1883.
7. Arya Samaj rejects idol worship and caste by birth.
8. Gurukul Kangri = Munshi Ram; DAV = Hansraj.
9. Bharatiya Hindu Shuddhi Sabha (1923) = Shraddhanand.
10. "India for the Indians" and first use of Swaraj = Dayananda, not Tilak.

content.text:
STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Growth of Nationalism – Factors; Pre-congress Political Associations

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Factors of Indian Nationalism
## Unintended Results of British Rule
Political and administrative unification: railways, telegraph, post and uniform laws tied India together.
Western education: liberal ideas (liberty, equality, democracy); English as a link language across regions.
Rise of a new educated middle class – lawyers, journalists, teachers – who led the early associations.
Press and literature spread political ideas; history-writing revived pride in India's past.
Inspiration from the American, French and Italian freedom struggles.
## Reactions to British Rule
Economic critique: the drain of wealth and the ruin of artisans.
Racial arrogance: Lytton's policies and the Ilbert Bill agitation.
Early associations trained the English-educated class in petitions, memorials and all-India teamwork – this led straight to the INC in 1885.
# Lytton's Resented Measures (1876-80)
Measure | Year | Why resented
Delhi Durbar | 1877 | Proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India while millions starved in the 1876-78 famine
Vernacular Press Act | 1878 | Gagged the Indian-language press
Arms Act | 1878 | Disarmed Indians but spared Europeans
Second Afghan War | 1878-80 | Drained Indian revenue
ICS age cut | 1876 | Maximum age lowered from 21 to 19 (by Secretary of State Salisbury), shutting out Indians
"Which was NOT a measure of Lytton?" – the Ilbert Bill (1883) was Ripon's, not Lytton's.
Amrita Bazar Patrika turned English overnight in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
# Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883)
Particular | Fact
Viceroy | Lord Ripon
Drafted by | Sir Courtenay Ilbert (Law Member)
Provision | Allowed Indian magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects
Reaction | Strong European protest ("White Mutiny")
Compromise | A European accused could claim a jury with at least half Europeans
Passed | 25 January 1884, in a weakened form
Lesson for Indians: organised agitation works – the Europeans' success pushed Indians towards an all-India body.
# Pre-congress Associations – All-india List
Association | Year | Founder / leader | Place
Landholders' Society (Zamindari Association) | 1838 | Dwarkanath Tagore, Prasanna Kumar Tagore, Radhakanta Deb | Calcutta
Bengal British India Society | 1843 | – | Calcutta
British Indian Association | 1851 | Merger of the two above; Radhakanta Deb president, Debendranath Tagore secretary | Calcutta
Madras Native Association | 1852 | Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty | Madras
East India Association | 1866 | Dadabhai Naoroji | London
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha | 1870 | M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, S.H. Chiplunkar | Poona
Indian Association | 1876 | Surendranath Banerjee, A.M. Bose | Calcutta
Madras Mahajana Sabha | 1884 | P. Rangaiah Naidu, P. Anandacharlu, M. Viraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer | Madras
East India Association was founded in London, not in India.
# Madras and Andhra Associations
## Madras Native Association (26 February 1852)
First political body of Madras; first such organisation in South India.
Founder and first president: Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty; secretary Somasundaram Chettiyar.
Began as an adjunct of the British Indian Association, later independent.
Petition (1852) to the British Parliament before the Charter renewal of 1853 – against the ryotwari oppression, torture by revenue collectors and heavy taxes such as moturpha (a tax on trades and occupations).
Its agitation helped lead to the Torture Commission (1854).
## Madras Mahajana Sabha (16 May 1884)
Second major body of Madras.
President P. Rangaiah Naidu; secretary P. Anandacharlu; other founders M. Viraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer.
Demanded larger councils and more Indian representation.
## Kakinada (Coconada) Literary Association
Sent memorandums (1884-85) to raise the ICS age limit and hold simultaneous examinations in India.
## Krishna District Association (1892)
Founded by Ramaswamy Gupta; first district association in the Madras Presidency.
Formed on the INC's advice to set up district bodies.
First meeting at Guntur (1892, APPSC key); second at Machilipatnam (1893).
Angalur conference (1900) demanded agricultural banks.
Its resolution of 1899 led to Krishna Patrika (first issue 1902).
1852 – 1884 – 1892 = Native Association – Mahajana Sabha – Krishna District Association; 1900 = Angalur conference, not the founding.
Body | Year | Exam-key point
Madras Native Association | 1852 | Correct pair (APPSC-GS 2025)
Madras Mahajana Sabha | 1884 | Correct pair (APPSC-GS 2019, 2025)
Krishna District Association | 1892 | "1900" is wrong (APPSC-GS 2021, 2025)
Stimulus in the South: S.N. Banerjee's tour for the Indian Association (1878).
# Surendranath Banerjee
Passed the ICS (1869) → disqualified over an age dispute → reinstated → dismissed in 1874 on a minor irregularity.
Toured India against the cut of the ICS maximum age from 21 to 19.
Founded the Indian Association (1876) with A.M. Bose.
Convened the Indian National Conference (1883, 1885) → merged with the INC in 1886.
Title: "Rashtraguru"; paper: The Bengalee.
INC president: Poona 1895 and Ahmedabad 1902 (not Surat 1907).
Banerjee's presidencies were Poona 1895 and Ahmedabad 1902 – not Surat 1907.
# Nationalist Literature
Work | Author | Year / note
Nil Darpan (Neeldarpan) | Dinabandhu Mitra | 1860; cruelty of indigo planters (before Satyendranath Tagore's ICS, 1864)
Anandamath | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | 1882; set in the Sannyasi Rebellion (1763-1800); contains Vande Mataram
Durgeshnandini | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | His first novel
Rajasimha, Rajani, Indira | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | Other novels

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Constitutional Government
Constitutional government = limited government, limited by the terms of the Constitution (UPSC 2020, 2021); it defines, restrains and checks power to stop executive tyranny.
Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy = separation of powers (UPSC 2021).
Constitutionalism: limits + rule of law + checks and balances + judicial review + FRs.
A majoritarian position cannot override constitutionalism.
PIL widens access to justice for the poor but is not indispensable for the rule of law, which existed before PIL via Arts. 14, 32, 226.
# Montesquieu and the Indian Degree
Montesquieu: division of powers best protects liberty; "The Spirit of Laws" (1748); drew on the British constitution.
Parliamentary system = fusion: executive drawn from and accountable to the legislature; ministers must be legislators. Presidential = separation.
Nominal head President; real executive Council of Ministers.
Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability; reasons: familiarity (1919/1935 Acts), diversity, avoid American-style conflict.
India: no rigid separation; implicit, not absolute; overlapping functions → checks and balances.
Art. 50 (DPSP): separate judiciary from executive in public services. Judiciary insulated: Arts. 50, 121, 211, 235.
Munro's Madras Regulations (1816): reversed the Cornwallis separation – the Collector again got magisterial and police powers, and village heads got petty police and judicial powers.
# Legislature Over Executive
In India the executive is subordinate to the legislature (BPSC 2001).
Device | Purpose
Question Hour, Zero Hour | Daily watch
No-confidence motion | Removes government – Lok Sabha only
Impeachment (Art. 61) | Removes President
Collective responsibility | Art. 75(3) Lok Sabha; 164(2) Assembly
# Executive Over Legislature
Power | Union | State
Summon/prorogue; max 6-month gap | Art. 85 | Art. 174
Dissolve lower House | Art. 85(2) | Assembly
Address / messages | 86, 87 | 175, 176
Ordinance | 123 | 213
Assent / veto | 111 | 200; reserve 201
Ordinance only when the legislature is not in session; subject to judicial review; laid before the House.
# Judicial Checks
Judicial review of laws and executive action: Arts. 13, 32, 226; ultra vires law is void.
Art. 121: no discussion in Parliament on an SC/HC judge's conduct, except on a removal motion; Art. 211 for State Legislatures.
Arts. 122, 212: courts cannot question legislative proceedings for irregular procedure.
Art. 142 complete justice: Vishaka guidelines before POSH Act, 2013; scope undefined, overreach risk.
121/211 = legislature cannot discuss judges; 122/212 = courts cannot question procedure.
# Cases
Case | Holding
Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) | No rigid separation; executive power covers matters on which legislature can legislate
Kesavananda (1973) | Separation of powers = basic feature
Raj Narain (1975) | Legislature cannot decide an election dispute; 39th Amendment validation of PM's election struck
Minerva Mills (1980) | 42nd Amendment bar on review struck
I.R. Coelho | Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries reviewable
# Overriding A Judgment
Option | Limit
Constitutional amendment | Basic structure
Validating law | Must remove the basis; cannot declare judgment void
Ninth Schedule (76th, TN 69%) | Coelho review
Ordinance (123/213) | Judicial review
Review Art. 137; reference Art. 143 | Art. 143 advice not binding
Amendment | Overrode
1st | Champakam Dorairajan
24th | Golaknath
26th | Madhav Rao (privy purses)
77th | Indra Sawhney (promotion quota)
One Nation One Election Bill: amends Arts. 83, 172, 327; critics: fixed tenure weakens collective responsibility (75, 164).
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Pair | Union – State
Summon | 85 – 174
Assent | 111 – 200
Responsibility | 75(3) – 164(2)
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2 Mains (syllabus) | Checks and balances – Articles
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Parliament cannot overrule a judgment by simple resolution.
2. No-confidence motion: Lok Sabha only.
3. Art. 143 advice not binding.
4. Art. 50 is a DPSP.
5. India: no rigid separation (Ram Jawaya Kapur).
6. 77th followed Indra Sawhney.
7. PIL not indispensable for rule of law.
8. Executive subordinate to legislature.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Separation of powers — definitions, thinkers and degree in India
Constitutional government: = limited government → limited by the terms of the Constitution (UPSC 2020, 2021 keys)
Constitutionalism: powers within constitutional limits + rule of law + checks and balances + judicial review + protection of FRs
Best safeguard of liberty: in a liberal democracy = separation of powers (UPSC 2021 key)
Person | Statement / contribution
Montesquieu | Division of powers = most effective way to protect liberty; "The Spirit of Laws" (1748); drew on the British constitution
Ambedkar | Preferred responsibility over stability
Feature | Parliamentary (India, UK) | Presidential (USA)
Principle | Fusion - cooperation and coordination | Separation of powers
Executive | Drawn from and accountable to legislature | President independent of Congress
Heads | Nominal (President) and real (Council of Ministers) | Single real executive
Checks | Questions, confidence/no-confidence votes | Checks and balances among three organs
Why parliamentary system: familiarity (1919/1935 Acts) + diversity + avoid American-style executive-legislature conflict
Degree in India: no rigid separation; separation implicit, not absolute; overlapping functions → checks and balances

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.
