STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Vice-president; Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers – Articles 74, 75, 77, 78

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Vice-president – Office and Election
## Office (Articles 63, 64, 79, 89)
Article 63: second-highest office; modelled on the US Vice-President.
Articles 64 and 89(1): VP is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; has only a casting vote in a tie.
VP is not a member of either House – RS is chaired by a non-member.
Article 79: Parliament = President + Council of States + House of the People; the VP is not a part of Parliament.
Does not preside while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
Ex officio President of ICWA (Indian Council of World Affairs).
## Election (Articles 66, 71)
Elected (not appointed) by members of both Houses – elected and nominated MPs (788 when full); State Legislatures have no role.
PR-STV, secret ballot; Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.
Article 71: all disputes decided by the Supreme Court – final; acts done before a void election is declared remain valid.
39th Amendment (1975) removed the SC's power over election disputes of President, VP, PM and Speaker; 44th Amendment (1978) restored it.
State Legislative Assemblies vote in electing the President, Rajya Sabha members and Legislative Council members – not the VP.
# Vice-president – Qualifications, Term, Removal, Acting President
## Qualifications and term (Article 67)
Citizen; 35 years; qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha (not Lok Sabha); no office of profit.
Term 5 years; continues till successor takes charge (Art 67(c)); re-election any number of times.
Oath by the President (Art 69).
## Removal (Article 67(b))
Resolution moved only in the Rajya Sabha by a majority of all the then members, agreed to by the Lok Sabha; 14 days' notice; no grounds stated; no impeachment.
Point | President | Vice-President
Qualified to be member of | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
Resigns to | Vice-President (Art 56(1)(a)) | President (Art 67(a))
Removal | Impeachment (Art 61), two-thirds, 14 days' notice | RS resolution + LS agrees
Vacancy filled | Within 6 months (Art 62) | "As soon as possible" – no deadline (Art 68)
On the President's resignation the VP immediately informs the Speaker (Art 56(2)).
## Acting President (Article 65)
On vacancy (death, resignation, removal) or the President's inability; maximum 6 months.
While acting: ceases to do Chairman's duties – the Deputy Chairman presides; draws the President's salary, not the Chairman's.
# Vice-presidents – Firsts and Records
Fact | Person
First VP (1952–62); earlier Ambassador to the USSR (1949–52) | Dr. S. Radhakrishnan
Two full terms | S. Radhakrishnan (1952–62) and Hamid Ansari (2007–17)
Second VP (1962–67) | Dr. Zakir Husain
12th VP (2007), re-elected 2012 | Mohammad Hamid Ansari
VPs who became President | Radhakrishnan (1962), Zakir Husain (1967), V.V. Giri (1969)
Became President without being VP | Neelam Sanjiva Reddy
First President to die in office | Zakir Husain – V.V. Giri then acted as President (1969)
Diplomats: V.V. Giri (High Commissioner, Sri Lanka 1947–51), K.R. Narayanan (Ambassador, China 1976–78); also S. Radhakrishnan (Ambassador, USSR). ⚠ APPSC key (2010) gave Radhakrishnan and Zakir Husain – Zakir Husain held no diplomatic post.
July 2025: Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (health, Art 67(a)) – third mid-term vacancy after V.V. Giri (1969) and Krishan Kant (2002, died); Sep 2025: C.P. Radhakrishnan elected – present VP.
AP angle: M. Venkaiah Naidu (Nellore) was VP 2017–22.
S. Radhakrishnan = first VP; C.P. Radhakrishnan = present VP (2025).
# Prime Minister – Appointment, Oath, Membership
## Appointment (Article 75(1))
Appointed by the President; by convention the leader of the LS majority. Other Ministers on the PM's advice; PM has full discretion in choosing them. ⚠ APPSC key (2002) gave "PM is elected by the Parliament"; under Art 75(1) the President appoints the PM.
Oath by the President (Art 75(4)).
May be from either House; need not be an MP when appointed – must become one within six months (Art 75(5)).
UK PM must belong to the House of Commons; Indian PM – either House.
Article 53(1): executive power in the President (nominal, de jure); real executive = PM (de facto). The President "represents the nation but does not lead the nation".
Art 54 = President's election; 75 = PM and Ministers; 155 = Governor; 164 = CM and State Ministers.
## Tenure and responsibility
No fixed tenure; formally at the President's pleasure, in practice while he has the Lok Sabha's confidence.
PM resigning on losing majority (e.g. Budget defeated in LS) is a convention, not written in the Constitution.
# Prime Minister – Powers, Functions, Bodies Chaired
Selects Ministers, allocates portfolios, can ask any Minister to resign; advises on summoning/prorogation and dissolution of LS – not on the CJI (collegium).
Article 78 (not 74) – PM's duties to the President (see section 6).
Administering ministers' oaths is not an Article 78 duty.
Body chaired by the PM | Note
NITI Aayog, NDC, Inter-State Council, National Integration Council, National Defence Committee | Chairman
Planning Commission (1950) | Ex-officio Chairman; Deputy Chairman = Cabinet rank, first Gulzarilal Nanda
NDMA | Disaster Management Act (23 Dec 2005)
CSIR | President
Gandhi Peace Prize (started 1995, Gandhi's 125th birth anniversary): jury of five incl. PM, CJI, Leader of Opposition in LS – not the President.
# Articles 74, 75, 77, 78 – Content
Article | Content
74(1) | CoM headed by PM to aid and advise the President; President may ask reconsideration once; then advice is binding
74(2) | Advice not inquired into by any court
75(1A) | Size cap 15% of LS (91st Amdt)
75(1B) | Defector disqualified cannot be Minister till re-elected
75(2) | Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure
75(3) | Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha
77(1) | All executive action in the President's name
77(2) | Authentication of orders
77(3) | Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 and Transaction of Business Rules, 1961; President allocates portfolios on PM's advice
78 | PM communicates CoM decisions, furnishes information, puts a Minister's lone decision before the CoM
Article 74(3) does not exist.
During a National Emergency the President gets no discretion; CoM advice stays binding.
"All executive action of the GoI is taken in the name of the President" = Article 77.
# Council of Ministers – Responsibility and Non-members
## Collective and individual responsibility
Article 75(3): Council collectively responsible to the House of the People only – even if the PM or Ministers are RS members.
Individual responsibility: Ministers hold office at the President's pleasure (Art 75(2)) – not legally the PM's; President removes a Minister only on PM's advice.
## Non-member Ministers (Article 75(5))
Any person (incl. PM) may be a Minister; a non-member for six consecutive months ceases to be one.
S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001): a non-member cannot be re-appointed repeatedly without getting elected.
## Ministers in Parliament (Article 88)
A Minister may speak in both Houses and joint sittings, but votes only in his own House (an RS Minister or RS PM cannot vote in the Lok Sabha).
24 Jul 2026: MoS Ravneet Singh Bittu's resignation accepted "under Article 75(2)" after his RS term ended.
Giriraj Singh (Begusarai) – Union Textiles Minister, 18th LS.
# Size of the Council of Ministers – 91ST Amendment, 2003
Before 2003 the number of Ministers was not in the Constitution.
Article 75(1A): Ministers incl. PM not more than 15% of LS total strength (543 → max 81).
Article 164(1A) (States): 15% of Assembly incl. CM; minimum 12. West Bengal (294): 15% = 44.1 → max 44.
Aims: limit ministry size; strengthen anti-defection law.
The APPSC key gave the "97th Amendment" for limiting cabinet size; the 97th Amendment (2011) dealt with cooperative societies – the size cap is the 91st (2003).
130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025: PM/CM/Minister detained 30 consecutive days for an offence punishable with 5+ years is removed on the 31st day; touches Articles 75, 164, 239AA.
# Categories of Ministers; Cabinet; Non-constitutional Posts
## Council vs Cabinet
Basis | Council of Ministers | Union Cabinet
Size | About 60–80 | About 15–20
Composition | Cabinet Ministers, MoS (independent charge), MoS, Deputy Ministers | PM + Cabinet-rank Ministers only
Role | Arts 74–75 body | Supreme decision-making body
Cabinet Ministers head major ministries, attend Cabinet; MoS (independent charge) own ministry; MoS attached; Deputy Ministers only assist.
The Constitution does not classify Ministers into ranks – convention and PM's choice.
Word "Cabinet" not in the original Constitution; inserted in Article 352(3) by the 44th Amendment, 1978 (Cabinet's written advice for Emergency).
## Non-constitutional posts
Post | Facts
Deputy PM | Not in the Constitution; political need; oath as ordinary Minister; no PM powers; first Sardar Patel (15 Aug 1947 – 15 Dec 1950), also Home Minister
Leader of the House (LS) | Not constitutional; PM if LS member, else his nominee; first Nehru; Pranab Mukherjee under Manmohan Singh (RS PM)
PMO | Extra-constitutional staff agency
AP angle: 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement – united AP cabinet 60% Andhra : 40% Telangana.
# Prime Ministers – Firsts and Unique Facts
Fact | PM
First PM; longest total tenure (1947–64) | Jawaharlal Nehru
First woman PM; first PM from RS (1966) | Indira Gandhi
First non-Congress PM | Morarji Desai
First acting PM, twice (27 May–9 Jun 1964; 11–24 Jan 1966) | Gulzarilal Nanda
Died abroad – Tashkent (11 Jan 1966); second PM | Lal Bahadur Shastri
Never faced the Lok Sabha (28 Jul 1979 – 14 Jan 1980) | Charan Singh (not an RS PM)
Shortest tenure – 13 days (1996) | A.B. Vajpayee
PM without being an MP (1991); first from South India | P.V. Narasimha Rao – won Nandyal (AP)
RS PMs | Indira Gandhi, H.D. Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral, Manmohan Singh (RS from Assam, PM 2004–14)
LS member while PM (Balia, 1990–91); never a CM before | Chandra Shekhar
Order: Nanda (1966) → Indira → Morarji → Charan Singh → Rajiv → Chandra Shekhar.
Held office more than once with gaps: Nanda, Indira Gandhi, Vajpayee (not Nehru or Shastri).
July 2025: Narendra Modi passed Indira Gandhi's continuous tenure; Nehru keeps the record.
# Oaths, Resignations and Removal – Executive Heads
Office | Oath Article | Oath by | Resigns to
President | 60 | CJI | VP
PM, Union Ministers | 75(4) | President | President
Governor | 159 | HC Chief Justice | President
CM, State Ministers | 164(3) | Governor | Governor
Governor holds office at pleasure (Art 156) – no impeachment; State Ministers dismissed by the Governor on the CM's advice.
Oaths of President, VP and Governor are written in Articles 60, 69, 159 – not the Third Schedule; ministers' oaths are in the Third Schedule.
Speaker takes no oath of office; resigns to the Deputy Speaker (Art 94).
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
Acting President maximum | 6 months
Non-member Minister | 6 consecutive months
Size cap | 15% (91st Amdt, 2003); State minimum 12
130th Amdt Bill detention | 30 days → out on 31st
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 1 | 91st Amendment – 15% cap on Union Ministers
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 1 | Vice-President – election and removal
Group 2 Mains 2017 | State ministry: 15% and minimum 12
APPSC (earlier) | VP in office (Venkaiah Naidu); PMs from Rajya Sabha; Article 75(5)
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. VP: elected by both Houses only; removal starts only in RS.
2. Ministers hold office at the President's pleasure, not the PM's.
3. Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha only (Art 75(3)).
4. PM's duties = Article 78, not 74; 74(3) does not exist.
5. Size cap = 91st (2003), not 97th; includes the PM.
6. Constitution does not classify Ministers; Deputy PM and Leader of House are not constitutional.
7. "Cabinet" added by 44th Amdt in Art 352(3).
8. No presidential discretion during National Emergency.
9. RS Minister may speak in LS but cannot vote there.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Vice-President — office, qualifications and election (Arts 63, 64, 66)
## 1. Office & qualifications
Art. 63: there shall be a Vice-President
Art. 64: ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; not a member of RS; holds no other office of profit
Only a casting vote on a tie
Ex officio: also President of ICWA (Sep 2026)
Qualifications: citizen, 35 years, eligible for election to the Rajya Sabha
## 2. Election (Art. 66)
Electoral college: members of both Houses (elected and nominated) by PR by single transferable vote (PR-STV), secret ballot
State legislatures have no role → State MLAs are NOT in it; nominated MPs ARE
Size = all MPs, 788 (543 LS + 245 RS) when full
Conduct: by ECI under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952
Exam angle: "Who elects the VP" (both Houses only) and "Where can the removal resolution first be moved" (Rajya Sabha).
# Vice-President vs President — oath, term, removal, acting, disputes (Arts 65, 67-71) — Oath and term
## 1. Oath and term
Term: Term 5 years from entering office; continues till successor takes charge (Art 67(c)); re-eligible any number of times
## 2. Resignation, removal, vacancy - compared with the President
Resignation to | Vice-President | President (Art 67(a)), effective immediately
Removal | Impeachment, Art 61, either House, 2/3 | Art 67(b): resolution only in RS, by majority of all its then members (effective majority); LS agrees by simple majority; 14 days' notice; no grounds stated

★ President removed by impeachment (Article 61)
## Executive
★ Article 53(1) — executive power of the Union vested in the President
★ PM — appointed by the President; head of the Council of Ministers
★ Convention: the person commanding majority support in Parliament is invited to head the government
★ Article 54 — election of the President; Article 75 — appointment of PM and Council of Ministers
★ A non-member can join the Cabinet for up to 6 months (Article 75(5)) — membership is not restricted to MPs
## PM facts
★ Lal Bahadur Shastri — died outside India, in Tashkent (11 January 1966); second PM
★ Chandra Shekhar — never a Chief Minister before becoming PM
★ PM — President of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
★ Gandhi Peace Prize jury includes the PM, the CJI and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (not the President)
★ Prize instituted in 1995 (125th birth anniversary of Gandhi); jury of five
★ During a National Emergency the President does not acquire discretionary powers; acts on the Council of Ministers' advice
★ Real executive power in the parliamentary form — Prime Minister (Article 75)
★ All executive power vested in the President
★ Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the House of the People — a constitutional obligation, Article 75(3)
★ 91st Amendment Act, 2003 — Council of Ministers incl. PM capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha's total membership
★ Inserted Article 75(1A) (Union); amended Article 164 — clause (1A): State ministry incl. CM within 15% of the Assembly
★ Before 2003 the number of ministers was not in the Constitution (PM's/CM's discretion)
★ Aims: curb the size of ministries; strengthen anti-defection law
★ APPSC key credited the 97th Amendment with "limiting cabinet size to 10%"; the 97th Amendment (2011) actually dealt with cooperative societies
★ Cabinet = PM + Ministers of Cabinet rank only; the supreme decision-making body
★ Article 75 — appointment of the Council of Ministers
★ 75(1) — President appoints PM, and other Ministers on the PM's advice; 75(2) — office during the President's pleasure
★ Article 77(3) — business rules; the President allocates portfolios among Ministers on the PM's advice
★ Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — first Deputy PM (15 Aug 1947 – 15 Dec 1950); also Home Minister; integrated 500+ princely states
★ Office of Deputy PM — not in the Constitution; an extra-constitutional growth (political necessity)
★ Naming a Deputy PM is a political decision; confers no power of the PM
★ Order: Gulzari Lal Nanda (caretaker, 1966) → Indira Gandhi → Morarji Desai → Charan Singh → Rajiv Gandhi → Chandrashekhar
★ Chaudhari Charan Singh — PM (28 July 1979 – 14 Jan 1980); never attended the Lok Sabha (Congress withdrew support)
★ Jawaharlal Nehru — a Prime Minister (odd one out among Presidents)
★ Held PM office more than once: Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Gulzari Lal Nanda (acting, twice), Atal Bihari Vajpayee
★ Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha only (Article 75(3)), though Ministers may be from either House
★ Constitutionally all Ministers in the Union Council are equal; Cabinet/State/Deputy hierarchy is informal practice
★ M. Venkaiah Naidu — Vice-President at the time of the APPSC question
★ Council collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; Ministers hold office at the President's pleasure (not the PM's)
★ More than once with gaps: Gulzarilal Nanda, Indira Gandhi, Atal Bihari Vajpayee (not Nehru or Shastri)
★ Nanda: 27 May – 9 June 1964 and 11–24 January 1966

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

content.text:
STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Legislative Procedure – Ordinary, Money, Financial and Constitutional Amendment Bills; Joint Sitting

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Bills – Basics
A Bill is proposed legislation; it becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Article 111).
Article 79: Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha. The President is an integral part of Parliament but not a member of either House.
Ordinary Bill: in either House. Money Bill: only in the Lok Sabha. Creation of a new All-India Service starts with a Rajya Sabha resolution (Art. 312).
## Articles at a Glance
Article | Provision
107–108 | Ordinary Bills; 108 = Joint sitting
109 | Special procedure for Money Bills
110 | Definition of Money Bill
111 | Assent to Bills
112 | Annual Financial Statement (Budget)
113 | Demands for Grants
114 | Appropriation Bill
116 | Vote on Account
117 | Special provisions as to Financial Bills
118(4) | Speaker presides over joint sitting
119 | Regulation by law of financial business
121 | Restriction on discussion in Parliament
200 / 201 | Governor's / President's assent to State Bills
368 | Constitutional amendment
# Government Bill vs Private Member's Bill
Feature | Government Bill | Private Member's Bill
Introduced by | A minister | Any MP who is not a minister (not necessarily nominated)
Notice | 7 days | 1 month
Drafted by | Concerned department with the Law Ministry | The member
Defeat | Signals loss of confidence | No bearing on the government
Same procedure: Government and Private Members' Bills pass through the same readings and stages in each House.
Lok Sabha: time is allotted by the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions; it classifies them and examines private members' constitutional amendment bills before introduction.
Rajya Sabha has no such committee; its Business Advisory Committee allots time.
Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law; the last in 1970.
# Ordinary Bill – Stages and President's Assent
## Three Readings in Each House
Stage | What happens
First reading | Leave to introduce; introduction; title and objectives read; published in the Gazette
Second reading | General discussion → committee stage (select/joint committee) → consideration stage: clause-by-clause voting on amendments
Third reading | Bill accepted or rejected as a whole
APPSC 2018: General discussion on a Bill takes place at the Second Reading – not the First or Third.
## Second House
Same three stages. It may pass, amend, reject or keep it pending for 6 months → deadlock → joint sitting.
For an ordinary Bill the second House has no time limit; for a Money Bill the Rajya Sabha has 14 days.
## President's Options – Article 111
Bill | Assent | Withhold | Return for reconsideration
Ordinary Bill | Yes | Yes | Yes (once)
Money Bill | Yes | Yes | No
Financial Bills I and II | Yes | Yes | Yes
Constitutional Amendment Bill | Must assent (24th CAA, 1971) | No | No
Suspensive veto: if a returned Bill is re-passed, with or without amendment, the President must assent.
Pocket veto: no time limit is fixed → possible. India has no qualified veto.
A Money Bill is normally assented to, because it is introduced on the President's recommendation.
# Money Bill – Articles 109 and 110
## Definition – Art. 110(1)
A Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only these matters:
1. Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
2. Regulation of borrowing by the Government of India.
3. Custody of the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund, and money into or out of them.
4. Appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI).
5. Declaring any expenditure charged on the CFI.
6. Receipt, custody or audit of money of the CFI or Public Account.
7. Matters incidental to the above.
## NOT Money Bills – Art. 110(2)
Bills only for fines or penalties.
Fees for licences or fees for services.
Taxes by local bodies for local purposes.
## Procedure
Introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Art. 109(1)), only by a minister, only on the President's recommendation (APPSC 2019).
Speaker certifies it; the decision is final (Art. 110(3)); no need to consult anyone. The certificate is endorsed when sent to the Rajya Sabha (Art. 109) and to the President (Art. 111).
Rajya Sabha: only recommends within 14 days; cannot amend or reject. Lok Sabha is not bound to accept the recommendations (Art. 109(2)). Not returned in 14 days → deemed passed by both Houses.
No joint sitting; President cannot return it.
Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill: Rajya Sabha need not pass it; it is treated as passed if not returned in 14 days.
AP angle: the AP Legislative Council also only recommends on a Money Bill within 14 days; it cannot reject or amend it finally. Article 200: a Governor cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
## Aadhaar Cases
Case | Year | Holding
K.S. Puttaswamy | 2018 | Upheld the Aadhaar Act passed as a Money Bill
Rojer Mathew | 2019 | Money Bill question referred to a larger 7-judge bench
# Money Bill vs Financial Bills vs Finance Bill
## Article 117 – Three Categories of Financial Bills
Money Bills (Art. 110), Financial Bill (I) (Art. 117(1)), Financial Bill (II) (Art. 117(3)).
Feature | Money Bill (Art. 110) | Financial Bill I (Art. 117(1)) | Financial Bill II (Art. 117(3))
Art. 110 matters | Only | Some, plus general matters | None – only spending from CFI
Speaker's certificate | Required | Not required | Not required
House of introduction | Lok Sabha only | Lok Sabha only | Either House
Who introduces | Minister only | Minister only | Minister or private member
President's recommendation | At introduction | At introduction | At consideration stage only
Rajya Sabha | Recommend only (14 days) | Amend or reject | Amend or reject
Joint sitting | Not allowed | Allowed | Allowed
President can return | No | Yes | Yes
In FB-I: an amendment reducing or abolishing a tax needs no recommendation; one increasing a tax needs it.
Finance Bill: gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals; usually certified as a Money Bill.
"No Bill imposing tax without the President's recommendation" – Article 117.
Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.
Not all financial bills start only in the Lok Sabha: FB-II can start in either House. A Bill only involving expenditure can start in either House.
# Bills by House of Introduction and Prior Recommendation
Cannot originate in the Rajya Sabha: Money Bills and Financial Bills (I).
Bill | Article | President's prior recommendation
New States, alter boundaries/names | Art. 3 | Required (either House)
Money Bills and FB-I | Art. 117(1) / 110 | Required
FB-II / expenditure from CFI | Art. 117(3) | Before consideration
Taxation in which States are interested | Art. 274 | Required
State level: a Bill restricting inter-state trade needs the President's previous sanction before introduction in a State legislature.
# Budget – Articles 112–117
Annual Financial Statement = Article 112; prepared by the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement but cannot vote on the Demands for Grants (Art. 113); voting is only in the Lok Sabha.
Appropriation Bill (Art. 114) – no withdrawal from CFI without it.
Vote on Account (Art. 116) – grant in advance for part of the year until the budget is passed.
FIRST Union budget of independent India: 26 November 1947, by R.K. Shanmukham Chetty.
## Cut Motions (only in Lok Sabha)
Motion | Reduction | Purpose
Policy cut | Demand reduced to Re 1 | Disapproval of the policy
Economy cut | By a specified amount | Economy in spending
Token cut | By Rs 100 | A specific grievance
Guillotine: on the last day allotted, all remaining demands are put to vote without discussion.
# Joint Sitting – Article 108
## Grounds (deadlock after one House passes a Bill)
1. The other House rejects it.
2. Houses finally disagree on amendments.
3. More than six months pass without it being passed (prorogation and adjournments of over 4 consecutive days are excluded).
Summoned by the President, who "notifies his intention" to summon it; then neither House proceeds further with the Bill.
If the President does not summon it → the Bill comes to an end (APPSC G2 2017).
Presides: Lok Sabha Speaker (Art. 118(4)) → Deputy Speaker → Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman → member chosen by those present.
Quorum: one-tenth of total membership; decided by simple majority of members of both Houses present and voting together.
Excluded: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills (Art. 368). Applies to ordinary bills; Financial Bills I and II can go.
The Vice-President / Rajya Sabha Chairman does NOT preside over a joint sitting.
## Joint Sittings Held (only three)
Year | Bill
1961 | Dowry Prohibition Bill
1978 | Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill
2002 | Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA)
# Constitutional Amendment Bill vs Ordinary Bill
Feature | Ordinary Bill | Constitutional Amendment Bill (Art. 368)
House | Either House | Either House
Introduced by | Minister or private member | Minister or private member
President's prior recommendation | Not needed (except listed cases) | Not needed
Majority | Simple majority | Special majority – majority of total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting, in each House separately
State ratification | No | Half the States for federal provisions
Deadlock | Joint sitting possible | No joint sitting
President | Assent / withhold / return | Must give assent
Latest: Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 (One Nation One Election, new Article 82A) – still with the JPC, not passed; opposition argues the government lacks a two-thirds majority (Aug 2026).
# Lapsing of Bills – Dissolution, Prorogation, Adjournment
## On Dissolution of Lok Sabha
Lapses | Does not lapse
Bill pending in Lok Sabha (originated there or sent by RS) | Bill pending in Rajya Sabha, not yet passed by LS
Bill passed by LS, pending in RS | Bill for which a joint sitting was notified before dissolution
Bill passed by RS, pending in LS | Bill passed by both Houses, pending assent
— | Bill returned by the President for reconsideration
Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
No joint sitting can be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed; a joint sitting already summoned is held as scheduled even after dissolution.
APPSC G1 2024: "A Bill passed by LS but not taken up in RS does not lapse" = FALSE.
## Effect of Other Events
Event | Bills | Motions / notices
Adjournment / adjournment sine die | Do not lapse – taken up next session (APPSC 2025) | Continue
Prorogation | Do not lapse | Pending notices lapse, except notices for introducing Bills
Dissolution | As in the table above | All pending Lok Sabha business lapses
# Latest and State Angle
Monsoon Session 2026: 12 Bills passed; FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 referred to a JPC; Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 (Art. 3, to "Keralam") passed by RS; RS returned several money bills to the Lok Sabha.
Governor (Art. 200): assent, withhold, return a non-Money Bill, or reserve for the President (Art. 201).
Tamil Nadu Governor judgment (April 2025): "deemed assent" and fixed timelines. November 2025 advisory opinion (five-judge Bench, Presidential Reference): courts cannot fix timelines or declare deemed assent.
AP: Andhra State Bill introduced in Parliament 10 Aug 1953; assent 14 Sep 1953.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Correct Fact
RS time limit on Money Bill | 14 days
Notice – govt / private bill | 7 days / 1 month
Private Members' Bills made law | 14 (last 1970)
Joint sittings held | 3 (1961, 1978, 2002)
Joint sitting quorum | One-tenth
Delay ground for joint sitting | 6 months
Token cut | Rs 100
Policy cut | Re 1
Aadhaar bench | 7 judges (Rojer Mathew, 2019)
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First joint sitting: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition); last: 2002 (POTA).
First Union budget: 26 Nov 1947, R.K. Shanmukham Chetty.
Only Bill whose certificate makes the Speaker's word final: Money Bill (Art. 110(3)).
Only Financial Bill that may start in Rajya Sabha: FB-II.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 1 Prelims 2024, Paper 1 | Bills; Consolidated Fund
Group 1 Prelims 2024, Paper 1 | Bills; Sessions of Parliament – lapse on dissolution
APPSC GS 2025 | Effect of adjournment sine die on Bills
APPSC GS 2019 | Money Bill introduced only by a minister in LS
APPSC GS 2018 | General discussion = Second Reading
Group 2 2017 | Joint sitting not summoned – Bill ends
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Art. 108 vs 109: joint sitting vs Money Bill procedure.
2. Joint sitting chaired by the Speaker, not the Vice-President.
3. No joint sitting for Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills; FB I and II can go.
4. RS holds a Money Bill 14 days at most; ordinary Bill – no time limit.
5. Fines, licence fees, local taxes – not Money Bills.
6. President cannot return a Money Bill; can return FB I and II.
7. Bill passed by LS and pending in RS lapses on dissolution.
8. Prorogation and adjournment sine die do not end Bills.
9. FB-II can start in either House; recommendation needed only at consideration.
10. Puttaswamy 2018 upheld; Rojer Mathew 2019 referred to 7 judges.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Bills → types: government vs private member's
Government bill | Private member's bill
Introduced by a minister | Any MP who is not a minister
7 days' notice | 1 month's notice (one month's notice)
Drafted by department with Law Ministry | Drafted by the member
Rejection signals loss of confidence | Defeat has no bearing on / does not affect the government
LS committee: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
Classifies them, allots time, examines constitutional amendment bills by private members before introduction
RS has none → its Business Advisory Committee (BAC) allots time
Record: Only 14 private members' bills have become law, the last in 1970
# Ordinary bill → stages and President's assent (Art. 111)
## 1. Introduction and readings
Introduction: In either House (government bill: by a minister, 7 days' notice; private member: 1 month)
Three readings in each House (APPSC-GS 2018):
First reading | Leave to introduce; introduction; title and objectives; published in the Gazette
Second reading | General discussion → committee stage (select/joint committee) → consideration/report stage: clause-by-clause voting on amendments
Third reading | Bill accepted or rejected as a whole; no amendments of substance [GK]
## 2. Second House
Transmission: Same stages in second House; may pass, amend, reject, or keep it for 6 months
Deadlock: → joint sitting
## 3. President's assent - Art. 111
Options: Give assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration (non-money bills only)
Re-passage: If re-passed with or without amendment → President must assent
Pocket veto: No time limit fixed → "pocket veto" possible
# Money Bill → Article 110 provisions, procedure and cases
## 1. Contents - Art. 110(1)
Scope: Deals only with Art. 110(1) matters
Tax: imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, regulation
Borrowing by GoI
Custody of Consolidated/Contingency Fund + money in or out of them
Appropriation from CFI; declaring expenditure charged
Receipt/custody/audit of CFI or Public Account money; incidental matters
Not money bills: Fines/penalties, fees for licences or services, taxes by local bodies for local purposes
## 2. Procedure
Art. 110(3) | Speaker certifies it; decision is final
Art. 109 | Certificate endorsed when sent to the RS; Rajya Sabha must return within 14 days with or without recommendations
Art. 111 | Certificate endorsed when sent to the President; President may assent or withhold but cannot return for reconsideration
Introduction: Only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, only on the President's recommendation (APPSC-GS 2019)
Rajya Sabha: LS may accept or reject its recommendations; if not returned → deemed passed
No joint sitting
President: In practice assents, since introduced on his recommendation (some notes say he "cannot withhold")
## 3. Aadhaar cases
K.S. Puttaswamy | 2018 | Upheld Aadhaar Act passed as a Money Bill
# Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill
Art. 110 matters | Exclusively | Partially, plus other matters | Not at all - only expenditure from the CFI
House of introduction | Only LS | Only LS | Either House
Rajya Sabha | Recommend only | Amend or reject | Amend or reject
President returns it? | Cannot | Can | Can
FB-I amendments:
Amendments reducing/abolishing a tax need no recommendation
Amendments increasing a tax need the President's recommendation
Finance Bill: Gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals; usually certified a Money Bill
Relation: Every money bill is a financial bill vs not every financial bill a money bill
⚠ Trap: Some notes reverse the definitions and say all financial bills start in LS only → FB-II can start in either House
# Articles → House of introduction and President's prior recommendation
Only in the Lok Sabha (cannot originate in RS): Money Bills and Financial Bills (I)
Bills to form new states or alter boundaries/names | Art. 3 | Required (either House)
Money bills and FB-I | Art. 117(1) | Required
FB-II / bills involving expenditure from the CFI | Art. 117(3) | Before consideration
Bills affecting taxation in which states are interested | Art. 274 | Required
State level: No bill restricting inter-state trade can be introduced in a state legislature without the President's previous sanction
# Joint sitting → Article 108 provisions and instances
## 1. Grounds (deadlock)
After one House passes a bill, the other:
Rejects it
Houses finally disagree on amendments
Does not pass it for more than six months (6 months); periods of prorogation/adjournment over 4 consecutive days excluded

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Parliamentary Form of Government – Features, Merits, Demerits; Comparison with Presidential System

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Meaning of Parliamentary Government
Also called cabinet or responsible government: stays in power while it has a majority in the popular House.
Based on cooperation and co-ordination of legislature and executive (fusion of powers); presidential = separation of powers.
India adopted the British model (influenced by the UK); parliamentary system at the Centre and in the States; both get power from the Constitution.
Defining test: India is parliamentary because the executive is responsible to the legislature (Council of Ministers headed by PM, to the Lok Sabha) – A and R both true, R explains A (UPPSC 2025).
# Features of Parliamentary Government (india)
1. Nominal and real executive: President = de jure head (Head of State); PM + Council of Ministers = real executive. Executive powers of the Union are vested in the President.
2. Art. 74(1): President acts on aid and advice; advice binding.
3. Majority party rule: leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha becomes PM.
4. Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75); ministers individually responsible to the President.
5. Dual membership: ministers must be MPs; a non-member must enter Parliament within six months, else stops being minister.
6. Leadership of the PM: heads Council of Ministers; Leader of the Lok Sabha; chief spokesperson.
7. Dissolution of the lower House possible.
8. Government can be removed by Parliament (no-confidence); ministers stay while they keep its confidence.
The President is not the real head of the executive (APPSC G2 2017). India is not a presidential system.
India is democratic and has a written constitution, but the written constitution does not explain democracy (UK is democratic without one).
# Presidential System – Features
President = Head of State and Head of Government; single executive; power centralised.
Directly elected; fixed term; removable only by impeachment.
Not accountable to the legislature; cannot dissolve the legislature.
Appoints his own Council of Ministers (secretaries); US secretaries do not sit in the legislature.
APPSC G2 2025 key: head of State, head of Government, directly elected = correct; "accountable to the legislature" = wrong.
## Parliamentary vs Presidential
Parliamentary | Presidential
Nominal head + real head (PM) | One person is both heads
Collective executive (cabinet) | Single executive
Fusion of powers; ministers are legislators | Separation of powers
Removable by no-confidence | Fixed tenure; only impeachment
Lower House can be dissolved early | No dissolution
# Origin Countries and Semi-presidential Systems
System | Origin | Examples
Parliamentary | Britain (Westminster model) | UK, Japan, Canada, India
Presidential | USA – oldest and purest form | USA, Brazil, most of Latin America
Semi-presidential | — | France (Fifth Republic, 1958), Russia, Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)
Semi-presidential: directly elected President with real powers + PM responsible to the legislature; both may be from different parties.
India's President is indirectly elected and nominal – India is not semi-presidential.
Westminster | Britain | Parliamentary
Oldest presidential | USA | Presidential
# India vs Britain
Feature | India | Britain
Head of State | Indirectly elected President, 5 years | Hereditary monarch
Supremacy | Constitutional supremacy (written Constitution) | Sovereignty of Parliament
Constitution | Written | Unwritten (conventions)
Judicial review | Courts can strike down laws; basic structure | Courts cannot question Acts of Parliament
PM from | Either House | House of Commons
Ministers | Six months as non-member allowed | Must be MPs
Shadow cabinet / legal responsibility of ministers | No | Yes
Latest: UK PM Keir Starmer announced resignation as PM and Labour leader. UK: ruling party can replace the PM; India: removal needs loss of Lok Sabha confidence.
# India vs Usa
Feature | India | USA
Executive | Parliamentary | Presidential
Residuary powers | Parliament (Union) | States
Judicial review | Narrower – "procedure established by law" | Wider – "due process of law"; SC called a "third chamber"
Term limit | None for PM | 22nd Amendment (1951)
Common: written Constitution, federal structure, independent judiciary with judicial review, Fundamental Rights / Bill of Rights.
Latest: on 22 March 2026, Narendra Modi completed 8,931 days as head of an elected government, passing Pawan Kumar Chamling (8,930).
# Merits and Demerits
System | Merits | Demerits
Parliamentary | Responsible government – executive continuously accountable; harmony; fresh elections break deadlock | Unstable coalitions; no fixed tenure; ministers not specialists; cabinet dictatorship with large majority
Presidential | Stable, fixed-term executive | Executive-legislature deadlock; personality cult
Main advantage of parliamentary government: executive stays responsible to the legislature (collective responsibility, Art. 75).
# Constituent Assembly's Choice
Familiarity under the 1919 and 1935 Acts.
India's vast size and diversity.
Avoid US-style executive-legislature conflict and a personality cult.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar: a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility; India chose responsibility over fixed tenure.
# Presidential System Debate in India
Person / body | Contribution
Vasant Sathe | Proposed a presidential form, 1970s-80s
NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02) | Advised keeping the parliamentary system
One Nation, One Election: amendments to Arts 83, 172, 327; critics say fixed tenures graft presidential mechanics and weaken accountability.
Shamsher Singh (1974): Governor publicly criticising Cabinet policy runs "counter to the Parliamentary system"; Governor's discretion also rests on parliamentary logic.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
Non-member minister | 6 months
Advice binding | Art. 74(1)
France Fifth Republic | 1958
Sri Lanka Constitution | 1978
US term limit | 22nd Amendment, 1951
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First parliamentary form: Britain; first presidential: USA.
Longest-serving elected head (22 Mar 2026): Narendra Modi, 8,931 days.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 1 | President – features of presidential system
Group 2 2017 | President is not real head of executive
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Presidential executive is not accountable to the legislature.
2. Residuary powers: India – Union, USA – States.
3. "Procedure established by law" = India; "due process" = USA.
4. PM from either House in India; Commons only in UK.
5. Shadow cabinet is British only.
6. Semi-presidential: France, Russia, Sri Lanka – not India.
7. Ambedkar: responsibility over stability.
8. NCRWC kept the parliamentary system.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Parliamentary government — meaning and features
Basis: India adopted the British parliamentary system = cooperation and co-ordination of legislature and executive
vs presidential system = separation of powers
Features:
Nominal and real executive: President = de jure head; PM + Council of Ministers = de facto executive (Art. 74(1): ministers aid and advise; advice binding)
Majority party rule: leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha becomes PM
Dual membership: ministers must be MPs; a non-member must be elected within six months
Leadership of the PM/CM + dissolution of the lower House possible
Responsibility: ministers individually responsible to the President
⚠ Trap: the President is not the real head of the executive (APPSC-G2 2017 key)
Exam angle: Assertion-Reason: "India is parliamentary because the executive is responsible to the legislature" - both true, R explains A (UPPSC 2025).
# Countries → system of government
Presidential | USA (origin) | Brazil, most of Latin America
Semi-presidential | — | France, Russia, Sri Lanka
France (Fifth Republic, 1958) + Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution): directly elected President with real powers + PM responsible to the legislature
⚠ Westminster = Britain; presidential origin = USA
# Presidential and semi-presidential systems → features
## 1. Presidential system
President = both Head of State and Head of Government; single executive
Directly elected; fixed term
Not accountable to the legislature
⚠ Trap: APPSC-G2 2025 key: correct = head of State, head of Government, directly elected; "Accountable to the legislature" is wrong
Cabinet: members may or may not sit in the legislature (US secretaries do not)
## 2. Parliamentary vs presidential
Collective executive (cabinet) | Single executive (President)
Fusion of powers; ministers are members of the legislature | Separation of powers
Executive responsible to the legislature; can be removed by no-confidence | Fixed tenure; removable only by impeachment [GK]
Lower House can be dissolved early | No dissolution of the legislature [GK]
## 3. Semi-presidential system
Concept: President + PM coexist, possibly from different parties
India vs: India's President is indirectly elected and nominal
# India vs Britain and USA → feature comparison
## 1. Indian vs British parliamentary system
Head of State | Indirectly elected President, 5-year term | Hereditary monarch
Supremacy | Constitutional supremacy - Parliament bound by a written Constitution | Sovereignty of Parliament - can enact or repeal any law
Constitution | Written | Unwritten (conventions) [GK]
Judicial review | Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws | Courts cannot question Acts of Parliament (CDI)
State structure | Federal | Unitary
PM | From either House | From the House of Commons
Sources: LENS (Jun 2026); CDI
Membership: Britain - ministers must be MPs vs India allows six months as a non-member
Britain only: legal responsibility of ministers + institutionalised shadow cabinet; India has neither
Both: PM's role grown so much that scholars call it "Prime Ministerial Government"
## 2. India vs USA
Residuary powers | Parliament (Union) (IYB) | States[GK]
Division of powers | Three lists - Union, State, Concurrent (strong centre) [GK] | Enumerated federal powers; rest with states [GK]
Judicial review | Narrower - "procedure established by law" | Wider - "due process of law"; SC called a "third chamber" (APP)
⚠ "Procedure established by law" = India; "due process of law" = USA
# Merits, demerits and the Constituent Assembly's choice
## 1. Merits and demerits
Parliamentary | Responsible government; executive continuously accountable; executive-legislature harmony; fresh elections break deadlock | Unstable coalitions, no fixed tenure, ministers not always specialists, cabinet dictatorship when majority is large
Presidential | Stable, fixed-term executive | Executive-legislature deadlock; danger of a personality cult around a single executive
## 2. Why the Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary form
Reasons:
Familiarity with the system under the 1919 and 1935 Acts
Avoid US-style executive-legislature conflict
Risk of a personality cult under a single executive
# Persons, commissions and Articles → the presidential-system debate
Person / body | Statement / contribution
Dr B.R. Ambedkar | A democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility; India chose responsibility (continuous accountability) over guaranteed tenure
Vasant Sathe | Early proposals for a presidential system, 1970s-80s
NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02) | Reviewed the question; advised keeping the parliamentary system
One Nation, One Election: amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327
Critics: fixing tenures grafts presidential mechanics onto parliamentary democracy + weakens accountability
# Universal angles
Current relevance: UK PM Keir Starmer announced resignation as PM and Labour leader
UK: ruling party can replace the PM vs India: removal needs loss of Lok Sabha confidence
Criticism & debates: on 22 March 2026, Narendra Modi completed 8,931 days as head of an elected government, passing Pawan Kumar Chamling (8,930)
India: no term limit vs US: 22nd Amendment (1951)
Significance: Governor's discretion also rests on parliamentary logic
Shamsher Singh (1974): Governor publicly criticising Cabinet policy runs "counter to the Parliamentary system"

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Supreme Court – Composition, Appointment, Collegium, Njac and Jurisdictions

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Establishment and Constitutional Basis
Part V, Chapter IV – Articles 124-147.
Article 124: establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court (Court of Record is Art. 129, not 124).
Federal Court set up 1937 (GoI Act, 1935); Privy Council appeals abolished 1949.
SC replaced the Federal Court and the Privy Council's Judicial Committee on 26 Jan 1950; first sitting 28 January 1950 (two days later), in part of the old Parliament House.
Moved to its Tilak Marg building in 1958.
Art. 130: seat at Delhi, or elsewhere as the CJI decides with the President's approval. No regional benches yet.
Custodian / guardian of the Constitution through judicial review; final interpreter and guardian of Fundamental Rights.
Benches usually 2 or 3 judges; Constitution Bench ≥ 5 (Art. 145(3)); Art. 145 – SC frames its own rules.
Art. 348(1)(a): all SC and HC proceedings in English.
1937 Federal Court; 1949 Privy Council appeals end; 26 Jan 1950 SC replaces it; 28 Jan 1950 first sitting; 1958 Tilak Marg. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, not a court.
# Number of Judges – Article 124(1)
Parliament alone increases the number, by ordinary law (simple majority) – APPSC-G2 2025 key. Law: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956.
Year | Strength (incl. CJI)
1950 | 8 (CJI + 7)
1977 | 18
1986 | 26
2009 | 31
2019 (Amendment Act 37 of 2019) | 34 (CJI + 33)
16 May 2026 | 38 (CJI + 37) – Ordinance
6 May 2026: Cabinet approved four more judges. Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 (Art. 123), notified 16 May 2026, replaced "thirty-three" with "thirty-seven"; a Bill to replace it was listed for the Monsoon Session 2026.
Older figure 34 (2019) is out of date; present sanctioned strength 38 (May 2026).
# Appointment, Qualifications, Tenure
## Appointment – Art. 124(2)
President appoints judges after consulting the CJI and such judges as he thinks needed; consulting the CJI is compulsory for other judges (an autonomy safeguard).
CJI appointed by the President (APPSC-GS 2025 key); by convention the senior-most judge; the collegium only recommends.
Convention broken: A.N. Ray (1973), M.H. Beg (1977); Second Judges Case later upheld the senior-most convention.
## Qualifications – Art. 124(3)
Citizen of India and: 5 years as HC judge, or 10 years as HC advocate, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion – never used in 76 years (Justice Bhuyan, 31 Aug 2026).
L. Nageshwara Rao – not earlier an HC judge; 7th elevated directly from the Bar.
## Tenure, Oath, Resignation
Retire at 65; age determined as Parliament provides by law (Art. 124(2A), 15th Amendment 1963).
Oath before the President (form in Third Schedule) – to uphold the Constitution and the law. Resignation in writing to the President.
CJI has no fixed term in years – serves till 65.
Salaries fixed by Parliament by law (Art. 125(1)); until then, Second Schedule.
Oath (Art. 124(6)): an SC judge takes the oath before the President or a person appointed by the President for this purpose.
# Acting, Ad Hoc and Retired Judges
Article | Who | Appointed by
126 | Acting CJI | President
127 | Ad hoc judge (qualified HC judge) – when no quorum | CJI with President's previous consent, after consulting the HC Chief Justice
128 | Retired judges sitting | CJI with President's prior consent + judge's consent
Art. 128 judge has full powers of an SC judge but is not deemed a regular judge.
No additional judges in the SC – additional and acting judges only in High Courts (Art. 224).
APPSC-G2 2025 key only statement i (Art. 128: CJI, with the President's prior consent, may request a retired SC judge, who must also agree); statement ii on HC review power was rejected. Ad hoc judge is appointed by the CJI, not by the President on collegium advice.
# Judges Cases, Collegium and Njac
## Judges Cases
Case | Year | Holding
First – S.P. Gupta | 1981 | Consultation ≠ concurrence; executive primacy
Second – SCAORA | 1993 | Consultation = concurrence; judicial primacy; collegium born (CJI + 2)
Third – Presidential Reference (Art. 143(1)) | 1998 | Collegium CJI + 4 senior-most; plural consultation; if two give adverse opinion, name not sent
Fourth – SCAORA (NJAC case) | 2015 | NJAC and 99th Amendment struck down; collegium restored
Assertion-Reason: the Second Judges Case created the collegium BECAUSE it held consultation means concurrence (R explains A).
## Collegium
Not in the Constitution, not created by an Act – judicially evolved (adopted 1993; present form since 1998).
Formal appointment by the President – SC judges Art. 124(2), HC judges Art. 217(1).
Zero executive members; Government (IB checks) may return a name once – bound to appoint if reiterated.
Collegium | Members | Handles
Supreme Court | CJI + 4 senior-most (5 members) | SC appointments; HC transfers (with CJs of both HCs)
For HC appointments (SC side) | CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges | HC judges and HC Chief Justices
High Court | HC Chief Justice + 2 senior-most HC judges | Initiates HC appointments
June 2026 collegium: CJI Surya Kant, Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh, P.S. Narasimha (joined after J.K. Maheshwari retired, 29 Jun 2026).
## NJAC – 99th Amendment, 2014
99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 + NJAC Act, 2014; inserted Art. 124A (APPSC-GS 2022).
Stage | Date
Passed Lok Sabha | 13 Aug 2014
Ratified | 16 States
Assent | 31 Dec 2014
In force | 13 Apr 2015
Struck down | 16 Oct 2015
Six members: CJI (Chairperson), 2 senior-most SC judges, Union Law Minister, 2 eminent persons (chosen by PM, CJI and Leader of Opposition; one from SC/ST/OBC/minority/women). Attorney-General NOT a member.
Fourth Judges Case: 5-judge bench led by J.S. Khehar, 4:1; lone dissent J. Chelameswar (upheld NJAC). Ground: executive role hurt judicial independence – Basic Structure. India has no NJAC now.
Earlier attempt: Constitution (98th Amendment) Bill – National Judicial Commission, brought by Arun Jaitley (Law Minister, NDA).
## Transfers and Memorandum of Procedure
Art. 222: President transfers HC judges (incl. Chief Justices) after consulting the CJI.
MoP: CJI + 2 recommend HC Chief Justices (from outside parent HC) → Law Minister → State consulted → President appoints after consulting CJI and Governor.
Sep 2026: Punjab Cabinet objected that the State was bypassed in appointing the Punjab and Haryana HC Chief Justice.
# Jurisdictions → Article
Jurisdiction | Article | Key point
Original | 131 | Centre-State, State-State legal disputes; exclusive
Writ | 32 | FRs only; original but not exclusive (HC Art. 226)
Appellate | 132 / 133 / 134 | Constitutional / civil / criminal
Special leave | 136 | Any court or tribunal except military (136(2))
Review | 137 | Own judgments; subject to Parliament's law and Art. 145 rules
Advisory | 143 | Opinion not binding
President / VP election | 71 | Original, exclusive, final
Enlarged Union List jurisdiction | 138(1) | By Parliament
## Original Jurisdiction – Art. 131
Only disputes on legal rights between Centre and States or between States – SC as a federal court; main body for Centre-State fiscal disputes.
Excluded: inter-State water disputes (Art. 262); Finance Commission matters (Art. 280); pre-Constitution treaties; political questions; Art. 290 expense adjustments; private party suits for damages against the Union; disputes between private companies; Centre-UT disputes; election disputes of Parliament and Legislatures (go to High Courts – APPSC-G1 2022 key "II and III").
## Appellate Jurisdiction
Art. 132 (with 134A certificate): constitutional interpretation cases.
Art. 133: civil – substantial question of law of general importance, HC certificate.
Art. 134: HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death – appeal as of right, no certificate.
Art. 134(2): Parliament may by law enlarge the SC's criminal appellate jurisdiction.
Art. 136 SLP: discretionary, plenary, residual; needs no HC certificate.
## Advisory – Art. 143
143(1): President refers questions of law or fact of public importance; Court may give opinion. Only the President can seek it.
143(2): pre-Constitution treaty matters – Court must give opinion.
Examples: Gujarat Assembly elections delay – reference by President Abdul Kalam (Aug 2002); 16th Presidential Reference (Nov 2025) on Bill timelines.
# Special Powers
Article | Power
129 | Court of Record, power to punish contempt
141 | Law declared binding on all courts
142 | Complete justice – not constrained by ordinary laws; no HC equivalent (Anil Kumar Jain v. Maya Jain)
145 | Rules; ≥ 5 judges for constitutional questions
Art. 142 uses: deemed assent to 10 TN Bills (2025); ban on liquor shops near highways (2016); Right to Safe Travel under Art. 21 with nationwide directives (27 May 2026).
Curative petition: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002); after a review (Art. 137) is dismissed; inherent power anchored in Art. 142.
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (H.N. Sanyal Committee) defines civil and criminal contempt; the Constitution does not define it.
e-SCR – electronic Supreme Court Reports; free digital database of reported judgments, launched 2023.
V.V. Giri appeared in person before the SC as sitting President in a petition challenging his election.
# Removal of Judges
Art. 124(4): by order of the President after an address by Parliament; grounds proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Special majority in each House in the same session – majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting.
Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 (Art. 124(5)): motion signed by 100 LS / 50 RS members; Speaker / Chairman may admit or reject; 3-member committee (SC judge/CJI, an HC Chief Justice, a distinguished jurist).
Constitution says "removal"; "impeachment" only for the President (Art. 61). Neither the CJI nor the President alone can remove a judge.
Office | Article
SC judge / HC judge | 124(4) / 218
CAG / CEC – removed like an SC judge | 148 / 324(5)
Judge | Outcome
V. Ramaswami (1993) | Motion failed in Lok Sabha
Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC, 2011) | Rajya Sabha passed it; resigned (1 Sep 2011) before LS vote
Yashwant Varma (2026) | Speaker to table inquiry report despite his resignation (11 Jul 2026)
No judge removed so far.
In-House Procedure (1999), after C. Ravichandran Iyer (1995), for misconduct short of removal; Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997), 16 points.
# Independence Safeguards
Safeguard | Provision
Security of tenure | Removal only per Art. 124(4) / 217
Salaries | Fixed by Parliament (Arts 125, 221); not cut after appointment except Financial Emergency (Art. 360)
Expenses | SC salary and pension – Consolidated Fund of India; HC salary – State fund, HC pension – CFI
Conduct not discussed | Parliament (Art. 121), State Legislature (Art. 211), except on removal motion
Post-retirement practice | Retired SC judge – no court or authority (Art. 124(7)); retired HC judge – only SC and other HCs (Art. 220)
Contempt power | Art. 129 / 215
Judicial independence is part of the Basic Structure – why NJAC fell.
# High Court vs Supreme Court
Basis | High Court | Supreme Court
Strength fixed by | President (216) | Parliament (124(1))
Appointment | President by warrant (217) – not the Governor | President by warrant (124)
Oath | Governor (219) | President
Resignation | President | President
Retirement | 62 | 65
Court of Record | 215 | 129
Writs | FRs + legal rights (226); superintendence (227) | FRs only (32)
SC review of own judgments | – | Art. 137
Advisory | None | 143
HC Articles: 214 HCs for States, 216 constitution, 217 judges, 233 District Judges. AP High Court at Amaravati since 1 Jan 2019.
# Chief Justices and Firsts
Fact | Person
First CJI | H.J. Kania (Harilal Jekisundas); then M. Patanjali Sastri
First woman SC judge | M. Fathima Beevi (1989) – also first Muslim woman in higher judiciary
Longest-serving | Y.V. Chandrachud, 16th CJI, 22 Feb 1978 – 11 Jul 1985
Shortest | Kamal Narain Singh, 18 days (25 Nov – 12 Dec 1991)
CJIs from AP | K. Subba Rao (1966-67), N.V. Ramana (2021-22)
Present CJI | Surya Kant (from 24 Nov 2025, after B.R. Gavai)
Other short tenures: R.M. Lodha (Apr-Sep 2014), S. Rajendra Babu (May 2004), G.B. Pattanaik (Nov-Dec 2002).
A.S. Anand – 29th CJI (1998-2001); S.H. Kapadia – 2010; S.A. Bobde – 47th (Nov 2019); D.Y. Chandrachud – 50th; Khare – CJI in 2002.
Fathima Beevi later became the first woman member of the NHRC (1993-97; first chairperson was Ranganath Misra) and the first Muslim woman Governor (Tamil Nadu).
# Reform Proposals and India vs Usa
Body | Recommendation
Law Commission, 14th Report (1958) | Appoint Bar members directly; not strictly by seniority
Law Commission, 214th Report (2008) – not 1998 | Review appointment procedure
NCRWC – Venkatachaliah (set up 2000, report 2002) | National Judicial Commission
Parliamentary Standing Committee (2023) | MoP to ensure women and marginalised candidates
Reforms: Judicial Standards and Accountability law, permanent disciplinary authority, asset disclosure, RTI (administrative side) – not abolition by executive notification.
Criticism: collegium "imperium in imperio", judges selecting judges; transparency debate revived by Justice Ujjal Bhuyan (26 Aug 2026).
P. Wilson's (DMK) private member's Bill (19 Feb 2026): social diversity, 90-day limit to notify names, regional benches.
Point | India | USA

143(2): SC must (is bound to) tender its opinion on pre-constitutional disputes
Opinions are strictly advisory — not binding on the President
The 16th Presidential Reference (Nov 2025) answered questions on bill timelines (see B-37)
Article 141: Law declared by the SC is binding on all courts in India
Article 142: Pass any decree or order for complete justice in any cause pending before it — unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations
Curative petition: Evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) — from the SC's inherent powers anchored in Article 142
Available after a review petition (Article 137) is dismissed; prevents abuse of process and cures gross miscarriage of justice

=== Complete2 notes ===
## History and placement
Federal Court set up 1937
Supreme Court inaugurated 28 January 1950 (two days after the Constitution came into force, 26 January)
Shifted to Tilak Marg building in 1958
Constitution: Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147)
## Strength (including the CJI)
Year | Strength
1950 | 8
2026 Ordinance | 38 (37 + CJI)
Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 — notified 16 May 2026 under Article 123; judges other than CJI raised from 33 to thirty-seven
## Judges: appointment, tenure, pay
Distinguished jurist route — in the opinion of the President; never used; must be a citizen of India
NJAC — six members, to be chaired by the CJI; Attorney-General not a member
Article 128 retired judge sitting in SC — has SC judge's powers but is not deemed a regular judge
SC judge retires at 65, resigns in writing to the President; HC retirement age 62
CJI — no fixed tenure in years, serves until 65; oath before and resignation to the President
HC judges' pension — charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (salaries on the State fund)
## Reports and courts
Law Commission 214th Report — submitted 2008 (not 1998)
NCRWC (Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah, set up 2000) — report 2002; recommended a National Judicial Commission
AP High Court at Amaravati since 1 January 2019
## Key Articles
Article 129 — Court of Record, power to punish contempt; Article 130 — seat at Delhi
Article 145(3) — Constitution Bench, at least five judges: hears substantial questions of constitutional interpretation and Article 143 references; Article 143 opinion does not bind the President
## CJI tenures
Shortest-serving CJI — Kamal Narain Singh, 18 days (25 November–12 December 1991)
Chandrachud served over seven years
## The Judges Cases
First (S.P. Gupta) | 1981 | Consultation does not mean concurrence; executive primacy
Second (SCAORA v. Union of India) | 1993 | Reversed 1981; consultation means concurrence; created the (two-judge) collegium; judges' primacy
Third (Presidential reference) | 1998 | Collegium enlarged to CJI + four senior-most judges; plural consultation; settled working of collegium
Fourth | 2015 | Struck down the NJAC
Collegium — judicial creation of the Three Judges Cases; no express constitutional mention
Assertion-Reason: Second Judges Case gave birth to the collegium because it held consultation means concurrence (R explains A)
## NJAC and the 99th Amendment
99th Constitutional Amendment, 2014 — inserted Article 124A (NJAC); sought to replace the collegium
Ratified by 16 States; assent 31 December 2014; in force 13 April 2015
Struck down in 2015 — executive role infringed judicial independence, part of the Basic Structure (R explains A)
Fourth Judges Case 4:1; lone dissent J. Chelameswar (upheld NJAC); Bench led by J.S. Khehar
## Appointment, transfer, misconduct
Formal appointment — Article 124(2) (SC judges) and Article 217(1) (HC judges), by the President
Transfer of an HC Chief Justice — Article 222
In-House Procedure (1999) — followed C. Ravichandran Iyer (1995); for misconduct not warranting removal
Retired HC judge may plead only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (Article 220); Article 124(7) bars a retired SC judge altogether
Reform ideas: judicial standards and accountability law, permanent disciplinary authority, asset disclosure, RTI (administrative side), transparent appointments — not abolition of the collegium by executive notification
## Jurisdiction and comparisons
Article 131 — federal disputes only; a dispute between private companies is outside it
Election disputes concerning Parliament and State Legislatures go to the High Courts
'Procedure established by law' (India) — narrower review than US 'due process of law' (substantive + procedural); US Court called a 'third chamber'
Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court (1935 Act) and the Privy Council's Judicial Committee; Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, not a court
Government may return a name once; bound to appoint if the collegium reiterates
HC appointments initiated by the HC Chief Justice + two senior-most HC judges, then to CJI + two senior SC judges
SC collegium — five members: CJI + four senior-most judges; no executive member
## Jurisdiction map
★ SC has Original (Article 131), Appellate (Articles 132–136) and Advisory (Article 143) jurisdiction
Article | Subject
32 | Writ jurisdiction
71 | Presidential / Vice-Presidential election disputes — original, exclusive and final
131 | Original jurisdiction
132 | Constitutional appeals
133 | Civil appeals
134 | Criminal appeals
136 | Special leave
137 | Review of its own judgments or orders
141 | SC law binding
142 | Orders for complete justice (SC only; no HC equivalent)
143 | Advisory jurisdiction
★ V.V. Giri — appeared in person before the SC as incumbent President, in a petition challenging his election (corrupt practices)
## Appeals
Article 134 — HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death: appeal lies as of right, no HC certificate
Article 136 — special leave discretionary, against any judgment of any court or tribunal, except military tribunals (136(2)); needs no HC certificate
Article 137 review = the Court's own judgments, distinct from judicial review of statutes
Curative petition — after dismissal of a review under Article 137; rests on inherent powers under Article 142
## Advisory (Article 143)
143(1) — President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance; Court may give its opinion
143(2) — pre-Constitution treaty/agreement matters: Court must give its opinion
Advice does not bind the President
## Appointment and transfer
CJI appointed by the President (Article 124(2)); by convention the senior-most judge; collegium only recommends
Article 222 — HC judge transferred by the President after consulting the CJI
Collegium in June 2026 — CJI Surya Kant, Justices Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh, P.S. Narasimha; J.K. Maheshwari had retired

Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 — defines civil and criminal contempt; the Constitution confers contempt powers but does not define contempt
"Imperium in imperio" — criticism of the collegium as an authority within an authority (opacity, judges selecting judges)
Private member's Bill — social diversity, 90-day limit for the Centre to notify collegium names, regional benches of the SC
US Supreme Court has no writ jurisdiction equivalent to Article 32
India synthesises American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
Longest-serving CJI — Y.V. Chandrachud (16th CJI), 22 February 1978 – 11 July 1985
Article 131 — only disputes on legal rights between the Centre and States or between States (the core of 131)
Excluded: inter-State water disputes (Article 262), Finance Commission matters (Article 280)
Private party suing the Union for damages — goes to ordinary courts, not Article 131
126 | Acting CJI

HC Chief Justice appointment begins with CJI + two senior-most SC judges, then Law Minister, State, appointment by President

HC judge retires at 62; SC judge at 65
## Removal
SC judge — Article 124(4); HC judge — Article 218
CAG (Article 148) and CEC (Article 324(5)) removed like an SC judge
No SC judge removed so far; motion against V. Ramaswami failed; Soumitra Sen resigned after Rajya Sabha passed the motion

SC judge — salary and pension both on the Consolidated Fund of India
HC judge — salary on the State's Consolidated Fund; pension on the Consolidated Fund of India

215 | HC Court of Record
216 | Constitution of HCs
217 | HC judges
226 | HC writ power
227 | Superintendence of HCs
233 | District Judges
Removal motion — signed by 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members
Constitution uses 'removal', not 'impeachment', for judges
Article 121 — judge's conduct discussed in Parliament only on a removal motion
Removal address needs special majority in each House (majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting), not simple majority
Grounds — proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Judges' salaries fixed by Parliament by law; cannot be cut after appointment except in a Financial Emergency (Article 360)
First CJI — H.J. Kania; M. Patanjali Sastri came after him
CJIs from Andhra Pradesh — K. Subba Rao (1966-67) and N.V. Ramana; P. Wilson linked to a private member's Bill on judicial diversity, not CJI

Second Judges Case later affirmed the senior-most convention

system.text:
You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.
