STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Finance Commission – Composition, Terms of Reference, Functions; 15TH and 16TH Finance Commission

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Nature and Constitutional Basis
Finance Commission (FC) = constitutional body under Article 280, Part XII.
Quasi-judicial body; the anchor of fiscal federalism.
Not permanent: constituted by the President within two years of the start of the Constitution, then every fifth year or earlier when necessary (Art. 280(1)).
Independent; recommendations advisory, not binding.
P.V. Rajamannar (4th FC) view: recommendations should not be rejected without very compelling reasons.
## Articles – Number Game
Article | Provision
280 | Constitution, composition and functions of the FC
280(2) | Parliament fixes qualifications by law
281 | President lays recommendations + explanatory memorandum on action taken before each House of Parliament
290 | Pensions – NOT the FC
APPSC-G2 2025: "Article 290 provides for the Finance Commission" is INCORRECT – it is Article 280.
# Composition and Qualifications
Chairman + four other members (5 in all), appointed by the President (Art. 280(1)).
Term: as the President specifies; members are eligible for reappointment; no fixed term in the Constitution.
Qualifications fixed by Parliament in the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951 – NOT by the President or the Union Cabinet.
Has powers of a civil court: summoning persons, production of documents.
## Qualifications – FC (Misc. Provisions) Act, 1951
Post | Qualification
Chairman | Experience in public affairs
Member | High Court judge or qualified to be one
Member | Special knowledge of government finance and accounts
Member | Wide experience in financial matters and administration
Member | Special knowledge of economics
No member post for an expert in monetary policy operations.
NOT "a Chairman and six members"; the FC does NOT report to NITI Aayog – it reports to the President.
# Functions – Article 280(3)
1. Distribution of net proceeds of taxes between Centre and States (vertical) and among States (horizontal).
2. Principles of grants-in-aid to States from the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 275).
3. Measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement resources of Panchayats and Municipalities (on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations).
4. Any other matter referred by the President in the interest of sound finance.
Main function: decide the share of States in central taxes.
Divisible pool = gross tax revenue − cesses, surcharges and cost of collection; net amount certified by the CAG.
Rising cesses and surcharges shrink the divisible pool.
The FC does not fix GST rates and does not itself release funds; it only recommends.
# Finance Commissions → Chairman, Award Period, Share
FC | Chairman | Award period | States' share
1st | K.C. Neogy | 1952–57 | –
10th | K.C. Pant | 1995–2000 | 29% (Alternative Scheme of Devolution)
11th | A.M. Khusro | 2000–05 | 29.5%
12th | C. Rangarajan | 2005–10 | 30.5%
13th | Vijay Kelkar | 2010–15 | 32%
14th | Y.V. Reddy | 2015–20 | 42%
15th | N.K. Singh | 2020–21 + 2021–26 | 41%
16th | Arvind Panagariya | 2026–27 to 2030–31 | 41% retained
First FC: constituted under a Presidential order in 1951; set up 6 April 1952.
M.V. Mathur (member, 3rd FC, 1960) suggested joining the Finance and Planning Commissions.
Dr. Manmohan Singh was never Chairman of a Finance Commission.
15th FC award period "2020-25" is a trap: correct = 2020-21 (first report) + 2021-26.
# 14TH Finance Commission (2015–20)
Constituted 2 January 2013; recommendations for 1 April 2015 – 31 March 2020; GoI accepted the report on 24 February 2015.
Share raised 32% → 42% = largest increase ever.
Made tax devolution the main route (not grants); ignored the Plan/non-Plan distinction.
Made no distinction between special and general category States.
Population base: 1971 and 2011.
Criteria: income distance 50%, population 1971 17.5%, population 2011 10%, area 15%, forest cover 7.5%.
Local-body grants ₹2,87,436 crore (panchayats ₹2,00,292 crore), as basic and performance grants.
After 42%, the Centre increased non-shareable cesses.
# 15TH Finance Commission (2020–26)
Formed 27 November 2017; Chairman N.K. Singh.
First FC to cut the vertical share: 42% → 41% due to the change in J&K's status.
Used 2011 population only (not 1971).
Added two new criteria: demographic performance and tax effort.
Local-body grants ₹4.36 lakh crore; urban local bodies share 36%.
# Vertical vs Horizontal Devolution
## Meaning
Vertical devolution | Centre ↔ States | share of divisible pool (41%)
Horizontal devolution | among States | criteria and weights
## Horizontal Criteria → Weight (%)
Criterion | 15th FC | 16th FC
Income distance | 45 | 42.5
Population (2011) | 15 | 17.5
Area | 15 | 10
Forest and ecology | 10 | 10
Demographic performance | 12.5 | 10
Tax and fiscal effort | 2.5 | dropped
Contribution to GDP | – | 10 (new)
16th FC: highest weight = income distance (42.5%).
16th FC is the first to use a Contribution to GDP criterion.
16th FC forest criterion now includes open forests too.
NUMBER GAME: 32 → 42 → 41 → 41 (13th → 14th → 15th → 16th)
# 16TH Finance Commission (2026–31)
## Constitution and Terms of Reference
Constituted 31 December 2023; Chairman Arvind Panagariya; award 2026-27 to 2030-31.
Members: T. Rabi Sankar, Annie George Mathew, Manoj Panda, Soumya Kanti Ghosh.
Terms of reference came straight from the Constitution, without detailed Central directives.
Population base 2011 (demographic performance measured against 1971).
## Report and Recommendations
Report to the President November 2025; tabled in Parliament 1 February 2026 (Budget day).
Devolution accepted by the Centre in the Budget 2026-27 speech; States got the full 41%; total transfers ₹25.44 lakh crore for 2026-27.
41% applies only to the divisible pool (excludes cesses, surcharges, cost of collection).
Total grants ₹9.47 lakh crore; revenue-deficit grants discontinued.
Local-body grants ₹7.91 lakh crore: rural ~₹4.35 lakh crore, urban ~₹3.56 lakh crore (= 45%); urbanisation premium ₹10,000 crore.
Disaster corpus ₹2.04 lakh crore; sharing 90:10 NE/Himalayan States, 75:25 others.
Heatwaves and lightning proposed as new notified disasters.
State deficits capped at 3% of GSDP.
All five southern States gained: Karnataka 4.131% (15th: 3.64%; 14th: 4.71%), Tamil Nadu 4.097%.
Kerala: fiscal stress – neither revenue deficit grants nor State-specific grants.
## Criticism and Debates
Rising cesses and surcharges are kept out of the divisible pool, so the real share of States in gross tax revenue is lower than 41%.
Southern States call the use of population and income distance unfair to better-performing States, even though all five gained under the 16th FC.
Ending revenue-deficit grants hurts States such as Andhra Pradesh and Kerala, which must now cut their revenue deficits on their own.
Local-body grants need duly constituted elected bodies, which pushes States to hold timely ULB and panchayat elections.
Devolution is "tax sharing" (formula-based, untied); grants are "transfers for a purpose" – the 14th FC shifted the weight from grants to tax sharing.

Grants under Art. 275 are for needy States; the FC does not decide Plan transfers.
# Special Category Status
Introduced in 1969 on the recommendation of the 5th Finance Commission (Mahavir Tyagi); funds allotted by the Gadgil formula (NDC).
First States: Assam, Jammu & Kashmir, Nagaland.
Criteria: hilly and difficult terrain, low population density or large tribal share, strategic border location, economic and infrastructure backwardness.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Civil Society, Ngos, Shgs and Pressure Groups in Governance; Fcra Regulation

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Civil Society – Meaning and Role
Civil society = pressure groups + trade unions + NGOs; the "third sector" alongside the State (first) and market (second).
World Bank: NGOs, unions, faith-based groups, professional associations, foundations.
CSOs = development partners and democratic watchdogs.
Shift: welfare delivery → rights and empowerment; service delivery → advocacy, policy formulation, watchdog work (e.g. ADR on candidate disclosure).
APPSC 2019 key: NGOs as "observationalists in development" (standard texts call them partners of government).
# Pressure Groups – Definition and Types
Organised group influencing public policy without contesting elections or seeking office; presses government, legislators, bureaucracy for one section's interest.
Also called interest groups, lobby groups; label: "Anonymous Empire".
Almond and Powell: institutional, associational, non-associational, anomic.
## Types → Indian Examples
Type | Examples
Business | FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM
Trade union | AITUC, INTUC, CITU, BMS, HMS
Professional | Indian Medical Association, Bar associations
Peasant | Bharatiya Kisan Union, All India Kisan Sabha
Caste | Maratha, Gujjar, Patel quota groups
Religious / student | Faith bodies; student unions
APPSC 2007 key: most powerful pressure group = AITUC (texts often rank business groups first).
## Pressure Group vs Political Party
 | Political party | Pressure group
Elections | Contests; answers to voters | Does not contest; answers to members
Scope | Whole range of policy | One section's interest

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Human Rights in the Indian Constitution; Protection of Human Rights Act 1993

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Fundamental Rights As Human Rights
Right to vote = statutory only.
Article | Content | UDHR
14 | Equality before law | Art. 7
19 | Six freedoms, 19(1)(a)-(g); citizens only | Arts. 13, 19, 20, 23
21 | Life, personal liberty | Art. 3
21A | Education 6-14 (86th CAA, 2002); both human and fundamental right | Art. 26
23 | Traffic, begar, forced and bonded labour | Art. 4
24 | No child below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work | Arts. 4, 25(2)
32 | Remedies: "Heart and Soul" (Ambedkar) | Art. 8
Art. 12 "State"; 13 judicial review; 15(4) by First Amendment; 17 untouchability; 18 titles; 29-30 minorities; Art. 40 = DPSP.
Citizens + foreigners: 14, 20, 21, 23, 25-28.
Right against Exploitation = Arts. 23 + 24.
# Article 21 Read by Courts
Right | Case
Legal aid | M.H. Hoskot (1978)
Speedy trial | Hussainara Khatoon (1979)
Dignity | Francis Coralie (1981)
Livelihood | Olga Tellis (1985)
Clean environment | Subhash Kumar (1991)
Arrest safeguards | D.K. Basu (1997)
Privacy | K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)
# DPSPs, Duties and Treaties
UDHR reflected in Preamble (justice, equality, liberty), DPSPs and Fundamental Duties (UPSC 2020: all three).
Article | Provision
39(a) / 39(d) | Livelihood / equal pay
42 | Humane conditions, maternity relief
43 | Living wage
51A(e) | Renounce practices derogatory to women
51(c) | Respect international law (DPSP)

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: United Nations – Principal Organs, Unga, Unsc and Reform; India's Candidature

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Un Charter and Membership
Signed by 50 nations at San Francisco, 26 June 1945; Poland ratified on 16 Oct 1945 as the 51st original member.
In force 24 October 1945 = UN Day (81st anniversary in 2026).
Members: 193.
Six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, Spanish. Working languages: English and French.
Amendment (e.g. UNSC reform): two-thirds of members, incl. ratification by all P5.
## Key Articles
Article | Provision
Art. 1 | Purposes – peace and security, friendly relations, cooperation, harmonising action
Art. 2 | Sovereign equality
Art. 18 | UNGA "important questions" = two-thirds majority
Art. 23 | No immediate re-election of a retiring non-permanent UNSC member
Art. 27 | Veto of the P5
Hindi is NOT an official UN language. Purposes = Art. 1; sovereign equality = Art. 2.
# Principal Organs
Organ | Composition / mandate
General Assembly | All members, one vote each
Security Council | 15 members; only body whose decisions bind members
ECOSOC | 54 members, 3-year terms; economic, social, SDG coordination
Trusteeship Council | Inactive since 1994, after Palau became self-governing
ICJ | Principal judicial organ; The Hague
Secretariat | Headed by the Secretary-General
Amnesty International is an NGO, not part of the UN. GA, ICJ and Trusteeship Council are principal organs.
## ECOSOC Functional Commissions
Commission on the Status of Women (1946) – CSW-70 held 2026.
Commission on Sustainable Development – reviewed Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration; replaced by the High-Level Political Forum in 2013 (APPSC 2018).
Others: Statistical Commission, Commission on Narcotic Drugs.
# Security Council
P5: China, France, Russia, UK, USA – veto (Art. 27); only P5 have veto.
10 non-permanent members: elected by UNGA, two-thirds secret ballot, for 2 years; no immediate re-election.
Germany is NOT a permanent member.
April 2024: full UN membership for Palestine – vetoed by the USA; UK and Switzerland abstained (BPSC 2024).
# General Assembly
One member, one vote; important questions need two-thirds (Art. 18).
Credentials Committee: 9 members appointed each session.
Uniting for Peace (Res. 377), 1950: lets UNGA act when a veto blocks the UNSC; first used in the 1956 Suez Crisis to send peacekeepers.
Emergency special sessions: e.g. the 10th – resolution ES-10/23 (10 May 2024) upgraded Palestine's rights as an observer State, without vote.
Non-member observer States (2): Holy See (since 1964) and State of Palestine (2012, res. 67/19).
81st UNGA President (2026-27): Khalilur Rahman (Bangladesh), defeating Cyprus.
Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit – President of the UNGA.
22 May 2026 climate resolution: India abstained (141-8-28), citing the ICJ's July 2025 opinion.
Uniting for Peace was adopted in 1950, not 1956 (1956 = first use).
# Sanctions and Counter-terrorism Committees
Resolution | Year | Subject
1267 | 1999 | Sanctions on Al-Qaida / ISIL (Da'esh); terrorist listings
1373 | 2001 | Counter-Terrorism Committee (after 9/11)
1540 | 2004 | Stopping WMD reaching non-state actors
Masood Azhar (Jaish-e-Mohammed) listed under the 1267 Committee (APPSC-G1 2019).
AP angle: India's first UNSCR 1540 capacity-building programme for Asia-Pacific – NACIN, Palasamudram (AP), Feb 2025.
# Unsc Reform
Group | Members / demand
G4 | Brazil, Germany, India, Japan – permanent seats, plus permanent seats for Africa
Uniting for Consensus ("Coffee Club") | Led by Italy; includes Pakistan; opposes new permanent seats
L.69 | Developing countries of Asia, Africa, Latin America, Pacific; India a member
Ezulwini Consensus (2005) | African Union: 2 permanent seats with veto + 5 non-permanent
IGN (Inter-Governmental Negotiations): informal UNGA process (not a UNSC body), set up 2008; annual "Elements Paper" maps agreements and disagreements.
India's PR criticised the 2026 Elements Paper and demands text-based negotiations (June 2026).
China opposes India's permanent seat; China is not in the G4 – already permanent (APPSC-G1 2012).
# Secretaries-general

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Environmental Degradation As A Development Challenge; Green Accounting and Green Gdp

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Functions of the Environment
Function | Meaning
Supplies resources (first function) | Both renewable (trees, fish) and non-renewable (fossil fuels)
Assimilates waste | Absorbs and neutralises wastes
Sustains life | Genetic and biodiversity
Aesthetic services | Scenery and amenity
First function of the environment = supply / production of raw materials (APPSC-GS 2023 key).
Absorptive capacity = power to take in degradation = maximum pollutants an ecosystem can process and neutralise without harm (APPSC-GS 2024 key).
Crisis comes when extraction > regeneration and waste > absorptive capacity; the environment then cannot sustain life. The world is at the threshold of an environmental crisis.
"Supplies renewable resources only" is wrong. Recycling is NOT a function of the environment; nor is "it disorganizes waste that benefits human life".
# Resource Depletion and Its Causes
## Key terms
Resource depletion = use faster than regeneration (APPSC-GS 2024 key: B).
A forest managed sustainably for timber while keeping biodiversity is NOT depletion.
## Resource -> cause (APPSC-GS 2025 match)
Resource | Cause
Groundwater | Deep bore tubewells for irrigation
Topsoil | Brick production
Biodiversity habitats | Expansion of agriculture
# Causes of Environmental Degradation
## Human-driven causes vs conservation practices
Human-driven causes | NOT causes (conservation)
Deforestation (APPSC-GS 2024 key) | Sustainable agriculture
Chemical-intensive farming | Renewable energy production
Groundwater over-extraction, dams | Wildlife conservation
Road and urban expansion, industrial emissions, overfishing | 
India's two threats: poverty-induced degradation + pollution from affluence and rapid industrial growth.
## Causes by sector
Factor | Effect
Green Revolution: HYV monoculture + chemical fertilisers | Cut soil fertility
HYV irrigation needs | Water-table depletion
Fertiliser, pesticide, herbicide use | Polluted land, water, air + reduced biodiversity
Soil: Urea = ~56% of fertiliser use | Overuse degrades soil and water
Air: urban particulate pollution + coal-based power | Main reasons for India's low EPI score
Urea alternative: green urea (green hydrogen + captured CO2) = low-carbon.
# Environmental Kuznets Curve
Feature | Fact
X-axis | Per capita income
Y-axis | Environmental degradation (pollution)
Shape | Inverted U
Logic | Pollution rises at low income, falls after a turning point
Named after | Simon Kuznets (his original curve: income inequality)
First shown for environment | Grossman and Krueger (1991)
Kuznets Curve = income vs inequality; Environmental Kuznets Curve = income vs degradation. Both inverted U.
# Growth vs Environment Debate
View | Argument
Trade-off view | Environmental rules slow growth; "grow first, clean up later" (EKC logic)
Necessity view | Degradation raises health costs and lowers labour efficiency (World Bank estimates)
Conventional GDP ignores depletion, so growth can hide loss of natural capital.
# Green Economy and Green Gdp
Green economy = reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcities; development decoupled from resource use and pollution; builds green industries and green jobs (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
Green jobs = preserve or restore environmental quality.
Green GDP = conventional GDP adjusted for environmental consequences = GDP net of natural-resource depletion and degradation costs.
Uttarakhand = first State to adopt green GDP, as Gross Environment Product (GEP).
# Green Accounting Frameworks
Person / body | Contribution
Sir Partha Dasgupta | Chaired the Expert Group on Green National Accounts (set up 2011, report 2013)
Paul Samuelson | NEW (Net Economic Welfare)
Nordhaus and Tobin | MEW (Measure of Economic Welfare)
World Bank | Developed the Green Index; 2013 cost-of-degradation estimate
MoSPI | Environment accounts on UN SEEA; EnviStats India
SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) Central Framework adopted by the UN Statistical Commission in 2012.
MoSPI ecosystem and natural-asset accounts released since 2018.
EnviStats India (annual) - six components: conditions and quality; resources and use; residuals; extreme events; human settlements and health; protection and management.
# Policy Tools
Tool | Year | Provision
EIA | First used 1978 (river valley projects) | -
EIA Notification | 1994, revised 2006 | Clearance compulsory for 39 project categories
Green Credit Rules | 2023 | Under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
AP angle: AP Common Zoning Regulations 2026 - development-restricted: forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas, CRZ. AP has 638 green building projects.
# Cost of Degradation and Land Degradation Data
## Cost to India
World Bank (2013): India's annual cost of environmental degradation about 5.7% of GDP (Rs 3.75 lakh crore, for 2009).
How: higher healthcare spending + lower labour productivity.
## Global
About one-third of global land transformed by humans; 60%+ of rivers dammed or diverted; about 40% of land degraded.
## ISRO-SAC Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021)
Period | Degraded area
2003-05 | 94.53 Mha (28.76%)
2011-13 | 96.40 Mha (29.32%)
2018-19 | 97.85 Mha (29.77%)
Leading processes: water erosion (10.98%), vegetation degradation (8.91%).
Desertification rose in 28 of 31 States/UTs between 2011-13 and 2018-19.
Restoration: 21.76 Mha restored in 2011-2020 (461.14 Mt carbon), beating the original Bonn pledge; Telangana first (4.18 Mha); AP among the top five.
AP districts: Anantapur, Kurnool and Kadapa are the most desertification-vulnerable.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Correct Fact
India's degraded land (2018-19) | 97.85 Mha = 29.77%
Water erosion / vegetation degradation | 10.98% / 8.91%
Land restored 2011-2020 | 21.76 Mha
Cost of degradation (World Bank 2013) | 5.7% of GDP
Urea share of fertiliser use | ~56%
EIA project categories (2006) | 39
Expert Group on Green National Accounts | 2011 / 2013
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First function of environment: supply of raw materials.
First State with green GDP: Uttarakhand (GEP).
First in land restoration: Telangana (4.18 Mha).
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
APPSC-GS 2023 | First function of the environment
APPSC-GS 2024 | Absorptive capacity; resource depletion; deforestation as cause; odd-one-out of causes
APPSC-GS 2025 | Green economy; resource -> cause match

For every PYQ return one result:

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: National Income Concepts – Gdp, Gnp, Ndp, Nnp, Factor Cost vs Market Price, Gva, Deflator

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Gdp – Definition and Elements
GDP = market value of all final goods and services produced within the geographical boundaries of a country during a year, whoever produces them (GS 2025 key).
Three elements: final goods only (no intermediate goods), domestic territory, time period (one year).
Gross = before deducting depreciation; Domestic = within the country irrespective of nationality.
GDP = Q x P; counts production by both residents and non-residents inside the territory.
GDP is place-based; it does NOT include NFIA.
National income = money value of final goods and services produced (no intermediate goods).
Income method: GDP = domestic factor incomes − transfer payments.
Hindu growth rate is related to GDP.
# Gnp and Gdp vs Gnp
## GNP
GNP (Gross National Product) = total money value of final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during a period, inside and outside the country's boundaries.
GNP is nationality/residence-based.
## Comparison
Basis | GDP | GNP
Based on | Domestic territory | Normal residents / nationals
Measures | Production within the country | Production by residents within and outside the country
Nature | Location-based | Residence-based
Indians earning abroad | Excluded | Included
Link | GDP = GNP − NFIA | GNP = GDP + NFIA
Main difference between GDP and GNP = net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
NFIA = factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad.
NFIA form: GNP = GDP + X − M (X = income of nationals abroad; M = income of foreigners in India).
## When one exceeds the other
Condition | Result
NFIA positive (residents earn more abroad than foreigners earn at home) | GNP > GDP
NFIA negative | GNP < GDP
NFIA zero | GNP = GDP
India: NFIA usually negative -> GNP lower than GDP.
An Indian resident's factor income earned in Saudi Arabia counts in India's GNP only, not GDP.
GDP is NOT equal to GNP – GNP considers nationality (factor income from abroad).
# Aggregates and Conversions
## Formula table
Aggregate | Formula
GNP | GDP + NFIA; also NNP + depreciation
NDP | GDP minus depreciation (not plus)
NNP | NDP + NFIA; also GNP − depreciation
NNP at MP | GNP at MP − depreciation
NNP (FC) | NNP (MP) − net indirect taxes
National Income | NNP at factor cost = NDP at FC + NFIA
National Income (long form) | GNP at MP − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies
National Income (from NNP) | NNP at MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies)
GDP at MP | GNP at MP − net income from abroad
Shortcut | NNP = GDP + NFIA − depreciation
## Three bridges
Bridge | Item | Rule
Domestic -> National | NFIA | GNP = GDP + NFIA
Gross -> Net | Depreciation | NDP = GDP − Dep; NNP = GNP − Dep
Market price -> Factor cost | Net indirect taxes | FC = MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies)
Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) is removed because output that only replaces worn-out capital is not new output.
## Path from GDP (MP) to National Income
1. GDP (MP)
2. + NFIA -> GNP (MP)
3. − depreciation -> NNP (MP)
4. − net indirect taxes -> NNP (FC) = National Income
National Income = NNP at factor cost – the standard measure.
# Factor Cost vs Market Price; Gva at Basic Prices
## Factor cost vs market price
MP = FC + indirect taxes − subsidies; FC = MP − indirect taxes + subsidies.
GDP at MP and GDP at FC differ by indirect taxes and subsidies – not direct taxes (APPSC-G2 2025).
Subsidies are added back when going from MP to FC; "− subsidies" in that step is the wrong sign.
## Production taxes vs product taxes
Type | Meaning | Examples
Production taxes | Levied irrespective of output | Land revenue, stamp duty, property tax
Product taxes | Levied per unit of product | Excise, sales tax/GST
## Three price levels
Step | Result
GVA at factor cost + net production taxes | GVA at basic prices
GVA at basic prices + net product taxes | GVA at market prices = GDP
GDP = GVA + taxes on products − subsidies (wider measure).
GVA vs NVA: GVA includes depreciation; NVA excludes it.
# Gva – Meaning and Headline Measure
GVA = value added by producers and sectors – a production-side measure; GDP = broader measure after net taxes on products.
Real GVA at constant prices (base year removes the effect of price changes); nominal GVA at current prices.
GVA at basic prices = headline sectoral measure since the 2011-12 series; still used in the 2022-23 series; NSO headline growth is on GVA at basic prices.
Sep 2026: Q1 2026-27 real GDP Rs 81.36 lakh crore vs real GVA Rs 73.82 lakh crore (difference = net product taxes).
# Inclusions and Exclusions
Included | Excluded
Wages and salaries, rent, profits, dividends, interest on productive loans | Transfer payments – pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance, prizes (no productive service in return)
Value added at each stage | Intermediate goods (double counting)
Commission on resale (payment for a productive service; NOT a transfer payment) | Second-hand sales (already counted when produced)
 | Interest on public debt, tax revenue (transfers, not factor payments)
 | Transfer earnings (not payments for factor services)
Factor income = wages, rent, interest, profit earned by the factors of production.
National income at factor cost = wages, rent, interest and profits of the country's normal residents.
Transfer payments are added back when moving from NI to personal income.
APPSC-G2 2025 A-R: Transfer earnings are excluded – both A and R true, R explains A.
# Personal, Disposable and Per Capita Income
## Derivation steps
Measure | Derivation
Personal Income | NI − undistributed corporate profits − social security contributions − corporate tax + government and business transfer payments + net interest paid by government
Personal Disposable Income | Personal income − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments (fines, fees) = what individuals can spend or save
National savings | National disposable income − consumption
Per Capita Income | National Income ÷ Population (APPSC 2025; GS 2025 key)
Per capita income = average income of a country; it rises only when NI grows faster than population.
## Flow vs stock
National income = flow (over a period); national wealth = stock (point of time).
## Growth measure
Sign of economic growth = sustained increase in real per capita income.
Most appropriate measure of economic growth = per capita real income (per capita product / per capita NNP).
Considered in growth: GDP, GNP, per capita GNP; NOT considered: growth in financial aid from World Bank.
# Nominal vs Real Gdp
Basis | Nominal GDP | Real GDP
Prices | Current-year prices | Constant / base-year prices
Includes price change | Yes | No
Better indicator of output growth | No | Yes
Real GDP = value of production at prices of a single (base) year.
Base year now 2022-23 (earlier 2011-12).
Example: nominal GDP 1,000 -> 1,200 while price index 100 -> 120 -> real GDP unchanged.
Prices and money income both doubled -> real income unchanged.
Nominal growth exceeds real by roughly the inflation rate; 2025-26: nominal 8.0% vs real 7.4% (estimates, old series).
Per capita income grows faster at current prices than at constant prices, because constant prices allow for the rise in price level.
# Gdp Deflator and Gnp Deflator
Item | Fact
GDP deflator | Nominal GDP / Real GDP x 100 = GDP at current prices / GDP at constant prices x 100 (APPSC-G2 2025)
GNP deflator | Ratio of nominal GNP to real GNP, as a percentage
Why most comprehensive | Covers all goods and services in GDP (consumption, investment, government, exports); WPI, CPI, CPI-IW use fixed baskets
Rising deflator | Higher prices -> purchasing power of money falls
GDP deflator = most comprehensive measure of inflation (G2 2025 key).
Double deflation (2022-23 series): deflates output and input prices separately for manufacturing and agriculture, replacing single deflation.
Sectoral deflators (2025-26): agriculture grew fastest -> services -> industry -> manufacturing; so manufacturing's nominal share fell while its real share stayed about 17-18%.
# New Gdp Series, Ppp and India's Rank
## New series
27 Feb 2026: NSO released the new GDP series (base 2022-23) with double deflation and Supply-Use Tables.
GDP at current prices: Rs 261.18 / 289.84 / 318.07 lakh crore for 2022-23 / 2023-24 / 2024-25.
## Purchasing Power Parity
PPP compares GDP by pricing a common basket at each country's own prices -> removes price-level differences.
Estimated under the International Comparison Program (ICP) of the UNSD; World Bank = global implementing agency; NSO = India's nodal agency.
India's PPP GDP is much larger than market-rate GDP because prices are lower in India.
## India's rank
Measure | India's rank
Nominal GDP, 2025 | 4th (overtook Japan; about USD 4.18 trillion)
Nominal GDP, IMF WEO April 2026 | 6th (USD 4.15 trillion)
PPP GDP | 3rd, after USA and China (ICP 2021)
Older facts: Japan was the third largest economy (UPPCS 2007); highest per capita income in World Development Report 2000 = Luxembourg ($44,640); in 2024 Singapore had the highest per capita GNI (PPP).
# State Domestic Product and Ap
State Domestic Product (APSES wording, asked word for word in APPSC-GS 2025) = aggregate economic value of all goods and services produced within the State's boundaries, counted without duplication, during a specified period, usually a year.
AP per capita income is computed on NSDP: Rs 2,68,653 vs India Rs 2,00,162 (2024-25 FAE).
Per capita GSDP = gross; per capita income = net -> compare gross with gross, net with net.
Goa = highest per capita income among Indian States; Bihar had the highest GSDP growth in 2010-11 among the States given.
Largest State economy (2024-25): Maharashtra has the largest GSDP among Indian States; Tamil Nadu is second.
# Investment Concepts – Saving, Multiplier, Accelerator
Concept | Meaning
Autonomous investment | Independent of income; driven by outside factors – new product, new technique, new market
Induced investment | Rises with income / demand for consumer goods
Gross vs net investment | Net = gross − depreciation; net addition to capital stock
Planned (ex-ante) vs unplanned | Unplanned = unintended change in inventories; realised = planned + unplanned
Saving-investment link | Equilibrium income where planned saving = planned investment
Multiplier (k) | k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS
Accelerator | Induced investment ÷ change in income; linked to J.M. Clark
If planned saving > planned investment, unsold goods pile up, output and income fall until saving = investment.
Gross investment that only covers depreciation -> net investment zero.
Multiplier works on MPC/MPS; accelerator works on the change in income, not its level.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Correct Fact
Example: GDP(MP) 500, Dep 50, NFIA −10, NIT 40 | GNP(MP) 490; NNP(MP) 440; NDP(FC) 410; NI 400
Example: GDP(MP) 110; Indians earn 20 abroad, foreigners 10 in India | NFIA +10 -> GNP 120; Dep 15 -> NNP 105; NIT 5 -> NI 100
Base year | 2022-23 (earlier 2011-12)
New series released | 27 Feb 2026
AP vs India per capita income (2024-25) | Rs 2,68,653 vs Rs 2,00,162
India's PPP rank | 3rd
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
National income proper: NNP at factor cost.
Most comprehensive inflation measure: GDP deflator.
Only bridge with subsidies: MP -> FC (subsidies added back).
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 2 | Investment, saving, multiplier concepts
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 2 | GDP deflator, inflation index
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 2 | GDP at MP vs FC – subsidies and taxes
Group 2 Mains 2025, Paper 2 | Transfer earnings A-R; GDP index
APPSC-GS 2025 | SDP definition; per capita income; GDP definition
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. National Income = NNP at FC, not GNP or GDP at MP.
2. NDP = GDP − depreciation, not plus.
3. MP vs FC differ by indirect taxes and subsidies, not direct taxes.
4. India's GNP < GDP because NFIA is negative.
5. Transfer payments and transfer earnings are excluded; commission on resale is included.
6. Interest on public debt and second-hand sales are excluded.
7. Rising GNP deflator decreases purchasing power of money.
8. Prices and money income both doubled -> real income unchanged.
9. GVA includes depreciation; NVA excludes it.
10. PPP nodal agency in India = NSO; global implementing agency = World Bank.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Terms → meaning (GDP, GNP, national income, SDP) — GDP
Stem | Term
Value of all final goods and services produced within the country in a year | GDP
Final output of the country's nationals/normal residents, wherever located | GNP
Wages, rent, interest, profit earned by the factors of production | Factor income
## 1. GDP
GDP definition: GDP = market value of all final goods and services produced within the geographical boundaries of a country during a year, whoever produces them (GS 2025 key)
GDP formula: GDP = Q x P; counts production by both residents and non-residents inside the territory
## 2. National income
Definition: NNP at factor cost = National Income
Total factor income (wages, rent, interest, profits) of a country's normal residents in a year
= Net domestic factor income + NFIA
Flow vs stock: National income = flow (per year); national wealth = stock
# Terms → meaning (GDP, GNP, national income, SDP) — State Domestic Product
## 1. State Domestic Product
State Domestic Product: Aggregate economic value of all goods and services produced within the State's boundaries, counted without duplication, during a specified period, usually a year (APSES wording; APPSC 2025; APSES 2024-25; GS 2025)
## 2. Other terms
Term | Meaning
Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) | Deducted because output that only replaces worn-out capital adds nothing new
NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad) | Factor income received from abroad - factor income paid abroad
Production taxes | Levied irrespective of output (e.g. land revenue, stamp duty, property tax)
Product taxes | Levied per unit of product (e.g. excise, sales tax/GST)
Transfer earnings | Not payments for factor services → not included in national income
Transfer earnings: APPSC-G2 2025 A-R: both true, R explains A
Comparative note: GDP = territorial; GNP = nationality/residence
# Aggregates → formula
Link | Formula
Domestic to National | GNP = GDP + NFIA (NFIA = factor income received from abroad - factor income paid abroad)
Gross to Net | NDP = GDP - Depreciation; NNP = GNP - Depreciation
Market price to Factor cost | FC = MP - Net Indirect Taxes (indirect taxes - subsidies)
National Income | NNP at FC = NDP at FC + NFIA
Aggregate | Derivation
GDP (MP) | Value of final output within domestic territory
NDP | GDP - Depreciation
GNP | GDP + NFIA
NNP (MP) | GNP - Depreciation
# Aggregates → formula — Market price vs factor cost
## 1. Market price vs factor cost
Difference: GDP at MP vs FC differ by indirect taxes and subsidies - not direct taxes (APPSC-G2 2025)
Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes - subsidies
GDPfc = GDPmp - Indirect taxes + Subsidies = GDP (FC) = GDP (MP) - indirect taxes + subsidies
⚠ Trap: Some notes print "- subsidies": sign is wrong - subsidies are added back
## 2. Three price levels
# Aggregates → formula — Personal, disposable and per capita income
## 1. Personal, disposable and per capita income
Personal Income: Personal Income = NI - undistributed corporate profits - social security contributions - corporate tax + government and business transfer payments + net interest paid by government.
Personal Disposable Income: Personal Disposable Income = Personal Income - personal direct taxes - non-tax payments (fines, fees) = what individuals can spend or save
National savings: National disposable income - consumption = national savings
Per Capita Income: Per Capita Income = National Income / Population (APPSC 2025; GS 2025 key)
PCI rises only when NI grows faster than population
# GNP vs GDP — rule and worked examples
## 1. When one exceeds the other
Rule: GNP > GDP when NFIA is positive (residents earn more abroad than foreigners earn at home); GNP < GDP when NFIA is negative
Indians abroad: Remittance-type factor income earned (e.g. Indians earning in Saudi Arabia) is excluded from GDP but included in GNP
## 2. Worked examples
Example 1: GDPmp 500, depreciation 50, NFIA -10, NIT 40
GNPmp = 490; NNPmp = 440; NNPfc (NI) = 400; NDPfc = 410
Example 2: GDP (MP) Rs 110 crore
Indians earn Rs 20 crore abroad; foreigners earn Rs 10 crore in India → NFIA = +10 → GNP = 120
Depreciation 15 → NNP (MP) = 105
Net indirect taxes 5 → NI = NNP (FC) = 100
Exam angle: numerical questions give GDP, NFIA, depreciation and net indirect taxes and ask for NI.
# Included vs excluded in national income
Wages and salaries, rent, profits, dividends, interest on productive loans | Transfer payments - pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance, prizes (no productive service rendered in return); added back when moving from NI to personal income
Commission on resale [GK] | Second-hand sales (already counted when produced) [GK]
⚠ Transfer earnings are not included in national income - not payments for factor services
# Nominal vs real GDP and the GDP deflator
## 1. Nominal vs real GDP
Nominal GDP: At current prices (includes price change)
Real GDP: At constant prices; values output at base-year prices; strips out inflation
Growth gap: Nominal growth exceeds real by roughly the inflation rate
2025-26: nominal 8.0% vs real 7.4% (estimates, old series)
## 2. GDP deflator
Formula: GDP deflator = Nominal GDP (current prices) / Real GDP (constant prices) x 100 = GDP at current prices / GDP at constant prices x 100 (APPSC-G2 2025)
Comprehensiveness: Most comprehensive measure of inflation (G2 2025 key)
Covers all goods and services in GDP (consumption, investment, government, exports), not a fixed basket like CPI/WPI
Purchasing power: Rising deflator = higher price level → purchasing power of money falls / lower purchasing power of money
GNP deflator: Same ratio for GNP
Double deflation (2022-23 series): Deflates both output and input prices for manufacturing and agriculture, replacing single deflation
Sectoral deflators (2025-26): Agricultural GDP deflator grew fastest → services → industry → manufacturing
Hence manufacturing's nominal share fell while real share stayed about 17-18%
# Data — GVA headline, PPP and India's rank

Q1 2026-27: Real GDP Rs 81.36 lakh crore vs real GVA Rs 73.82 lakh crore (difference = net product taxes) (Sep 2026)

Nominal (market exchange rate) GDP | 4th (overtook Japan in 2025, about USD 4.18 trillion)

AP angle:
APSES definition of SDP asked word for word in APPSC-GS 2025

NNP at factor cost = National Income
Based on | Domestic territory | Normal residents

# GDP and GNP — meaning and difference
GDP: The value of final goods and services produced within domestic territory
Gross: Before deducting depreciation
Domestic production: Within the country irrespective of nationality
## 2. GNP
Gross National Product (GNP): The total monetary value of final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during a given period
Includes production occurring inside and outside the country's boundaries
⚠ GDP is not equal to GNP — GNP considers nationality or factor income
## 3. GDP vs GNP
Based on | The domestic territory of a country | The normal residents or nationals of a country
Measures | Production within the country | Production by residents within the country and outside the country
## 4. Stems → term
# Terms → meaning (national income, SDP and other terms)
## 1. National income
## 2. State Domestic Product
## 3. Other terms
NDP | GDP minus (subtracting) depreciation
GNP | GDP plus (adding) Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA); also NNP plus depreciation
NNP — Net National Product | NDP plus NFIA; also GNP minus depreciation
NNP at market price | GNP at market price minus depreciation
National Income | NNP at factor cost = GNP at market price minus depreciation minus indirect taxes plus subsidies
## 1. Nominal vs real
Nominal GDP: Measured at current-year prices (includes price change)
Real GDP: Measured at constant or base-year prices — base-year prices are used to calculate it; real GDP growth is a better indicator of actual output growth
Strips out inflation
# GVA — meaning, headline measure, PPP and India's rank
## 1. GVA
Gross Value Added (GVA): Measures the value added by producers and by sectors to the economy — a production-side measure
GDP: A broader measure of domestic production after accounting for net taxes on products

## 4. India's rank

## Per capita income

## Deflator and GVA
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, i.e. GDP at current prices / GDP at constant prices × 100

GVA — production-side measure; GDP = GVA + taxes on products − subsidies (wider measure)
## NFIA, GDP and GNP
NFIA = factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad; added to GDP to get GNP
Indian resident's factor income earned in Saudi Arabia — counts in India's GNP only
India's GNP usually lower than GDP — NFIA is negative
GDP — location-based: all production inside the country's borders; does NOT include NFIA
Residents' production inside and outside the country — GNP (nationality-based)
## Other terms

Personal disposable income = personal income − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments (fines, fees)

Commission on resale — payment for productive service, included; NOT a transfer payment
Transfer payments: pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowances

Excluded: second-hand sales, interest on public debt
## Concepts
National wealth — a stock (point of time); national income — a flow (over a period)
National income = NNP at factor cost; NDP = GDP − depreciation; NNP = GNP − depreciation
GDP at FC = GDP at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies (not direct taxes)
## Worked examples

## Personal income and AP

GDP — value of all final goods and services produced within a country's geographical boundaries in a year, irrespective of who produces them

Real GDP — at constant (base-year) prices; nominal GDP at current prices
Real GVA — base year used to remove the effect of price changes
GDP deflator — most comprehensive measure of inflation (covers all goods and services in GDP; WPI, CPI, CPI-IW price fixed baskets)
2022-23 series: GVA at basic prices continues to be used; double deflation replaced single deflation for manufacturing and agriculture (separately deflates output and input prices)
India's PPP GDP much larger than market-exchange-rate GDP — prices are lower in India
Transfer earnings — not payments for factor services; excluded from national income
Rent, productive interest, profit — factor incomes
★ Main difference between GDP and GNP — net factor income from abroad
★ National Income = Net National Product at factor cost
★ NDP = GDP − depreciation (not plus)
★ GNP — Gross National Product
★ National Income = GNP at MP − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Demography of India – Census 2011 Findings, Population Growth, Density, Sex Ratio, Literacy

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Census History
First Census attempted: 1872 (not 1871); first synchronous / regular Census: 1881; held every 10 years since.
Census 2011: 15th national Census; motto "Our Census, Our Future"; the last Census published.
Census 2027: includes caste enumeration; population enumeration from February 2027; mascots Pragati and Vikas.
Delimitation Bill 2026 is reported to use 2011 Census data.
Census Town definition criticised as it may undercount urbanisation (MoHUA, Sep 2026).
# Phases of Population Growth
## Phases
Phase | Feature
1901-21 | Stagnant; population fell in 1911-21
1921 | "Year of the Great Divide" / "Demographic Divide"
1921-51 | Steady growth
1951-81 | Rapid growth; 1961-71 = "explosion"
1981-2011 | High but slowing
1921 Census: the only Census with negative decadal growth (−0.31%); faster growth after it. 1951 is NOT the demographic divide.
## Decadal Growth Record
Decade | India's decadal growth
1961-71 | 24.80% (highest)
1971-81 | 24.66%
1981-91 | 23.87%
1991-2001 | 21.54% (about 21%)
2001-11 | 17.70% – India's lowest decadal growth after 1921
Highest average annual exponential growth: 1971-81 (2.22%); 1991-2001 about 1.97%; 2001-11 1.64%.
Largest decadal growth of urbanisation: 1971-81 (46.1%); UP's highest urban population growth also 1971-81 (60.89%).
Highest literacy increase: 1991-2001 (about 12.62 points); 2001-11 about 8.20 points.
## Population Totals
Year | Population
1951 | About 36 crore
1991 | 84.6 crore
2001 | 102.87 crore (1028.74 million) – almost tripled since 1951
2011 | 121.09 crore (1,21,08,54,977; 1210.85 million)
2025 (State of World Population) | 1463.9 million
India = about 17.5% of world population (not 18.5%); high growth, likely to overtake China.
Replacement level for zero population growth: 2.1 children per woman.
World population by religion (descending): Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists.
# India at A Glance – Census 2011
Indicator | Figure
Population | 121.09 crore; decadal growth 17.7%
Density | 382 per sq km
Sex ratio | 943 final (provisional 940); rural 949, urban 929
Child sex ratio (0-6) | 919 final (provisional 914)
Literacy | 72.98% (73.0%) final (provisional 74.04%); male 80.9%, female 64.6%; up 8.2 points over 2001
Rural population | 68.9% (72.2% in 2001)
STs | 10.43 crore (8.6%); 89.97% rural; growth 23.66%; sex ratio 990 (8.2% in 2001)
Literate (Census): person aged 7 years or above who can read and write with understanding in any language.
# Sex Ratio
## National Trend
Census | Sex ratio
1901 | 972
1941 | 945
1951 | 946
1961 → 1971 | 941 → 930 (sharpest decline)
1991 | 927
2001 | 933
2011 | 943
Trend is fluctuating, not steadily falling. Male : female = 1000 : 933 (2001); 1000 : 943 (2011 final).
Child sex ratio (0-6) has continuously decreased: 976 (1961), 962 (1981), 927 (2001), 919 (2011).
## States and UTs
Item | Fact
Highest State | Kerala 1,084 (1,059 in 2001) – only State above 1,000
Highest UT | Puducherry 1,037 (females outnumber males)
Lowest State | Haryana 879 (861 in 2001) – though rich by per capita income
Lowest UT | Daman and Diu 618 (710 in 2001; highest decline 1991-2001, 960 → 710)
Descending order 2011 | Kerala, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh
Southern order | Kerala 1,084 → TN 996 → AP
UP | 912 (2011); 898 (2001)
Lowest among States asked (2001) | Gujarat (920)
Highest rise 1991-2001 | Arunachal Pradesh (859 → 893)
Rose 1991-2001 | Uttarakhand (936 → 962)
Fell 1991-2001 | Delhi (827 → 821), Haryana (865 → 861), Punjab (882 → 876)
Metro with highest sex ratio | Chennai (957 in 2001; 985 in 2011 P)
Persons aged 7+ (2011 P): males outnumber females in Bihar, Maharashtra, UP and West Bengal (all four).
Religious sex ratio (descending): Christian 1023, Buddhist 965, Jain 954, Muslim 951.
Cities: northern cities mostly unbalanced; eastern cities scattered, western cities concentrated; western cities have less rural migration.
## Child Sex Ratio (0-6)
Lowest: Haryana (834) in both rural and urban areas; most boys per 100 girls (0-6): Haryana (120); fewest: Arunachal Pradesh (102).
2011 provisional: Mizoram 971, Meghalaya 970, Punjab 846, Haryana 830; highest among States asked: Chhattisgarh (969).
## International and NFHS
Sex ratio (2011) decreasing order: Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, China; most favourable among countries asked: Finland.
Fear of falling world sex ratio: rising sex-determination tests.
NFHS-5 (2019-21): overall sex ratio 1,020 (NFHS-4: 991) – first time more women than men; sex ratio at birth 929 (up from 919).
# Density
India 2011 | 382
Highest State | Bihar 1,106
Top four (descending) | Bihar 1,106, West Bengal 1,028, Kerala 860, UP 829
Highest UT / overall | NCT Delhi 11,320 (11,297 P); then Chandigarh 9,258
Highest UT (among options) | Puducherry 2,547

Lowest UT | Andaman and Nicobar Islands 46
Below 100 | Mizoram (52)
Ascending 2011 | Odisha (270), AP (308), Tripura (350), Punjab (551)
Lowest among Rajasthan, MP, Gujarat, Karnataka | Rajasthan (200)
Most dense UP city | Ghaziabad (3,971)
2001: highest West Bengal (903), lowest Arunachal Pradesh (13).
1991: most dense West Bengal (767); descending West Bengal, Kerala, Bihar, UP; lowest among Sikkim, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Manipur = Sikkim (57); most sparse among options = J&K (77).
Kerala: high density (819, 3rd in 2001) and highest literacy (90.9%) – but literacy does not explain density.
Lowest density among countries asked: Canada; continent (among options): North America.
U.P. R.O./A.R.O. 2016 key: lowest density among the States asked = Uttar Pradesh.
# Literacy
## Trend
18.33% (1951) (male 27.2%, female 8.9%) → 72.98% (2011).
Female literacy 2011 provisional about 65.5%; final 64.6%. M.P.P.C.S. 1991 key gives India's female literacy as 63.0 percent.
1991-2001: male-female gap narrowed 24.8 → 21.6; 2011 national gap 16 points.
## State Rankings
Highest | Kerala ~94.0% (93.9% P; 90.9% in 2001; 89.81% in 1991)
Second | Mizoram (91.3%) – after Kerala in 2001 and 2011
Descending | Kerala (94.0), Mizoram (91.3), Goa (88.7), Maharashtra (82.3)
Descending (2011 P) | Tripura (87.75), Himachal (83.78), Sikkim (82.20), Nagaland (80.11)
Lowest | Bihar 61.8% (63.82% P; also lowest in 1991); male 71.2%, female 51.5%
Ascending lowest four | Bihar (61.8), Arunachal (65.4), Rajasthan (66.1), Jharkhand (66.4)
Maximum increase 2001-11 | Bihar (47.0% → 61.8%)
Highest UT | Lakshadweep 91.8% (also highest UT female and male literacy)
Highest rural (2001, among options) | Goa (79.67%); overall rural – Kerala
Highest religion group | Jains
Female literacy: Kerala 92.1, Mizoram 89.3, Goa 84.7 (highest); lowest final Bihar 51.5%; provisional lowest Rajasthan (52.66%); Rajasthan 52.1% lowest among States asked; 2001 lowest Bihar (33.1%); highest 2001 among States asked Mizoram; 1991 descending Kerala, Mizoram, Goa, Nagaland.
Gender gap: largest Rajasthan (28 points); largest among States asked UP (77.3% vs 57.2%); smallest Meghalaya (3.1 points).
Districts: most literate Serchhip (Mizoram) 98.76%; least Alirajpur (MP) 37.22% (2011 P). UP: Gautam Buddh Nagar (80.1%), then Kanpur Nagar (79.7%); 2001 PYQ – Auraiya; UP 2001 literacy 56.3% (male 68.8%, female 42.2%).
Kerala's highest literacy is not explained by Christian share (highest Christian share is Nagaland).
# Population, Growth and Urbanisation – State Rankings
## Population
Most populous | Uttar Pradesh (19,98,12,341)
Order | UP, Maharashtra (11,23,74,333), Bihar, West Bengal, undivided AP
Over one-third of India | UP, Maharashtra, Bihar
Least populous State | Sikkim (also 2001)
Least populous UT | Lakshadweep (64,473 final; 64,429 P)
Largest rural population | UP; highest rural share Himachal (90.0%), then Bihar (88.7%)
Delhi's largest migrant source | Uttar Pradesh
## Growth
Period | Highest | Lowest
2001-11 | Meghalaya (27.9%); UT Dadra and Nagar Haveli | Nagaland −0.6% (only negative State)
1991-2001 | Nagaland (64.41%); then Sikkim, Manipur, Meghalaya | Kerala
1981-91 | Nagaland (56.08%) | Kerala (annual 1.34%)
Nagaland: 19,90,036 (2001) → 19,78,502 (2011).
## Urbanisation
Most urbanised State Goa (~62%); least Himachal (~10%).
UT order: Delhi (97.5%), Chandigarh (97.3%), Lakshadweep (78.1%), Daman & Diu (75.2%).
Mega cities (40 lakh+): 6 in 2001 (not four); 9 UAs in 2011 (P); growth rates vary.
# Religion, Castes and Tribes
Religion (2011) | Population | Share
Hindus | 96.6 crore | 79.8% (84.1% in 1951)
Muslims | 17.2 crore | 14.2% (9.8% in 1951)
Christians | 2.78 crore | 2.3%
Sikhs | – | 1.7%
Christians: 10.7 (1961), 14.3 (1971), 16.2 (1981), 18.9 million (1991) = 2.25%; highest share Nagaland (90%, 1991).
Largest Muslim and SC population: Uttar Pradesh; largest SC share: Punjab (2001 and 2011); zero SC: Nagaland.
Highest ST share: Mizoram (94.4%); UT Lakshadweep (94.8%); lowest among States asked UP (0.6%).
Largest tribe: Bhil (1,70,71,049), then Gond, Santhal.
PVTG criteria: declining/static population, extremely low literacy (not caste, not sex ratio).
Household amenity (Census 2011) | All | SC | ST
Electricity as main lighting source | 67% | 59% | 52%
Latrine within premises | 47% | 34% | 23%
ST households lag SC households on both electricity and latrines.
Lowest share of child population in rural areas: Kerala (10.4%).
# Workers – Cultivators vs Agricultural Labourers

Census 2011: for the first time agricultural labourers outnumbered cultivators.
# Andhra Pradesh in the Census
## Historical (present AP)
Year | Fact

1961 | About 233 lakh
Year | Pop. (lakh) | Sex ratio | Density | Urban %

## AP in 2011
10th in population; 4.09% of India; undivided AP = 8.46 crore (8,45,80,777), density 308.

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Urban Development – Urbanisation Trends, Challenges (housing, Slums, Transport, Waste, Finance)

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Urban Settlement Classification
## Statutory vs census town
Type | Criteria
Statutory town | Any place with a municipal corporation, municipality, nagar panchayat, cantonment board or notified town area; notified by the State by law; run by a ULB
Census town | Administratively a village but meets all 3: population ≥5,000; ≥75% of male workers non-agricultural; density ≥400/sq km
Same three tests define an urban area (Census 2001).
Census towns: 3,892 in 2011 (3,894 provisional); 1,362 in 2001.
Towns (2011): 7,933-7,935 ≈ 4,041 statutory + 3,892 census towns.
Census 2027 keeps the 1981 census-town criteria; RGI retained them despite MoHUA's objection before the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Affairs (chair Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy).
"60% of males in non-agricultural work" is wrong – correct is 75% (UPPSC 2010).
Census town = 5,000 – 75% – 400 (population – male non-farm workers – density)
## Size classes
Six population-size classes, Class I to VI (CGPSC answer "06").
Class | Population
Class I | 1 lakh+
Class III | 20,000-49,999
Class IV, V, VI | Small towns (under 20,000)
Class VI | Below 5,000

# Causes of Urbanisation

Push: monsoon failure, rural unemployment, non-growing farm land, rural-urban imbalance.
Pull: magnetic features of cities – jobs, amenities; plus industrialisation, commercialisation, transport, social change.
Philip M. Hauser – "Population Implosion" (rural-urban concentration); "New Population Bomb" = fast-growing Third World urban population.

You check the answer keys of previous-year exam questions (PYQs: APPSC, UPSC, other state PSCs, SSC) for an APPSC exam-preparation app. For each PYQ you get the question, its numbered options and the key the app currently gives. Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:
- AGREE: the notes clearly support the given key.
- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Irrigation – Sources, Projects, Groundwater, Micro-irrigation, Pmksy and Watershed Development

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Sources of Irrigation
Source of net irrigated area (India, 2021-22) | Share
Tubewells | 47.3%
Canals | 24.7%
Other wells | 13.2%
Other sources | 12%
Tanks | 2.8%
Groundwater meets about 64% of irrigation needs; India ≈ 25% of global extraction.
Uttar Pradesh: largest tubewell-irrigated area.
Tanks matter in AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu – undulating hard-rock terrain.
# Project Classes and Aibp
Class | Culturable Command Area (CCA)
Minor | Up to 2,000 ha (AP: ayacut up to 5,000 acres)
Medium | 2,000-10,000 ha
Major | Above 10,000 ha
Minor irrigation: about 65% of irrigated area.
AIBP: speeds up ongoing major and medium projects; 99 prioritised projects funded through NABARD's LTIF since 2016 (8 in AP); potential created 26.71 vs 34.63 lakh ha target.
2,000 ha = minor/medium line; 10,000 ha = medium/major line
# Canals – State and Source
Canal | State | Source
Indira Gandhi Canal | Rajasthan | Sutlej and Beas via Harike Barrage (Punjab), not Ghaggar; ~650 km
Sirhind Canal | Punjab | Sutlej at Ropar
Upper Ganga Canal | Uttar Pradesh | Ganga at Haridwar
Nagarjuna Sagar | AP/Telangana | Krishna: Right = Jawahar Canal, Left = Lal Bahadur Shastri Canal
# Pmksy and Watershed Development
## PMKSY
Launched 1 July 2015; umbrella irrigation scheme.
Components: AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani (assured irrigation; CAD and water management), Per Drop More Crop (micro-irrigation; now under PM-RKVY), Watershed Development.
PMKSY planning: District Irrigation Plans feed State Irrigation Plans; State Level Sanctioning Committee chaired by the Chief Secretary.
Micro Irrigation Fund: corpus Rs 5,000 crore with NABARD.
## Watershed
Hariyali guidelines: from 1 April 2003.
Hariyali, IWDP, NWDPRA merged into IWMP (2008 common guidelines); IWMP subsumed in PMKSY as WDC-PMKSY (guidelines 26 Oct 2015); funding 90:10 → 60:40; WDC 2.0 adds springsheds.
Neeranchal National Watershed Project: World Bank ($178.5 million, approved 2014; CCEA Oct 2015); nine States incl. AP and Telangana; 2016-2022.
Tarun Bharat Sangh: Rajasthan NGO founded by Dr Rajendra Singh.
Watershed Development Fund: set up at NABARD in 1999-2000; initial corpus Rs 200 crore, shared by the Centre and NABARD.
# Groundwater – Cgwb and Atal Bhujal
CGWB categories (stage of extraction): Safe, Semi-critical, Critical, Over-exploited, + Saline; not "adequately exploited".
India stage: 60.63% (2025), up from 60.47% (2024).
GRACE satellite studies: severe groundwater depletion in north-west India – Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi.
Atal Bhujal Yojana: December 2019; World Bank-aided Central Sector; Ministry of Jal Shakti.
7 States: Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP; AP NOT included.
Focus: demand-side community management via GP Water Security Plans.
# Apwalta Act, 2002
AP Water, Land and Trees Act, 2002: against careless borewell digging; controls groundwater use; promotes tree planting.
Rainwater harvesting compulsory on plots of 200 sq m and above.
Over-exploited villages notified (GEC 2024-25: 258 villages proposed).
# Pm-kusum and Micro-irrigation
PM-KUSUM (2019, MNRE) | Content
A | 10,000 MW decentralised grid-connected solar plants (0.5-2 MW)
B | 14 lakh standalone solar pumps (up to 7.5 HP); none in dark zones
C | Solarisation of grid-connected pumps, incl. feeder-level
Objective: end diesel/kerosene dependence, energy security, raise farmers' income; helps raise non-fossil capacity to 40%.
JPSC PYQ: PM-KUSUM = "agricultural solar pump system".
Concern: solar pumps may encourage over-drawing of groundwater.
APMIP (since 2003): 42.25 lakh acres; 15.09 lakh farmers; Rayalaseema 64%; AP ranks 1st in micro-irrigation.
Atal Bhujal = Jal Shakti (groundwater demand); PM-KUSUM = MNRE (solar pumps).
Drip irrigation: sends water straight to the root zone of plants; soluble fertiliser can be given through the same lines (fertigation).
# Andhra Pradesh Irrigation
Project | River | Facts
Polavaram | Godavari | National Project (APRA 2014); 194.6 TMC; 960 MW; 7.20 lakh acres; diverts 80 TMC to Krishna; 89% complete; dedication by March 2027
Galeru-Nagari | Krishna | 38 TMC; 2.60 lakh acres
Veligonda (Poola Subbaiah) | Krishna (Srisailam tunnels → Nallamala Sagar) | 43.5 TMC; 4.47 lakh acres
AP 2024-25: GIA 36.77 lakh ha; NIA 30.33 lakh ha; groundwater 41% of GIA (~19 lakh borewells).
38,862 tanks; ayacut 25.60 lakh acres; 57% utilisation gap.
Groundwater (GEC 2024-25): stage 31.5% (Safe); 12 of 679 mandals over-exploited, 3 critical, 24 semi-critical, 39 saline, 601 safe.
White Paper (Jul 2026): 36 projects by Dec 2028, Rs 35,555 crore.
Handri-Neeva Sujala Sravanthi (HNSS): lift canal (about 550 km) taking Krishna flood water from the Srisailam backwaters at Malyala (Kurnool) to Kurnool, Anantapur, Kadapa and Chittoor.
Neeru-Chettu (AP, 2015): water-conservation mission to make the State drought-free; main work desilting of minor irrigation tanks and channels, check dams and farm ponds.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
Tubewells / tanks share | 47.3% / 2.8%
Minor CCA | Up to 2,000 ha
AIBP projects | 99 (8 AP)
Atal Bhujal States | 7
PM-KUSUM B pumps | 14 lakh
APWALTA plot | 200 sq m
India / AP extraction | 60.63% / 31.5%
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
Largest tubewell area: UP.
AP ranks first in micro-irrigation.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
APPSC earlier papers | APWALTA purpose; rainwater harvesting plot size
APPSC earlier papers | Largest tubewell-irrigated State; Indira Gandhi Canal
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. Indira Gandhi Canal from Harike, not Ghaggar.
2. Polavaram = Godavari; Galeru-Nagari, Veligonda = Krishna.
3. AP is not an Atal Bhujal State.
4. CGWB has no "adequately exploited" category.
5. Atal Bhujal = Central Sector, World Bank.
6. PM-KUSUM is under MNRE, not Agriculture.
7. Minor = up to 2,000 ha CCA.
8. Jawahar = Right, LBS = Left canal.

- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED).
