STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Monetary Policy – Objectives, Instruments (crr, Slr, Repo, Reverse Repo, Msf, Omo, Laf), Transmission

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Monetary Policy – Authority and Objectives
Formulated and implemented by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 (APPSC GS 2023).
Main objective: price stability, keeping growth in mind; also financial stability, external balance, development goals.
The MPC sets the repo rate to hit the inflation target; liquidity is kept so money-market rates stay near repo.
Monetary policy instruments: Repo, Reverse Repo, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR. Fiscal deficit and public revenue belong to fiscal policy.
Repurchase option (Repo) is used by RBI to regulate money supply and inflation.
# Evolution of the Framework
Phase | Framework | Landmarks
1985–1998 | Monetary targeting with feedback (M3) | Chakravarty Committee 1985; Vaghul Committee 1987 (money market)
1998–2016 | Multiple indicator approach (growth, inflation, exchange rate, credit) | LAF 2000; MSS 2004; Base Rate 2010; MSF 2011; MCLR 2016
2016 onwards | Flexible inflation targeting | Urjit Patel Committee 2014; MPFA 2015; RBI Act amended 2016; SDF 2022
Key post-1991 change: deregulation of interest rates (APPSC GS 2023).
Multiple indicator approach dropped: opaque; markets could not predict RBI when indicators conflicted.
"Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy": Shaktikanta Das, 24 Jan 2020, St. Stephen's College (APPSC GS 2024).
Repo − reverse repo gap was 1.00% (June 2010–June 2011); from 2011-12 only repo is fixed, reverse repo set automatically.
# Quantitative vs Qualitative Instruments
Basis | Quantitative (general) | Qualitative (selective)
Aim | Volume and cost of total credit | Direction of credit
Other name | Traditional methods | Selective credit control
Tools | Bank rate, repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR (variable reserve ratio) | Margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing, direct action, credit ceilings, minimum interest on advances for sensitive goods, consumer credit regulation
Main instrument: policy repo rate – the single operating rate under FIT and most-watched signal.
OMOs: main tool for durable liquidity.
Margin = value of security − loan; higher margin = smaller loan against the same security.
Variable reserve ratios and Bank Rate policy are quantitative, not selective. Moral suasion, margin requirements, direct action = qualitative.
# Policy Rates and the Laf Corridor
## Instruments at a Glance
Instrument | Meaning | Rate (Aug 2026)
Repo | RBI lends short-term funds to banks against G-secs; principal policy rate | 5.25% (MPC, 5 Aug 2026, unanimous, neutral)
SDF | Banks park surplus with RBI without collateral; floor | 5.00%
MSF | Overnight emergency borrowing at penal rate, dipping into SLR up to 2% of NDTL; ceiling, repo + 25 bps | 5.50%
Bank Rate | RBI's lending/discount rate; rediscounts bills of exchange or commercial paper; long-term; penal rates linked to it | 5.50%
Fixed reverse repo | RBI borrows from banks against G-secs; at RBI's discretion since SDF | 3.35% (May 2026)
CRR | Share of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; no interest | 3%
SLR | Share of NDTL kept by bank in cash, gold, approved G-secs | 18%
OMO | RBI buys/sells G-secs (through banks, not directly with the public) | –
Corridor: SDF 5.00% < Repo 5.25% < MSF = Bank Rate 5.50%; width 50 bps.
MSF began May 2011 at repo + 100 bps, borrowing up to 1% of NDTL; now repo + 25 bps, up to 2%. MSF aligned to Bank Rate in Feb 2012.
NBFC access to LAF: only Primary Dealers (classed as NBFCs).
## Comparisons
Basis | Repo | Reverse repo | Bank Rate | MSF
Who borrows | Bank from RBI | RBI from bank | Bank from RBI | Bank from RBI
Use | Inject liquidity | Absorb surplus | Monetary policy signal | Marginal emergency need
Against | Eligible securities | G-secs | Bills of exchange/CP | SLR portfolio
Cost | Policy rate | Lower | = MSF | Higher than repo
Reverse repo = rate at which banks lend to RBI. MSF rate and NDTL are terms of banking operations.
## Stance Terms
Stance | Meaning
Accommodative | Supports growth; rate cuts likely
Neutral | Either way, data-dependent
Hawkish | Worried about inflation; tightens
Dovish | Worried about growth; easing bias
Path: neutral → accommodative (Apr 2025) → neutral (June 2025), retained through Aug 2026.
Calibrated tightening: a stance in which rate cuts are off the table; rate hikes are measured and need not come at every meeting.
# Crr vs Slr
## Comparison
Basis | CRR | SLR
Kept | With RBI | By the bank itself
Form | Cash only | Cash, gold, unencumbered G-secs, T-bills, SDLs, approved securities
Returns | No interest | Earns interest on G-secs
Law | Sec 42, RBI Act 1934 | Sec 24, BR Act 1949
Limits | No floor or ceiling (since 2006) | 0%–40% of NDTL
Now | 3% | 18% (Sep 2023)
APPSC 2023: "Required reserve ratio" = CRR.
## SLR Details
Minimum share of NDTL banks keep in liquid assets before lending; mechanism by which banks provide credit to Government.
MSS securities count towards SLR.
25% floor removed by BR (Amendment) Act, 2007.
Trend: 38.5% (1991-92) → cut on Narasimham Committee advice → 19.25% (2019) → 18%. Since reforms, both SLR and CRR reduced.
Shortfall penalty: bank rate + 3% → bank rate + 5% if it continues.
An SLR cut of 50 bps → banks may cut lending rates. Lower CRR → banks have higher leverage to liquidity.
# Tool → Effect
## Dear Money vs Cheap Money
Tool | Control inflation (dear, contractionary) | Boost growth (cheap, expansionary)
CRR, SLR | Raise | Cut
Repo, reverse repo, Bank Rate | Raise | Cut
OMO | Sell G-secs | Buy G-secs
Raising CRR: less money in circulation + lower demand for goods and services (APPSC G1 2022: statements I and II); reduces liquidity; helps control inflation.
Raising CRR does NOT raise purchasing power or lending capacity. Purchase of G-secs does not control inflation. Reducing interest rates is expansionary, not anti-inflation.
Lower bank rate → cheaper borrowing, more liquidity (expansionary); higher bank rate → tight.
CRR/SLR cut → more lendable funds, higher money multiplier (M3/M0 = 6.21, 31 Dec 2025).
More money supply than real output growth → inflation.
Expansionary policy cannot stop the rupee's slide (it depreciates the rupee); rupee support = curb non-essential imports, promote exports, Masala Bonds, ease ECB conditions.
Policy rates directly regulate capacity for credit creation.
# Liquidity Management and Sterilisation
## Short-term Windows
Tool | Feature
LAF | Repo + reverse repo/SDF; primary window for day-to-day liquidity
SDF | Proposed 2015; enabled by Budget 2018-19; began April 2022; absorbs without collateral (APPSC G2 2025)
VRR / VRRR | Auction-based; VRR injects, VRRR absorbs for longer than overnight SDF
Fine-tuning operations | Short VRR/VRRR auctions in line with stance; 49 in FY24 (APPSC G2 2025)
## Durable Liquidity and Reserve Tools
I-CRR: temporary 10%, announced 10 Aug 2023; impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore (APPSC G2 2025: both statements correct).
OMO purchases: ₹2.39 lakh crore (Apr–May 2025) + ₹1 lakh crore (Dec 2025, to stabilise bond yields); more in March 2026.
LTRO (2020): 1–3 year funds at repo.
USD/INR buy-sell swap ($5 bn, 3-year, Dec 2025): injects rupees without changing RBI's balance-sheet size.
## Sterilisation
Forex inflows swell rupee liquidity → RBI sells G-secs (OMO/MSS) or runs VRRRs to cancel the effect on money supply.
MSS (April 2004): T-bills/MSBs issued; proceeds in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
## Surplus vs Deficit Liquidity
Surplus liquidity speeds transmission and pulls rates below repo; deficit weakens it.
Dec 2025 tightness (currency leakage, tax outflows) → OMO + $5 bn swap.
By 3 Sep 2026: surplus about ₹10.32 lakh crore after FCNR(B) inflows; call rate below repo; on 4 Sep 2026 RBI absorbed ₹6.02 lakh crore via two 3-day VRRRs.
# Lending-rate Benchmarks
## Who Sets Which Rate
Fixed by RBI/MPC | Set by each bank | Market-determined
Repo, SDF, MSF, Bank Rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR | PLR/BPLR (old), Base Rate, MCLR, spread over EBLR | Call money rate (WACR), TREPS, T-bill and G-sec yields
RBI does not fix the PLR.
## Evolution
Benchmark | From | Key point
PLR | 1994 | Rate for best borrowers, set by each bank
Base Rate | 1 July 2010 | Average cost of funds → slow transmission
MCLR | 1 April 2016 | Marginal cost of funds + CRR/SLR carry + operating cost + tenor premium; internal benchmark
EBLR | 1 Oct 2019 | New floating-rate personal/retail and MSME loans linked to repo, 3/6-month T-bill yield or FBIL rate; fastest
MCLR purpose (UPSC 2016, both correct): faster transmission.
Janak Raj Internal Study Group (2017): MCLR transmission weak → external benchmark → EBLR mandate.
Base Rate (2010, replaced BPLR): minimum lending rate set by each bank; actual rate charged = base rate + borrower-specific charges.
Draft RBI (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026: from 1 April 2027; banks, RRBs, co-ops, AIFIs, NBFCs/HFCs; floating personal and MSME loans stay on external benchmark; interest on daily reducing balance.
# Transmission – Channels, Lags and Yields
## Channels
1. Repo up → 2. money-market rates up → 3. costlier credit → 4. lower consumption and investment → 5. lower aggregate demand → inflation cools.
Channel | How a rate cut works
Interest rate | Cheaper loans raise consumption and investment
Credit | Banks lend more
Exchange rate | Weaker rupee helps exports
Asset price | Bond and equity prices rise (wealth effect)
Expectations | Credible target anchors expectations (does not remove all uncertainty)
Rate cut → higher investment expenditure (UPSC 2014), not higher savings or tax collection.
## Lags
EBLR loans reprice quickly; deposit rates and MCLR adjust slowly. Outstanding-loan WALR 9.26% (Sep 2025).
Repo cut 125 bps (Feb 2025–Feb 2026, 6.50% → 5.25%); fresh-loan WALR fell about 93 bps (Feb 2025–Mar 2026), about 80 bps from rate changes and 13 bps from loan mix.
## G-sec Yields
Driven by US Fed actions + RBI actions + domestic inflation and short-term rates (all three, UPSC 2021).
Narrower spread of Indian over US yields → lower borrowing costs.
# Obstacles and Challenges
## Challenges after 1991
Factor | Effect
Exchange-rate volatility from capital flows | Main challenge (APPSC GS 2023)
Open capital account | Moves liquidity and rupee → sterilisation
External shocks | Oil, global rate cycles, West Asia conflict (2026)
Fiscal dominance | Large borrowing; ad hoc T-bills ended 1997 → Ways and Means Advances
Forex reserves were NOT a problem; inflation was not low; revenue was not in surplus.
## Obstacles to Transmission
Obstacle | Effect
Administered small-savings rates | Hold deposit rates up
NPAs | Weak balance sheets (GNPA now 2.2%, Sep 2025)
Deposit dependence | Banks reprice only new deposits
Heavy Government borrowing | High yields (crowding out)
Informal credit | Outside RBI's reach
Structural rigidities | Banking rigidities (2026)
Rakesh Mohan Committee (2004): on administered interest rates and small savings; urged aligning small-savings rates with market (G-sec) yields.
## Monetary vs Fiscal Policy
Basis | Fiscal | Monetary
Authority | Government (Finance Ministry, Parliament) | RBI / MPC
Tools | Spending, taxes, subsidies, borrowing | Repo, OMO, CRR/SLR, LAF
Effect | Direct | Indirect
Speed | Slow; legislative and implementation lags | Quick (bi-monthly)
Monetary tools are demand-side only; food inflation is supply-driven → needs buffer-stock releases, duty cuts, farm reform.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Date | Rate
30 Sep 2014 | Repo 8.00%
29 Sep 2015 | Bank Rate 7.75%
Oct 2001 | Bank Rate cut 7% → 6.50%
5 Dec 2019 | Repo 5.15%, reverse repo 4.90%
Apr 2025 | Repo 6.0%, SDF 5.75%, MSF 6.25%
5 June / Aug 2026 | Repo 5.25%, SDF 5.00%, MSF = Bank Rate 5.50%, reverse repo 3.35%
CRR | 4% → 3% (100 bps cut, ~₹2.5 lakh crore released)
SLR | 38.5% (1991-92) → 18%
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First flexible inflation targeting: 2016 (Urjit Patel Committee 2014).
Latest LAF tool: SDF (April 2022), the only collateral-free absorption tool.
Fastest-transmitting benchmark: EBLR.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
G1 Prelims 2022 | Effect of raising CRR
APPSC GS 2023 | Required reserve ratio; RBI authority; post-1991 challenge
APPSC GS 2024 | Seven Ages speech
G2 Mains 2025 Paper 2 | RBI; repo; reverse repo
G2 Mains 2025 Paper 2 | SDF; I-CRR; fine-tuning operations; CRR
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. SDF = floor, no collateral; MSF = ceiling.
2. CRR with RBI (cash, no interest); SLR with bank (earns interest).
3. Sec 42 RBI Act = CRR; Sec 24 BR Act = SLR.
4. Variable reserve ratio and OMO = quantitative.
5. Reverse repo = banks lend to RBI.
6. MCLR set by each bank; call rate by the market; CRR/SLR by RBI.
7. Base rate = average cost; MCLR = marginal cost.
8. EBLR from 1 Oct 2019 for retail and MSME loans.
9. Main post-1991 challenge = exchange-rate volatility.
10. Rate cut raises investment, not savings.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Monetary policy — authority, objectives and framework phases
## 1. Monetary policy basics
Authority: Formulated and implemented by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 (APPSC-GS 2023)
Objectives: Price stability (paramount), growth, financial stability, external balance, development goals
## 2. Phases and key changes
1985-1998 | Monetary targeting (M3) with feedback | Chakravarty Committee 1985; Vaghul Committee 1987 (money market)
Multiple indicator approach dropped: Opaque → markets could not predict RBI's moves when indicators conflicted
## 3. Persons
Seven Ages: Governor Shaktikanta Das traced the phases in "Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy", 24 Jan 2020, St. Stephen's College (APPSC-GS 2024 statement)
# Instruments — quantitative vs qualitative, main instrument
Aim | Volume and cost of total credit | Direction of credit to sectors or borrowers
Other name | Traditional methods of control | Selective credit control
Tools | Bank rate, repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR (variable reserve ratio) | Margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing, direct action, selective credit control, consumer credit regulation
Main instrument: The policy repo rate
Single operating policy rate under FIT + most-watched signal
MPC sets it to hit the inflation target; liquidity kept so money-market rates stay near it
OMOs: Main tool for durable liquidity (e.g. ₹1 lakh crore of purchases in Dec 2025)
Margin requirement: Gap between the value of the security and the loan
Higher margin = smaller loan against the same security → cuts credit against it
⚠ Moral suasion, margin requirements, direct action = qualitative; CRR, SLR, OMO = quantitative
# Terms → meaning: policy rates, LAF corridor, stance — Policy rates
## 1. Policy rates
Instrument | Meaning | Liquidity effect when raised | Rate now
Repo rate (policy repo rate) | RBI lends overnight to banks against approved collateral (G-secs); the policy rate | Tightens | 5.25% (MPC, 5 Aug 2026)
SDF (rate) | Banks park surplus / overnight deposits with RBI without collateral; floor of the LAF corridor | Absorbs more | 5.00%
MSF (rate) | Penal overnight borrowing by dipping into SLR portfolio up to 2% of NDTL; ceiling of the corridor, repo + 25 bps | Tightens | 5.50%
Bank rate | Rediscount rate / longer-term lending, rediscounting of bills with no collateral; aligned with MSF; penal rate for CRR/SLR shortfalls (penal rates linked to it) | Tightens | 5.50%
Fixed-rate reverse repo | RBI absorbs funds against G-secs; used at RBI's discretion since SDF | Absorbs more | 3.35% (May 2026)
CRR | Share of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; earns no interest | Reduces lendable funds | 3% of NDTL
SLR | Share of NDTL held by banks themselves in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved G-secs) | Reduces lendable funds | 18%
OMO | Outright purchase or sale of G-secs, done through banks and not directly with the public | Sale absorbs; purchase injects | -
Rate sources: Rates as of 6 Aug 2026 (MPC unanimous; neutral stance); CRR/SLR/reverse repo as of May 2026
Repo cuts: 125 bps since Feb 2025 (6.50% → 5.25%)
# Terms → meaning: policy rates, LAF corridor, stance — MSF and the corridor
## 1. MSF and the corridor
MSF design:
Began May 2011 at repo + 100 bps, borrowing up to 1% of NDTL (older notes)
Now 25 bps above repo (5.25% vs 5.50%)
Exam angle: order of the corridor - SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = bank rate (ceiling).
⚠ MSF borrowing limit: 1% of NDTL (2011, older notes) vs 2% now; spread 100 bps then vs 25 bps now
## 2. Policy stance terms
Accommodative | Supports growth, ample liquidity, rate cuts likely
Neutral | Rates can move either way, data-dependent
Calibrated tightening | No cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
Hawkish | Worried about inflation; tightens (raises rates, drains liquidity)
Dovish | Worried about growth; bias towards easing [GK]
Stance path: Neutral → accommodative (Apr 2025) → neutral (June 2025) → neutral retained through Aug 2026
# CRR and SLR — features, legal basis, floor and ceiling
SLR form of holding: Held by banks themselves (not deposited with RBI) as cash, gold, unencumbered G-secs/T-bills/SDLs and approved securities (UPSC)
SLR statutory range: 0% to 40% of NDTL
Earlier 25% floor removed by Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007
SLR trend: 38.5% of NDTL in 1991-92 → cut gradually on the Narasimham Committee's advice → 18% now
SLR shortfall penalty: Bank rate + 3% a year → bank rate + 5% if shortfall continues
Point | CRR | SLR
Form | Cash balance with RBI | Cash, gold, unencumbered approved securities held by the bank itself
Law | Sec 42, RBI Act[GK] | Sec 24, Banking Regulation Act, 1949[GK]
Limits | No floor or ceiling since 2006 [GK] | Ceiling 40%; RBI range 0-40%
Interest | None | Earns interest on G-secs
Current level | 3% of NDTL (100 bps cut released about ₹2.5 lakh crore by Dec 2025, ES 2025-26) | 18% (UPSC notes; your current lane has no newer value)
Trap: "Required reserve ratio" = CRR (APPSC 2023)
⚠ Sec 42 RBI Act = CRR; Sec 24 BR Act = SLR
# Tool → effect: money supply, demand, transmission channels, bond yields — Dear money vs cheap money
## 1. Dear money vs cheap money
Tool | To control inflation (dear money, contractionary) | To boost growth (cheap money, expansionary)
CRR | Raise | Cut
SLR | Raise | Cut
Repo transmission chain: Repo up → money-market rates up → costlier credit → lower consumption and investment → lower aggregate demand → inflation cools
CRR/SLR cut: Raises lendable funds and the money multiplier
M3/M0 = 6.21 on 31 Dec 2025; 6.0 adjusted for SDF
Raising CRR: Less money in circulation + lower demand (APPSC-G1 2022: statements I and II)
⚠ Trap: Does NOT raise purchasing power or banks' lending capacity
# Tool → effect: money supply, demand, transmission channels, bond yields — Transmission channels
## 1. Transmission channels
Credit | Banks have more funds and lend more
Exchange rate | Lower rates can weaken the rupee, helping exports [GK]
Asset price | Bond and equity prices rise, creating a wealth effect [GK]
Expectations | A credible target anchors inflation expectations
Effect of rate cut: Increases investment expenditure (UPSC 2014)
⚠ Trap: Does not raise savings or tax collection
Mechanism: Repo change → money-market rates → aggregate demand → inflation
## 2. What moves G-sec yields
Drivers of G-sec yields: US Federal Reserve's actions + RBI's actions + inflation and short-term rates → all three (UPSC 2021)
OMO purchases: ₹1 lakh crore (Dec 2025) meant to stabilise bond yields
Sovereign spread: Spread of Indian yields over US bonds narrowed → lower borrowing costs
S&P upgraded India from BBB- to BBB (2025-26)
# Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Short-term windows
## 1. Short-term windows
Tool | Meaning / feature
LAF | Repo + reverse repo/SDF windows → main short-term liquidity tool; primary window for injecting and absorbing day-to-day liquidity (UPSC)
SDF | Proposed by RBI in 2015; enabled by Budget 2018-19 (RBI Act amendment); began April 2022; absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral → RBI need not hold G-secs to drain funds (APPSC-G2 2025)
VRR / VRRR | Auction-based (competitive) LAF tools; last accepted rate = cut-off; VRR injects liquidity; VRRR absorbs it for longer maturities than the overnight SDF → keeps short rates near repo
Fine-tuning operations | Short VRR/VRRR auctions to keep liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance; 49 in FY2024 (FY24) (APPSC-G2 2025)
# Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Durable liquidity and reserve tools
## 1. Durable liquidity and reserve tools
I-CRR: Temporary 10% incremental CRR announced 10 Aug 2023 → impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore (APPSC-G2 2025: both statements correct)
OMO: Outright purchase/sale of G-secs for durable liquidity
FY26 injections: ₹2.39 lakh crore OMO purchases (Apr-May 2025)
LTRO (2020): 1-3 year funds at the repo rate
USD/INR buy-sell swap: e.g. $5 bn, 3-year, Dec 2025 → injects rupee liquidity without changing the size of RBI's balance sheet
## 2. Sterilisation
Sterilisation: Forex inflows swell rupee liquidity → RBI sells G-secs (OMO/MSS) or runs VRRRs to offset
Sep 2026 case: FCNR(B) inflows of $127.23 bn
MSS (April 2004): For sterilisation; sells securities to mop up surplus liquidity
RBI issues T-bills/securities (MSBs) to absorb rupees created by forex purchases
Proceeds sit in a separate MSS account the Government cannot spend
# Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Liquidity conditions - surplus vs deficit
## 1. Liquidity conditions - surplus vs deficit
Surplus vs deficit: Surplus liquidity speeds transmission + pulls market rates below repo vs deficit liquidity weakens it
Dec 2025 tightness: Currency leakage, tax outflows, reserve needs → RBI injected ₹1 lakh crore via OMO + $5 bn swap
2026 stance: RBI to keep "sufficient liquidity" for transmission (Governor, Feb 2026)
By 3 Sep 2026: surplus about ₹10.32 lakh crore → had pushed the call rate below repo; RBI draining via VRRR
4 Sep 2026: RBI absorbed about ₹6.02 lakh crore through two 3-day VRRRs
# Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Who sets which rate
## 1. Who sets which rate
Repo (MPC), SDF, MSF, bank rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR | PLR/BPLR (old), Base Rate (1 Jul 2010), MCLR (1 Apr 2016), spread over EBLR | Call money rate (WACR), TREPS, T-bill and G-sec yields
⚠ Trap: SLR and CRR are set by RBI, not by banks; MCLR = each bank's internal benchmark (each bank computes its own)
# Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Benchmark evolution
## 1. Benchmark evolution
PLR | 1994 [GK] | Rate for the best borrowers, set by each bank
BPLR | 2003 [GK] | Opaque; banks lent below it
Base rate | 1 July 2010 | Minimum lending rate, based on the average cost of funds → slow transmission
MCLR | 1 April 2016 | Based on the marginal cost of funds (marginal cost of deposits) + cost of CRR/SLR carry + operating cost + tenor premium; an internal benchmark
EBLR | 1 October 2019 | All new floating-rate personal/retail and MSME (MSE) loans are linked to an external benchmark: the repo rate, the 3-month or 6-month T-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate; loans linked directly to repo → fastest route
Purpose of MCLR (UPSC 2016: both statements correct):
More transparency in how banks fix rates
Faster transmission of policy rates to borrowers
MCLR in practice: HDFC Bank raised MCLR by up to 10 bps on 8 Jun 2026 → 1-year MCLR 8.40%
# Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Committee and directions
## 1. Committee and directions
Committee / direction | Year | Provision
Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system - chaired by Janak Raj | 2017 | Finding: MCLR transmission weak; recommendation: move to an external benchmark; outcome: EBLR mandate from 1 Oct 2019
Draft RBI (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026 | Proposed effect from 1 April 2027 | Covers banks, RRBs, co-operative banks, AIFIs, NBFCs/HFCs; floating-rate personal and MSME loans stay tied to an external benchmark; interest on the daily reducing balance
# Data — policy rates then and now, pass-through
## 1. Policy rates to track
Rate | Aug 2026 (TH, 6 Aug 2026) | Earlier
Repo | 5.25% | 6.0% (Apr 2025); 6.5% after the 2022-24 hikes (CDI)
SDF | 5.00% | 5.75% (Apr 2025)
MSF = Bank rate | 5.50% | 6.25% (Apr 2025)
Fixed reverse repo | 3.35% (CDI, May 2026) | -
CRR | 3% | 4% before the 2025 cuts
SLR | 18% (UPSC notes, Sep 2023) | 38.5% (1991-92)
## 2. Lags - policy rate to deposit and lending rates
Fresh loans (FY26 pass-through): WALR on fresh loans fell 64 bps (some notes say 69 bps) → "robust pass-through" (ES 2025-26)
Credit growth 14.5% YoY in Dec 2025
WALR levels (Sep 2025):
Fresh rupee loans = 8.5%
Outstanding loans = 9.26% → lag because MCLR loans reset only periodically
Speed: EBLR loans reprice quickly vs deposit rates and MCLR adjust slowly
# Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Challenges after 1991
## 1. Challenges after 1991
Open capital account | Inflows/outflows move liquidity and the rupee → RBI sterilises (MSS, OMO, VRRR), e.g. FCNR(B) inflows of 2026
External shocks | Oil prices, global rate cycles, wars (West Asia conflict of 2026)
Fiscal dominance | Large Government borrowing; automatic monetisation through ad hoc T-bills ended in 1997 → replaced by Ways and Means Advances
Other | Weak transmission
⚠ Trap: Forex reserves were NOT a problem; inflation was not low; revenue was not in surplus
# Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Monetary vs fiscal policy - complementary roles against inflation
## 1. Monetary vs fiscal policy - complementary roles against inflation
Basis | Fiscal policy | Monetary policy
Effect on demand | Direct | Indirect, through interest rates
Flexibility | Rigid, slow; legislative lags (needs legislative approval) | Quick, fast (bi-monthly meetings)
Limit: Monetary tools are demand-side tools only
Food inflation: Mostly supply-driven → rate hikes cannot add onions or tomatoes to the market
Supply-driven food/fuel inflation needs fiscal steps too: buffer-stock releases, duty cuts and farm reform
# Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Obstacles to transmission
## 1. Obstacles to transmission
Administered small-savings rates | Hold deposit rates up → banks cannot cut lending rates
NPAs | Weak balance sheets (though GNPA now at a multi-decadal low of 2.2%, Sep 2025)
Dependence on deposits | Banks reprice only new deposits
Heavy Government borrowing | Keeps yields high (crowding out)
Informal credit | Large unorganised money market outside RBI's reach; people prefer cash
Structural rigidities | In banking (2026); liquidity mismatches
# Universal angles
Current relevance:
ES 2025-26: 100 bps repo cut to 5.25%; 100 bps CRR cut to 3%; OMO purchases ₹2.39 lakh crore (Apr-May 2025) + ₹1 lakh crore (Dec 2025)
Liquidity then swung to a record surplus by Sep 2026
Aug 2026 MPC minutes point to a possible hike
Draft Interest Rate Directions 2026 (in force from 1 Apr 2027): "improve transmission" + prevent excessive pricing for small borrowers (Aug 2026)
Significance: Corridor + SDF → collateral-free way to absorb large surpluses
Comparative note: MSF = repo + 25 bps; SDF = repo - 25 bps → LAF corridor 50 bps wide (5.00-5.50%)
Criticism & debates:
Weak pass-through to deposit rates; large firms shifting to non-bank credit
Repo = demand-side tool → cannot fix food or fuel supply shocks; RBI has little reach over food inflation
Weak transmission from rigidities in banking (Sep 2026)

=== One-liner notes ===
# Policy rates (Aug 2026)
Corridor: SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = bank rate (ceiling), 50 bps wide
Instrument | Meaning | Rate
Repo | RBI lends to banks vs G-secs; main policy rate | 5.25%
SDF | Banks park funds, no collateral; floor | 5.00%
MSF | Emergency overnight; dip SLR up to 2%; ceiling | 5.50%
Bank Rate | Rediscounting bills; penal rates | 5.50%
Reverse repo | RBI borrows; discretionary | 3.35%
CRR / SLR | Cash with RBI / liquid assets with bank | 3% / 18%
Kept | With RBI, cash only | By bank itself: cash, gold, G-secs
Interest | None | Earns on G-secs
Law | Sec 42, RBI Act | Sec 24, BR Act 1949
Range | No floor/ceiling (2006) | 0% to 40%; was 38.5% (1991-92)
# Quantitative vs qualitative
Quantitative (general) | Qualitative (selective)
Bank rate, repo, OMO, CRR, SLR | Margin requirements, moral suasion, direct action
Volume & cost of credit | Direction of credit
# Frameworks & benchmarks
1985-1998 — Monetary targeting (Chakravarty Committee)
1998-2016 — Multiple indicator approach; LAF 2000, MSS 2004, MSF 2011
1 July 2010 — Base rate (average cost)
1 April 2016 — MCLR (marginal cost); FIT from 2016 (Urjit Patel 2014)
1 October 2019 — EBLR for retail & MSME loans (Janak Raj group, 2017)
April 2022 — SDF begins
# Repo transmission
1. Repo ↑ ↓
2. Money-market rates ↑ ↓
3. Costlier credit ↓
4. Consumption & investment ↓ ↓
5. Aggregate demand ↓ → inflation cools
# Liquidity tools
LAF: repo + reverse repo/SDF; day-to-day liquidity
VRR injects / VRRR absorbs; 49 fine-tuning ops in FY24
I-CRR 10% (10 Aug 2023): ~₹1.1 lakh crore
MSS (April 2004): sterilisation of forex inflows
OMO purchases: ₹2.39 lakh crore (Apr-May 2025)
Repo cut 125 bps since Feb 2025; stance neutral
# Obstacles & limits
Heavy govt borrowing; informal credit; MCLR resets slowly
Post-1991 main challenge: exchange-rate volatility (APPSC 2023)
Food inflation supply-driven: repo can't fix it
Ad hoc T-bills ended 1997 → Ways and Means Advances
# Exam corner
"Required reserve ratio" = CRR (APPSC 2023)
SDF absorbs without collateral (APPSC 2025); I-CRR: both statements correct
Raising CRR: less money + lower demand, NOT more lending (APPSC 2022)
Rate cut → investment up (UPSC 2014); MCLR: both statements correct
Seven Ages speech: Shaktikanta Das, 24 Jan 2020
CRR/SLR set by RBI; MCLR by each bank; call rate by market
## 1. Instruments at a glance
Bank Rate | The RBI's lending or discount rate — a traditional rate associated with RBI lending or rediscounting; involves bills of exchange or commercial paper; rediscount rate / longer-term lending, rediscounting of bills with no collateral; aligned with MSF; penal rate for CRR/SLR shortfalls (penal rates linked to it) | Tightens | 5.50%
Repo Rate (policy repo rate) | Lending by the RBI to banks against securities — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks; overnight, against approved collateral (G-secs); the policy rate | Tightens | 5.25% (MPC, 5 Aug 2026)
Reverse Repo (fixed-rate reverse repo) | Enables the RBI to absorb liquidity from banks — the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks; against G-secs; used at RBI's discretion since SDF | Absorbs more | 3.35% (May 2026)
CRR — Cash Reserve Ratio | A cash reserve maintained with the RBI (share of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; earns no interest) | Reduces lendable funds | 3% of NDTL
SLR — Statutory Liquidity Ratio | Liquid assets maintained by banks themselves (share of NDTL in cash, gold, approved G-secs) | Reduces lendable funds | 18%
OMO | The RBI buying or selling government securities (outright, done through banks and not directly with the public) | Sale absorbs; purchase injects | -
MSF (rate) | An emergency overnight borrowing facility — penal overnight borrowing by dipping into SLR portfolio up to 2% of NDTL; ceiling of the corridor, repo + 25 bps | Tightens | 5.50%
Monetary policy instruments: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, Bank Rate, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio — ⚠ fiscal deficit is associated with fiscal policy
# Repo vs reverse repo, bank rate and MSF
## 1. Repo vs reverse repo
Basis | Repo Rate | Reverse Repo Rate
Use | Liquidity injection; regulate money supply | Liquidity absorption — absorb surplus liquidity
Mechanism | A bank borrows from the RBI | A bank parks money with the RBI
## 2. Repo vs Bank Rate
Basis | Repo Rate | Bank Rate
Nature | Short-term lending by the RBI | A traditional rate
Against | Eligible securities | Bills of exchange or commercial paper
Use | Liquidity management | Monetary policy
Associated with | Repo transactions | Bank lending or rediscounting
## 3. MSF vs repo
Basis | Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) | Repo
Nature | An overnight borrowing facility | A short-term borrowing mechanism
Borrower | Banks borrow from the RBI | Banks borrow from the RBI
Use | Marginal or short-term liquidity needs | Regular liquidity management
Collateral | Can involve dipping into the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio | Against eligible securities
Cost | ⚠ Traditionally a higher cost than the repo rate | Principal policy lending rate in the source framework
# Terms → meaning: policy rates, LAF corridor, stance — Bank rate, MSF corridor and stance
## 1. Bank rate and stance
Lower bank rate: Borrowing cheaper; expands liquidity — an expansionary stance
Higher bank rate: Borrowing costlier; contracts liquidity — a tight stance
Central bank policy rates directly regulate the capacity for credit creation
## 2. MSF and the corridor
## 3. Policy stance terms
# CRR vs SLR — features and legal basis
## 1. SLR in detail
The minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that commercial banks must maintain in liquid assets before lending
Eligible assets: Liquid cash, gold and other unencumbered approved securities
Government securities are commonly used — most commonly held in Government Securities (G-Secs), which earn interest income while meeting SLR requirements
## 2. CRR vs SLR
Kept | Deposited with the RBI — an RBI-held reserve | Maintained by the bank itself — not deposited with the RBI; the bank's own holdings
Form | Only cash (Cash balance with RBI) | Cash, gold and approved securities or other liquid assets (unencumbered approved securities held by the bank itself)
Returns | Do not earn interest | Can earn returns (earns interest on G-secs)
Role | Controls liquidity and credit — regulates credit and liquidity | Controls liquidity; a liquidity buffer — regulates credit and liquidity
# SLR — holding, statutory range, trend and penalty
## 1. Policy links
A decrease in the Bank Rate increases liquidity; an increase is contractionary
OMO: A monetary policy instrument; ⚠ public revenue is associated with fiscal policy
## 2. Monetary vs fiscal policy - complementary roles against inflation

=== Complete2 notes ===
## Objective
Price stability — paramount objective (RBI Act, 1934); growth, financial stability, external balance also pursued
Fiscal policy is not free from legislative and implementation lags
## LAF corridor
Corridor, floor to ceiling — SDF < Repo < MSF = Bank rate
MSF rate — upper end of the corridor; repo + 25 bps; SLR dip up to 2% of NDTL (older design: 100-bps spread, 1% limit)
Repo 5.25% → MSF 5.50%, SDF 5.00%
Fixed-rate reverse repo — absorbs funds against G-secs, used at RBI's discretion; SDF absorbs without collateral
Tool | Meaning
Repo | RBI's principal policy lending rate; banks borrow from RBI against securities; regular liquidity
Reverse repo | RBI borrows from banks to absorb surplus liquidity
MSF | overnight emergency borrowing above repo, dipping into SLR
SDF | absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral
OMO | RBI buys or sells government securities; a monetary-policy tool
Bank rate | RBI's lending rate
## CRR and SLR
CRR — cash balance with the RBI, earns no interest
SLR — held by banks themselves in cash, gold, unencumbered G-secs and T-Bills (incl. SDLs) and approved securities
SLR statutory range 0%–40% of NDTL; 25% floor removed by Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007
Contractionary policy — raise CRR, SLR, repo; sell G-secs
CRR/SLR cut → more lendable funds, higher money multiplier
## Transmission and markets
MCLR — aimed at faster transmission; an internal benchmark computed by each bank
Call money rate — market-determined; RBI fixes CRR and SLR (true, but not the explanation)
Repo cut works via five channels — interest-rate, credit, exchange-rate, asset-price, expectations
Informal credit markets — outside the full reach of RBI policy (an obstacle to transmission)
G-sec yields — moved by US Fed actions, RBI actions, domestic inflation and short-term rates
★ Repurchase option (Repo) — used by RBI to regulate money supply and inflation
SLR reduced from its 1991–92 level on advice of the Narasimham Committee
CRR — Section 42, RBI Act, 1934; SLR — Section 24, Banking Regulation Act, 1949
SLR — 38.5% (1991–92) → 18% (September 2023)
Quantitative tools — repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR
Qualitative / selective tools — margin requirements, moral suasion
Margin = value of security − loan; raising the margin reduces the loan available against the same security
## Timeline
Year | Development
1985–1998 | Monetary targeting with feedback (M3 the principal aggregate)
1998–2016 | Multiple indicator approach
2000 | LAF
2004 | MSS
2011 | MSF introduced
2014 | Urjit Patel Committee report (basis of flexible inflation targeting)
2015 | Monetary Policy Framework Agreement
2016 | RBI Act amended; flexible inflation targeting adopted
Base Rate — 1 July 2010; based on average cost of funds (slow transmission)
MCLR — 1 April 2016; marginal cost of funds (marginal deposit cost, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost, tenor premium)
RBI Internal Study Group on MCLR (2017) — chaired by Janak Raj; found weak transmission, recommended an external benchmark
EBLR mandatory from 1 October 2019 — new floating-rate personal, retail and MSME loans linked to an external benchmark (repo, 3- or 6-month T-bill yield, or FBIL-published rate)
EBLR-linked loans — fastest transmission; MCLR loans reset only periodically
Who sets the rate — MSF rate by RBI/MPC; MCLR by each bank; EBLR by external benchmark; call rate by the market
MSF rate is higher than repo (repo + 0.25%); overnight emergency window
MPC sets repo to achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates
Repo hike sequence — higher money-market rates → costlier credit → lower consumption and investment → lower aggregate demand
Surplus liquidity pulls market rates below repo, speeding transmission; deficit liquidity weakens it
Expectations channel — a credible target anchors expectations; does not remove all uncertainty
## Day-to-day liquidity
LAF — RBI's primary window: injects via repo, absorbs via reverse repo and SDF
VRRR — auction-based, absorbs liquidity for longer than overnight SDF; VRR injects
Fine-tuning operations (short-term VRR/VRRR) — keep liquidity in line with the policy stance
Hawkish — worried about inflation, tightens; dovish — worried about growth, easing bias
Higher CRR → reduces money in circulation
## Durable liquidity and sterilisation
OMO — outright purchase or sale of government securities; durable liquidity
I-CRR — 10%, announced 10 August 2023; impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore
USD/INR buy-sell swap (e.g. 3-year, $5 billion, December 2025) — injects rupee liquidity without changing RBI balance-sheet size
MSS (April 2004) — sterilises liquidity from forex purchases; T-Bills issued, proceeds in a separate account Government cannot spend
Sterilisation — offsetting excess rupee liquidity from forex inflows; tools MSS, OMO, VRRR
Supply-driven food/fuel inflation — buffer stocks, duty cuts, farm reforms (CRR, SLR, rates act on demand)
Ad hoc Treasury Bills (automatic monetisation) ended 1997 → Ways and Means Advances
Main post-1991 challenge — exchange-rate volatility from capital flows
Fiscal dominance — large government borrowing pressuring money supply and inflation
Narrower spread between Indian and US bond yields → cuts India's borrowing costs
"Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy" — Shaktikanta Das, 24 January 2020, St. Stephen's College
Required reserve ratio = CRR (share of NDTL kept as cash with RBI, Sec 42 RBI Act, no interest)
Repo cut → cheaper loans → higher investment expenditure (not higher savings or tax collection)
Lower bank rate — expansionary: cheaper borrowing, more liquidity
Reverse repo — absorbs surplus liquidity; Bank Rate — long-term rediscount rate on bills of exchange and commercial paper
SLR — controls liquidity, a buffer, held in assets that earn returns (government bonds); CRR controls liquidity and credit
★ Selective credit control — margin requirements, credit ceilings, minimum interest rates on advances for sensitive goods
★ Variable reserve ratios — not selective; a quantitative tool
★ Bank Rate policy — a quantitative tool
★ Variable reserve rates and OMO — tools of monetary policy
★ OMO — quantitative technique of credit control
★ Lower Bank Rate → more liquidity in the market
## Rates
★ Repo Rate — rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks (against G-secs); under monetary policy
★ LAF — means by which banks borrow through repos (and lend via reverse repos)
★ Bank Rate — rate at which RBI discounts bills of exchange; RBI's long-term lending rate to banks
★ Bank Rate cut 7% → 6.50% in October 2001; MSF aligned to Bank Rate in February 2012
## Reserve ratios
★ CRR — ratio of deposits banks must keep with RBI; CRR hike → less money to lend
★ SLR — mechanism by which banks provide credit to the government (investing in G-secs)
★ SLR 19.25% (RBI review, 2019)
★ SLR cut of 50 bps → banks may cut lending rates
★ Since the reforms (Narasimham Committee) — both SLR and CRR reduced; SLR from 38.5% in 1991
## OMO and inflation control
★ OMO — purchase and sale of government securities by RBI (trading in securities)
★ Inflation control — raise Bank Rate, CRR, SLR; not purchase of government securities
★ Lower CRR → banks have higher leverage to liquidity
★ Expansionary monetary policy — not a measure to stop the rupee's slide (it leads to depreciation)
rupee support — curb non-essential imports, promote exports, Masala Bonds, ease ECB conditions
★ Bank rate — official rate of interest charged by the central bank
★ Repo − reverse repo gap 1.00% (June 2010–June 2011); from 2011–12 only repo fixed, reverse repo adjusted automatically
★ SLR — ratio banks keep between cash in hand (liquid assets) and total assets; cash, gold, G-secs
★ CRR — mandatory proportion of deposits kept with the RBI
★ MSF rate and NDTL — terms of banking operations
MSF — overnight emergency borrowing from RBI, dipping into SLR at a penal rate
★ CRR increase → fall in money circulation and low demand for goods and services
★ Decreased money circulation helps control inflation
★ Lower interest rate → higher investment (and consumption) expenditure
★ Sterilisation — conducting Open Market Operations to offset forex operations' effect on money supply
★ Reverse Repo Rate — rate at which banks lend to RBI (RBI absorbs surplus, overnight, against G-secs)

★ NBFCs can access the LAF window — Primary Dealers (classified as NBFCs) access it
★ Reducing the interest rate — expansionary, not a method to control inflation (contractionary policy controls it)

★ 29 September 2015 | Bank Rate 7.75%

5 June 2026 | Repo 5.25%, fixed reverse repo 3.35%, SDF 5.00%, MSF 5.50%, Bank Rate 5.50%

Judge the key ONLY against the study notes supplied in the message (several apps' notes on the same topic). Do not use outside knowledge to overrule the notes; if the notes do not settle it, say so.

For every PYQ return one result:

- CONFLICT: the notes clearly support a different option. Give that option's number in "option" and quote or closely paraphrase the deciding line of the notes in "evidence". Also use CONFLICT when the notes contradict each other on this exact point (option = what the stronger/more specific note says; say "notes disagree" in evidence).
- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Deficit Financing - Meaning, Methods and Consequences

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Meaning - Indian vs Western Usage
Usage | Meaning
Indian | Budget gap met by borrowing from the RBI; RBI creates new money (government "buys money")
Western | Any financing of a budget deficit, mainly borrowing from the public/market
Effect | Increase in money supply; creates extra paper currency
Deficit financing is inflationary by nature.
Fiscal deficit (Union Budget) = budgetary deficit + net increase in internal and external borrowings and other liabilities.
In India, deficit financing = borrowing from the RBI, not from the public.
# Purpose in Indian Planning
Purpose: raising resources for economic development; a "pragmatic tool" to finance the Five Year Plans.
Needed after 1947 because of a low tax base, poor compliance, weak private banking and low domestic savings (not a high savings rate).
## Phases and Plans
Independence to late 1960s: little use, to fund plans.
Second Plan: deficit financing about ₹1,100 crore against ₹1,200 crore planned.
Third Plan: reliance on deficit financing to be strictly limited.
1970s onwards: heavy reliance (oil shocks, welfare spending) led to debt and inflation.
# Public Debt Classification
Head | Items
Internal debt | Market loans, Treasury Bills, special securities to NSSF
Other liabilities (Public Account) | Small savings, State Provident Funds, reserve funds and deposits
External debt | Loans from foreign sources
Market loans = 75% of AP's debt.
# Methods of Deficit Financing
Borrowing from the RBI (monetising the deficit).
Ad hoc Treasury Bills - automatic RBI financing, now abolished.
Ways and Means Advances (WMA) - temporary RBI advances from 1 April 1997.
Market borrowing; liquidity now managed by OMOs: sale of G-Secs drains liquidity, purchase adds it.
15 Sep 2026: RBI announced OMO sales of ₹1 lakh crore with 91/182/364-day T-bill auctions.
# Control Over Deficit Financing
Year | Step
Sep 1994 | RBI-Government agreement began phasing out ad hoc T-bills
Mar 1997 | Agreement ended ad hoc T-bills; WMA from 1 April 1997
2003 | FRBM Act
1 Apr 2006 | RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs
2018 | Monetised borrowing only on escape-clause grounds
Escape clause: slip limited to 0.5% of GDP a year.
# Consequences
Effect | Mechanism
Demand-pull inflation | Money supply and demand rise without more goods; hurts the poor most
Crowding out | Market borrowing raises interest rates, cuts private investment
Debt trap | Borrowing to pay interest; little room for health, education
Rating downgrades | Higher borrowing cost for government and firms
## Inflationary Ranking
Mode | Effect
Creation of new money | Most inflationary
Borrowing from banks | High
Borrowing from public | Lower (existing savings)
Repayment of debt | Not inflationary (withdraws money)
## Current Data

Appointed day = 2 June 2014; the Act got presidential assent on 1 March 2014.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: A.p. Reorganisation Act 2014 – Structure, Schedules and Key Provisions

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# The Act at A Glance
Full name: Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 (Act No. 6 of 2014).
Divided the old State of Andhra Pradesh into 2 States: Telangana and residual Andhra Pradesh.
Structure: 12 Parts, 108 sections and 13 Schedules.
Part V: authorisation of expenditure and distribution of revenues; Part VI assets and liabilities; Part VIII services.
Telangana became the 29th State of India.
# Timeline of Enactment
Event | Date
Bill introduced in Lok Sabha | 13 February 2014
Passed by Lok Sabha (voice vote) | 18 February 2014
Passed by Rajya Sabha (voice vote, no amendment) | 20 February 2014
President's assent; Gazette No. 6, 65th year of the Republic | 1 March 2014
Appointed day (territorial split) | 2 June 2014
President at the time of assent: Pranab Mukherjee.
"The Act came into effect on 2 March 2014" is WRONG. Enacted on 1 March 2014; the split took effect on 2 June 2014.
# Key Sections
## Territory, Capital and Governor
Section | Provision
3 | Telangana formed from 10 districts; the Khammam villages in the Polavaram submergence area stayed with AP (Polavaram Ordinance amended Sec 3)
4 | Residual State of Andhra Pradesh
5 | Hyderabad = common capital for up to 10 years; afterwards capital of Telangana, with a new capital for AP
7 | Common Governor for both States
8 | Governor's special responsibility for security of life, liberty and property in the common capital
10 | Amends the First Schedule of the Constitution; Telangana = 29th State
Under Section 8 the common Governor is helped by two advisors appointed by the Centre.
Greyhound Training Centre, Hyderabad: common training centre for a maximum of three years.
## Finance and Development
46 | 13th Finance Commission award split by population ratio and other parameters; grants and a special development package for backward areas, especially Rayalaseema and North Coastal AP
50 / 51 | Recovery of tax arrears and loans/advances by location (AP seeks amendment)
59 | Apportionment of pension liability (Eighth Schedule)
93 | Centre to take the Thirteenth Schedule measures within 10 years
94 | 94(1) fiscal measures incl. tax incentives; 94(2) backward-area infrastructure; 94(3) special support for the new capital (Raj Bhavan, High Court, Secretariat, Assembly, Council); 94(4) denotify degraded forest land for the capital
95 | Equal opportunities for quality higher education
## Water Resources (Sections 84-91)
84 | Apex Council: Union Water Resources Minister (chair) + both Chief Ministers (3 members)
85 | GRMB (HQ in Telangana) and KRMB (HQ in Andhra Pradesh) within 60 days; security by CISF
89 | KWDT (Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal) term extended for project-wise allocation
90 | Polavaram declared a national project; Telangana's consent deemed given
89 = KWDT; 90 = Polavaram. GRMB HQ = Telangana; KRMB HQ = AP (do not swap).
# Seat Allocation
House | Andhra Pradesh | Telangana | Total
Rajya Sabha | 11 | 7 | 18
Lok Sabha | 25 | 17 | 42
Legislative Assembly | 175 | 119 | 294
Legislative Council | not more than 50 | 40 | –
Section 26: delimitation can raise the AP Assembly from 175 to 225, subject to Article 170.
Section 18: each Governor could nominate 1 Anglo-Indian MLA (Article 333); ended by the 104th Amendment.
Section 13 / First Schedule of the Act: allotment of sitting Rajya Sabha members.
## District-wise Assembly Constituencies (13 districts of 2014)
District | Seats | District | Seats
Srikakulam | 10 | Prakasam | 12
Vizianagaram | 9 (fewest) | Nellore | 10
Visakhapatnam | 15 | YSR Kadapa | 10
East Godavari | 19 (most) | Kurnool | 14
West Godavari | 15 | Anantapur | 14
Krishna | 16 | Chittoor | 14
Guntur | 17 | Total | 175
Reserved: 29 SC and 7 ST Assembly seats.
# Amendments to the Constitution and Other Laws
Law / Article amended | Change
First Schedule of Constitution | New State added (names and territories of States and UTs) – Sec 10
Fourth Schedule of Constitution | Rajya Sabha seats: AP 18 → 11; new entry "Telangana – 7"
Art 168(1)(a) | Telangana added to States with a Legislative Council (Sec 96)
Art 371D | Now reads "Andhra Pradesh or Telangana" (Sec 97)
RP Act, 1950 | First Schedule amended for Lok Sabha seats
RP Act, 1951 | Section 15A amended for Telangana Council (Sec 98)
Other laws amended: Delimitation Order 2008, SC and ST Orders 1950, States Reorganisation Act 1956 (Sec 15).
APPSC 2021: Constitution Schedules amended = First and Fourth.
# Schedules of the Act
## Schedule → Subject (full list)
Schedule | Subject
I | Allotment of sitting Rajya Sabha members (Sec 13)
II | Amendments to the Delimitation Order, 2008 (Sec 15)
III | Delimitation of Council constituencies orders: Part I AP, Part II Telangana (Sec 24)
IV | Legislative Council members (Sec 22)
V / VI | Constitution (SC) Order 1950 / (ST) Order 1950 amendments
VII | List of Funds (provident, pension, insurance and other funds)
VIII | Apportionment of pension liability (Sec 59)
IX | Companies and corporations
X | Continuance of facilities in State institutions (e.g. APSCHE, Shilparamam); lists 107 institutions
XI | Principles for Godavari and Krishna River Management Boards
XII | Coal, Oil and Gas, Power
XIII | Education and Infrastructure commitments
VII = Funds (APPSC 2022); VIII = pension; IX = companies; X = institutions; XI = river boards; XII = coal/oil/power; XIII = education and infrastructure.
## Schedule XI (Water)
Priority order: drinking water > irrigation > power.
No new project on Krishna or Godavari without Apex Council sanction.
## Schedule XII (Power)
APGENCO units divided by location.
APERC = joint regulator for up to six months; SLDC shared for up to two years.
# Schedule Xiii – Central Commitments
## Education
IIT, NIT, IIM, IISER, Central University, Petroleum University, Agricultural University, IIIT, AIIMS-type hospital, Tribal University, NIDM.
NOT listed: Indian Institute of Science (IISc).
## Infrastructure
Duggirajupatnam port.
6-month feasibility studies: SAIL steel plant in YSR district (not Kurnool); refinery; Vizag-Chennai Industrial Corridor (modelled on DMIC); new railway zone.
SAIL steel plant study = YSR district (Kadapa), not Kurnool.
# High Court Bifurcation
30 | High Court at Hyderabad common to both States until a separate AP High Court is set up under Article 214; judges' salaries shared by population ratio
105 | Disputes over transfer of pending cases → decided by the Hyderabad High Court; its decision is final
The Act named no place for AP's High Court.
Section 31: provides a separate High Court for AP (Section 30 = common Hyderabad High Court meanwhile).
26 December 2018: Presidential order under Article 214 and the Act constituted a separate High Court for AP.
1 January 2019: High Court of Andhra Pradesh began functioning with its principal seat at Amaravati; the Hyderabad court became the High Court for Telangana.
# Capital Question – Latest Developments
3 March 2022: AP High Court order on the capital (Amaravati).
28 March 2026: AP Assembly resolution to insert "at Amaravati" in Section 5(2).
April 2026: Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026 (29 March and 1 April 2026).
2026 amendment = first time Parliament named a State's capital by law.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Correct Fact
Parts / sections / Schedules | 12 / 108 / 13
Assent / appointed day | 1 March 2014 / 2 June 2014
Common capital period | Up to 10 years (Sec 5)
Schedule XIII deadline | 10 years (Sec 93)
River boards set up within | 60 days (Sec 85)
Apex Council members | 3
Greyhound common centre | Max 3 years
Schedule X institutions | 107
AP Assembly increase | 175 → 225 (Sec 26)
AP HC began | 1 January 2019, Amaravati
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
Telangana = 29th State.
First law in which Parliament names a State's capital: the 2026 amendment.
Only Anglo-Indian MLA provision (Sec 18) ended by the 104th Amendment.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
APPSC 2021 | Constitution Schedules amended (First and Fourth); RP Act 1950 for Lok Sabha seats
APPSC 2022 | Seventh Schedule of the Act – List of Funds
APPSC 2023 | Key sections, Schedules and seat allocation
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. 1 March 2014 (assent) vs 2 June 2014 (appointed day); never "2 March 2014".
2. Sec 89 = KWDT; Sec 90 = Polavaram.
3. GRMB HQ = Telangana; KRMB HQ = AP; security by CISF.
4. Apex Council chaired by the Union Water Resources Minister, not the PM.
5. Constitution Schedules amended = First and Fourth, not Seventh.
6. VII = Funds, VIII = pension, XI = river boards.
7. SAIL steel plant study in YSR district, not Kurnool; IISc is not in Schedule XIII.
8. Schedule XI priority: drinking water first, then irrigation, then power.
9. Common capital = up to 10 years, not exactly 10 or 5.
10. The Act named no place for AP High Court; Amaravati HC from 1 January 2019.

- NOT_COVERED: the notes do not contain the fact needed, or the question is garbled/unanswerable as written (say which in evidence).

Rules: "option" is 1-based and 0 when there is no alternative option (AGREE / NOT_COVERED). For "which is NOT correct", "wrong pair" and statement-combination questions, work out which option the notes make right before judging. Keep evidence under 30 words; leave it empty for AGREE. Return exactly one result per PYQ id, in order.

STUDY NOTES

TOPIC: Disaster Management Framework – Dm Act 2005, Ndma, Ndrf, Early Warning Systems

=== APPSC Complete notes ===
# Key Terms – Hazard, Disaster, Vulnerability, Risk
Term | Meaning
Hazard | Potentially damaging event (e.g. an earthquake in an empty desert = hazard, not disaster)
Disaster | Hazard meeting a vulnerable population: Hazard × Vulnerability; Sec. 2(d) DM Act – catastrophe causing loss beyond the affected community's coping capacity (not the State Government's)
Risk | Likelihood of loss; rises with hazard, exposure, vulnerability; falls with coping capacity
Mitigation (DM Act) | Measures to reduce the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation
## Types of Vulnerability
Type | Example
Physical | Weak houses, floodplain settlements
Social | Age, gender, caste, disability discrimination
Economic | Poverty, daily-wage workers, small farmers
Environmental | Mangrove loss (raises cyclone impact), deforestation → landslides
Systemic / institutional | Weak governance, poor coordination, weak early warning
Community vulnerability factors: kutcha housing, farm-labour dependence, thin health infrastructure, weak early warning; high crop-insurance coverage reduces vulnerability.
Hazard types: geological (earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes, tsunamis); hydro-meteorological (cyclones, floods, droughts, cloudbursts, heat waves); biological (epidemics, pest attacks).
Natural vs man-made: natural disasters cause most damage in developing countries; Bhopal gas tragedy (2–3 December 1984, Methyl Isocyanate) was man-made; mangroves reduce cyclone impact. People killed by natural disasters in India, 1980–2010: 1,43,039.
# Evolution of Dm in India – Milestones and Firsts
Year | Milestone
1957 | CERTI (Central Emergency Relief Training Institute), Nagpur – first DM training institution
1958 | Central Water Commission (then Central Water & Power Commission) began scientific flood forecasting, on the Yamuna at Delhi
1987 | Disaster Management Institute, Bhopal, after the gas tragedy
1990s | DM Cell under Ministry of Agriculture, responding to the UN IDNDR
1995 | National Centre for Disaster Management (NCDM) at IIPA – first national DM training/research centre; became NIDM (2003)
Aug 1999 | High Powered Committee (HPC), chaired by J.C. Pant
2001 | Gujarat (Bhuj) earthquake → National Committee; reforms
2002 | DM shifted from Agriculture → Home Affairs (MHA)
2004 | Indian Ocean tsunami – catalyst for the Act
2005 | DM Act (23 Dec); Hyogo Framework 2005–2015
Nov 2006 | First India Disaster Management Congress, New Delhi, by NIDM
2009 | National Policy on DM (Cabinet, 22 Oct 2009)
2015 | Sendai Framework 2015–2030
2016 | First NDMP; revised 2019 (aligned with Sendai)
2025 | DM (Amendment) Act
Order: NCDM (1995) → DM Act (2005) → NPDM (2009) → Sendai (2015).
## High Powered Committee (1999)
Constituted August 1999; first chairman J.C. Pant; reported 2001; theme "Building a Culture of Prevention".
At first natural disasters only, later widened to man-made; classified disasters into five broad categories; recommended a separate Department of DM in GoI.
Uttarakhand: first State with a separate Ministry of Disaster Management.
## Shift in Approach
Basis | Pre-2005 | Post-DM Act 2005
Approach | 3 Rs – rescue, relief, rehabilitation | 3 Ps – prevention, preparedness, proofing (mitigation)
Nature | Relief-centric, reactive | Holistic, proactive, continuous cycle; Build Back Better
# Disaster Management Act, 2005
Act No. 53 of 2005; Presidential assent 23 December 2005; in force progressively from 2006; whole of India; 11 Chapters, 79 Sections.
Enacted after the 2004 tsunami exposed gaps; legal and institutional framework at national, state and district levels.
MHA = nodal ministry (except drought, pest attack, epidemics); primary responsibility lies with State Governments; Centre supports.
## Key Sections
Section | Provides for
2(d) | Definition of disaster
3 | NDMA
8 | National Executive Committee (NEC)
14 | SDMA – set up by the Governor (s.14(1), after notification under s.3(1))
25 | DDMA (in Chapter IV)
35 / 37 | Hazard-specific plans of Union ministries / Ministry DM Plans
42 | NIDM
44 | National Disaster Response Force
46 | National Disaster Response Fund
47 | National Disaster Mitigation Fund
48 | State Disaster Response Fund (s.48(1)(a))
NDRF = both the Force (s.44) and the Fund (s.46).
## DM (Amendment) Act, 2025
Urban Disaster Management Authorities (UDMA) in Municipal Corporation cities and State capitals, except Delhi and Chandigarh; headed by the Municipal Commissioner (not the Mayor).
Statutory status to the NCMC and High Level Committee; national and state disaster databases; definitions of risk, resilience, recovery, evacuation; aligned with Sendai; mandatory SDRF in every state; stronger NDMA powers (minimum relief standards, audits).
June 2026 – "Resilient India 2047": NDMA asks Union ministries for hazard-specific plans (s.35) and Ministry DM Plans (s.37).
# Authorities and Committees – Who Heads What
Body | Head | Role
NDMA | Prime Minister (ex officio) | Apex policy body; max nine members incl. Vice-Chairperson; formally constituted 27 Sep 2006
NEC | Union Home Secretary | Prepares and implements the National Plan (not the HLC)
SDMA | Chief Minister | State authority
SEC | Chief Secretary | Runs SDRF
DDMA | Collector / District Magistrate; elected local head = co-chair | District planning and response
NCMC | Cabinet Secretary | Highest coordination in major crises; can direct any ministry
State Crisis Management Committee | Chief Secretary | Daily review
High Level Committee | Union Home Minister | Approves aid from national funds
Cabinet Committee on Security | Prime Minister (not Home Minister) | Nuclear, biological, chemical emergencies
Cabinet Committee on Natural Calamities | — | Policy decisions
National Advisory Committee | Under NDMA | Expert advice
NPDRR | Union Home Minister | Multi-stakeholder DRR platform
Crisis Management Group (nuclear) | Department of Atomic Energy | —
Chain of command: hierarchy of officials and organisations responsible for decisions in a disaster.
APPSC key once gave NDMA formation = 2005 (the Act); the notification is 27 Sep 2006.
# National Institutions and Forces
## Institutions → Location
Institution | Location | Role / fact
NDMA | New Delhi | Apex body
NIDM | New Delhi (Rohini); Southern Campus at Kondapalli near Vijayawada (AP) (not Visakhapatnam) | Statutory (s.42); NCDM 1995 → NIDM 2003; President = Union Home Minister; journal "Disaster & Development" (biannual); runs IDRN, IUINDRR
NDRF Academy | Nagpur (2018) | Merged with National Civil Defence College; trains NDRF, SDRF, civil defence
National Fire Service College | Nagpur | Fire and rescue training
Centre for Disaster Management | LBSNAA, Mussoorie | Trains civil servants
INCOIS | Hyderabad | Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre
NRSC | Hyderabad | Remote sensing for disasters
IMD | New Delhi | Cyclone forecasting
GSI | Kolkata | Landslide forecasting, hazard zonation
CWC | New Delhi (not Hyderabad) | Flood forecasting
IDRN (India Disaster Resource Network): online inventory of response resources under NIDM/MHA; criticised for outdated data.
## NDRF – National Disaster Response Force
Raised 2006 under s.44 (2005 = year of the Act); Raising Day 19 January; world's largest dedicated response force.
Under MHA; superintendence of NDMA; Director General from senior IPS cadre; HQ New Delhi.
Motto: "Aapada Seva Sadaiv Sarvatra" ("Disaster Service Always Everywhere").
16 battalions (from an initial 8; 12 at the time of the APPSC 2018 key); ~1,149 personnel each, >18,000 in all; 18 search-and-rescue teams per battalion (engineers, technicians, dog squads, medics).
Parent forces (on deputation): BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles.
Skills: CSSR (Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue), flood and mountain rescue, MFR (Medical First Response), CBRN response; natural and man-made disasters; teams pre-positioned by vulnerability profile.
AP: 10th Battalion, regional HQ for AP, Telangana and Karnataka at Vijayawada. NDRF budget estimate 2021-22: ₹1,209 crore.
## SDRF – State Disaster Response Force
Raised by States/UTs; first responder in the state for the first 24–48 hours; trained by NDRF/NDRF Academy; battalion model.
Drawn from State Police, Armed Police, Fire Services, Home Guards, Civil Defence (NDRF draws on central forces).
Not yet set up in all states → strain on NDRF in simultaneous disasters.
# Disaster Funds and Notified Disasters
Fund | Section | Use
State Disaster Response Fund | 48 | First fund for immediate relief to victims of notified disasters; run by SEC (Chief Secretary); primary fund for drought relief
National Disaster Response Fund | 46 | Central fund; tops up SDRF in severe calamities (not the first fund)
NDMF / SDMF | 47 | Mitigation, long-term risk reduction (not relief); operationalised after the 15th Finance Commission; ₹4,645 crore approved for 9 states incl. AP
SDRF share (Centre : State) | — | General 75:25; NE/Himalayan 90:10
SDRF is not for individual compensation or long-term rebuilding. Up to 10% (not 25%) may go to state-specific disasters.
Finance Commission recommends calamities and amounts; MHA notifies.
Notified list: cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, pest attack, frost and cold wave; no man-made calamity.
Aug 2026: MHA added heatwaves and lightning – list 12 → 14 for 2026–31, on the 16th Finance Commission's recommendation.
Drought support: PMFBY – crop insurance; MGNREGA – employment.
AP: ₹277.63 crore (2025-26) + ₹479.01 crore (2026-27) released under SDRF/NDRF.
# Policy, Plans and International Frameworks
## National Policy on DM, 2009 and NDMP
NPDM: approved by Union Cabinet 22 Oct 2009; prepared by NDMA under the DM Act; vision "safe and disaster-resilient India"; covers prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, community participation, mainstreaming DRR.
NOT an objective: "promoting preparedness only after a disaster occurs" or relying only on post-disaster relief.
NDMP 2016: India's first national plan, all phases of the cycle, aligned with Sendai; time frames short (5-yr), medium (10-yr), long (15-yr); revised 2019.
Mainstreaming DRR is part of the PM's 10-Point Agenda.
## International Frameworks
Framework | Period / year | Key point
IDNDR | 1990s | UN decade; India set up DM Cell
Yokohama Strategy | 1994 | Mid-decade review
Hyogo Framework | 2005–2015 | Adopted at Kobe, Jan 2005; building resilience
Sendai Framework | 2015–2030 | Replaced Hyogo; 4 priorities – understand risk (first), strengthen risk governance, invest in DRR, enhance preparedness and "Build Back Better"; 7 global targets (mortality, affected people, economic loss … to multi-hazard early warning access), 38 indicators; goal: universal early warning by 2030
CDRI | 2019 | Launched by India at the UN Climate Action Summit, New York; secretariat New Delhi
IDNDR: UN General Assembly resolution 44/236 (22 Dec 1989) proclaimed 1990–1999 the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction.
# Disaster Management Cycle
Phase | Stage | Measures
Prevention | Pre | Proactive, long-term: land-use zoning, regulating deforestation, control of industrial siting, GIS hazard zonation
Mitigation | Pre | Most cost-effective; lowers likelihood of disaster: quake-resistant buildings, building codes, embankments, afforestation, hazard maps, retrofitting, insurance; vulnerability analysis and risk assessment
Preparedness | Pre | "First critical step": early warning (CAP-SACHET), mock drills, stockpiling, Aapda Mitra, Emergency Operation Centres, contingency plans, evacuation routes
Response | During | Time-critical: search and rescue, evacuation, first aid, shelter, food, restoring critical services
Recovery / Reconstruction | Post | Restore normal life; damage assessment, compensation, psycho-social care, livelihoods, Build Back Better
The cycle is continuous – lessons from recovery feed prevention; phases overlap.
During: early warning → evacuation → rescue → shelters → emergency medical/water. After: relief → restoration → reconstruction → resilient rebuilding.
Structural mitigation for earthquakes = building codes; cyclones = coastal tree planting. Non-structural mitigation = community awareness and education (public education).
Early warning is a crucial component of mitigation (timely information).
Terms: HAZOP study – checks adequacy of safety measures; MAT – Mitigation Assessment Team; hazard mapping – mapping areas at risk.
First responder: the community. Urban response is shared by civic bodies, fire brigade, police; district administration in charge (Collector pivotal).
"Planning Mitigation" is NOT a type of mitigation; "Non planning required" is NOT a hazard-specific control activity; recovery and reconstruction are NOT pre-disaster.
Types of mitigation: avoidance, minimization and compensatory mitigation.
Hazard-specific control activity: a measure aimed at one particular hazard, e.g. building flood levees against floods.
# Safety Drills and Awareness
Hazard | Safest action
Earthquake (indoors) | "Drop! Cover! Hold" under a strong table; away from windows, balconies, stairs (APPSC 2025)
Cyclone | Move to a cyclone shelter or safe building; never go to sea or stand under trees
Flood | Move to higher ground; avoid flowing water
Tsunami | Sudden sea recession → move inland/uphill at once
Tools: mock drills, Aapda Mitra volunteers, National School Safety Programme, tsunami escape-route signage.
Prakampana: super-cyclone preparedness exercise at Visakhapatnam by the Eastern Naval Command with civil agencies.
First forest-fire DM exercise: Uttarakhand, April 2017.
Tsunami Ready villages: India targets 100; 12 indicators; renewed every 4 years; verified by the National Tsunami Ready Recognition Board (MoES, chaired by Director, INCOIS).
CBDRR through PRIs: ₹507.37 crore; MoPR + NDMA; 20 states, 81 districts.
IMD colour code: Green all well – Yellow be aware – Orange be prepared – Red take action.
Subhash Chandra Bose Aapda Prabandhan Puraskar 2020: Uttarakhand's Disaster Mitigation & Management Centre.
# Early Warning Systems → Agency
Hazard | Agency | Detail
Cyclones (forecast, track, name) | IMD; RSMC New Delhi (North Indian Ocean) | 7 cyclone warning centres incl. Visakhapatnam; NDMA cyclone guidelines 2008
Lightning | IMD | Damini app; detection at 104 locations
Tsunamis, storm surge, high waves | INCOIS, Hyderabad | ITEWC (2007); alerts within 10 minutes; serves 25 countries; 32 major quakes monitored in 2025
River floods | CWC | —
Earthquakes | National Centre for Seismology (MoES) | IndiaQuake app; IIT Roorkee early-warning pilot, Uttarakhand
Landslides | GSI | Hazard zonation, susceptibility maps, Landslide Atlas
Glacial lakes | NDMA / ISRO | Indigenous GLOF alert tested at Sissu, HP; ISRO Glacial Lake Atlas
MHEW-DSS (IMD, 2024, Mission Mausam): WebGIS multi-hazard warning platform reaching ~80% of population.
CAP (Common Alerting Protocol) integrates public warnings. Cyclone/high-wind-prone coastline (NDMA): 5,700 km.
Tsunami = INCOIS; landslides = GSI; floods = CWC; NDEM = ISRO (not IMD).
# Technology – Gis and Remote Sensing
GIS stores, analyses, overlays and presents spatial data; maps disaster-prone areas and vulnerable people; plans camps, routes, resources; maps flood damage.
APPSC 2025: in floods, GIS analyses flood patterns and topography for proactive action (it builds nothing, pays nothing).
GIS cannot give details of individual victims and exact locations, nor fully resolve social issues.
Phase | GIS use
Prevention / mitigation | Hazard zonation, vulnerability and risk mapping
Preparedness | Evacuation routes, resource mapping, early warning
Response | Real-time damage assessment
Recovery | Build Back Better planning
Hazard | GIS use / programme
Flood | Inundation mapping, floodplain zoning
Cyclone | Track monitoring, storm surge modelling
Landslide | Susceptibility mapping (GSI NLSM)
Drought | NADAMS
Tsunami | Inundation modelling (INCOIS)
Tool | Use
Remote sensing | Synoptic, real-time view; inundation and damage mapping (not "hills management")
Google Earth Engine | Cloud platform for rapid flood mapping
INSAT-3D/3DR | Track cyclones
NDEM | GIS repository for the DM cycle, by ISRO
DEM | Digital Elevation Model – digital terrain
GSI Bhukosh | Landslide maps of 4.3 lakh sq km
Landslide Hazard Zonation (APPSC 2025): divides hill areas into homogeneous zones by degree of susceptibility, hazard or risk; maps are probabilistic.
Earth observation and communication satellites detect and deliver early warnings; social media and apps increasingly used.
# Apsdma and Ap Cyclones
APSDMA: apex statutory DM body of AP, chaired by the Chief Minister, under the AP DM Rules 2007 (APPSC 2025); pre-disaster planning + post-disaster restoration.
Runs the State Emergency Operations Centre at Kunchanapalli; coordinates districts; alert systems Vajrapath, Varuna, Red Message.
AP moved from relief-centric to mitigation-centric; a national leader in DRR. Cyclone measures: IMD warnings, cyclone shelters, evacuation, shelter belts, mangroves.
Cyclone | Year | Landfall
Hudhud | Oct 2014 | Visakhapatnam
Titli | Oct 2018 | Near Palasa, Srikakulam
Michaung | Dec 2023 | Near Bapatla
AP faces about 13–14 Bay of Bengal low-pressure systems a year, mostly from the northern Bay → Godavari-Krishna floods.
# Number Game and Quick Revision
Item | Fact
DM Act | No. 53 of 2005; 23 Dec 2005; 11 chapters, 79 sections
NDMA members | Max 9
NDRF battalions | 16 (initial 8)
SAR teams per battalion | 18
SDRF share | 75:25; 90:10 (NE/Himalayan)
State-specific use of SDRF | Up to 10%
Notified disasters | 12 → 14 (2026–31)
Tsunami alert time | 10 minutes
Hyogo / Sendai | 2005–2015 / 2015–2030
NDMP time frames | 5 / 10 / 15 years
## FIRST / LAST / SPECIAL FACTS
First DM training institution: CERTI, Nagpur (1957).
First scientific flood forecasting: 1958, CWC, Yamuna at Delhi.
First State DM ministry: Uttarakhand. First NDMP: 2016. First India DM Congress: Nov 2006.
# Appsc Previous Year Questions
Examination | Question Area
APPSC 2025 | Earthquake "Drop, Cover, Hold"; APSDMA and AP DM Rules 2007; GIS in floods; landslide hazard zonation; 1958 flood forecasting
APPSC 2018 | Number of NDRF battalions
APPSC (earlier years) | DM Act sections; NDMA chairman; DDMA head; HPC 1999; CERTI; DM cycle phases; NIDM
# High-probability Mcq Traps
1. NDRF force = s.44; NDRF fund = s.46; SDRF fund = s.48.
2. NDMA chair = PM; NEC = Home Secretary; NCMC = Cabinet Secretary; HLC = Home Minister.
3. NDRF raised 2006, not 2005.
4. NIDM Southern Campus near Vijayawada (Kondapalli), not Visakhapatnam.
5. CWC is in New Delhi, GSI in Kolkata, INCOIS in Hyderabad.
6. UDMA head = Municipal Commissioner, not Mayor.
7. SDRF is for immediate relief, not compensation; state-specific limit 10%.
8. Mitigation = most cost-effective; reconstruction = post-disaster.
9. CCS is chaired by the PM, not the Home Minister.
10. Sec. 2(d): coping capacity of the affected community, not the State.

=== APPSC Prep notes ===
# Terms → meaning (hazard, vulnerability, disaster, risk) and hazard types
Hazard | Potentially damaging event
Vulnerability | Exposure + inability to cope
Disaster | Hazard meeting a vulnerable population → Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster; Sec. 2(d) of the DM Act: Disaster = catastrophe causing substantial loss beyond the community's coping capacity
Earthquake in an empty desert = hazard, not a disaster
Community vulnerability factors: kutcha housing, dependence on farm labour, thin health infrastructure, low crop-insurance cover, weak early warning
Type | Examples
Geological | Earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes, tsunamis
Hydro-meteorological | Cyclones, floods, droughts, cloudbursts, heat waves
Biological | Epidemics, pest attacks
# Evolution of DM in India → year, milestone and FIRSTs
1958 | Central Water Commission (then Central Water & Power Commission) began scientific flood forecasting (APPSC 2025 key), starting on the Yamuna at Delhi
1987 | Disaster Management Institute, Bhopal, after the gas tragedy [GK]
1990s | DM Cell under the Ministry of Agriculture, in response to UN IDNDR (UPSC)
1995 | National Centre for Disaster Management at IIPA - India's first national DM training/research centre; became NIDM (2003) [GK]
1999 | High Powered Committee on DM plans, chaired by J.C. Pant [GK for name]
2001 | National Committee after the 2001 Gujarat earthquake
2005 | Disaster Management Act; Hyogo Framework 2005-2015
2006 | First India Disaster Management Congress, New Delhi, Nov 2006, by NIDM
2009 | National Policy on Disaster Management (NPDM) (UPSC) - prevention, mitigation, community, mainstreaming DRR
2015 | Sendai Framework 2015-2030 (Sendai, Japan) - 4 priorities: understand risk; strengthen risk governance; invest in DRR; enhance preparedness and "Build Back Better"
2016 / 2019 | First NDMP (2016) [GK] - India's first national plan, aligned with Sendai; revised NDMP 2019 aligned to Sendai
Dec 2020 | DM Cell in MoHFW
Sendai goal: Universal access to multi-hazard early warning by 2030
NDMP 2016 time frames: short (5-yr), medium (10-yr), long (15-yr)
⚠ Hyogo = 2005-2015; Sendai = 2015-2030; J.C. Pant = 1999 committee
# DM Act 2005 → bodies, sections and heads — Background and objective
## 1. Background and objective
Background: High-powered committee 1999; National Committee after the Gujarat earthquake
Enacted: Dec 2005 (23 Dec 2005)
Core shift: from relief-centric response to proactive prevention, mitigation and preparedness
Nodal ministry: Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) - overall coordination
Structure: three-tier structure: NDMA-SDMA-DDMA
# DM Act 2005 → bodies, sections and heads — Bodies and key sections
## 1. Bodies and key sections
Body | DM Act section / basis / year | Head / seat | Role
NDMA | Sec 3 (s.3) | Prime Minister; New Delhi | Apex; lays down policies, approves National Plan, guidelines, aid to other countries, NIDM policy
National Executive Committee (NEC) | Sec 8 (s.8) | Union Home Secretary | -
SDMA | Sec 14 (s.14) | Chief Minister; State Executive Committee under the Chief Secretary | -

NDRF (force) | Sec. 44 (s.44); raised 2006 | Director General; drawn from paramilitary forces; under NDMA superintendence | Specialist response force
NDRF Academy | - | Nagpur | -
NPDRR | Multi-stakeholder platform | Union Home Minister | -
DDMA co-chair: Detail most often tested - only tier where an elected representative sits with the bureaucratic head
⚠ s.3 NDMA - s.14 SDMA - s.25 DDMA - s.42 NIDM - s.44 NDRF
# DM Act 2005 → bodies, sections and heads — NDRF — the specialist response force
## 1. NDRF — the specialist response force
Composition: Specialist force drawn from the central paramilitary forces - search and rescue teams, engineers, dog squads
Superintendence: NDMA
Gap: SDRFs not yet set up in all states → strain on NDRF during simultaneous disasters
Suggested fix: mandatory SDRFs + joint NDRF-SDRF training
AP presence: NDRF 10th Battalion + an NIDM southern campus near Vijayawada/Gannavaram, AP
Not in your sources: the current number of NDRF battalions and the names and places of recent NDRF exercises.
# Disaster funds and notified disasters → sections
Fund | Section | Use / funding
National Disaster Response Fund | s.46 (per UPSC) | Central; tops up SDRF in severe calamities
State Disaster Response Fund | s.48 [GK] | First fund for relief in notified disasters; Centre:State 75:25 for general states (LENS Aug 2026)
